Chapter One

Blood Rain

Queen Aurelia Darkheart screamed as midnight approached.

The sound traveled through the birthing chamber, passed beneath iron-bound doors, and rolled through Castle Darkheart until guards stationed in distant towers heard the pain of their queen. Servants paused in torchlit corridors. Priests lowered their heads over unfinished prayers. Soldiers who had faced cavalry charges without flinching exchanged uneasy looks as the ancient fortress seemed to tighten around them.

Castle Darkheart had witnessed executions, coronations, betrayals, and wars older than the living memory of its kingdom. Its walls had endured siege fire and witchcraft. Its black towers had watched generations of rulers rise beneath the silver moon and descend into burial vaults beneath the throne.

Yet on this night, the castle felt afraid.

The wind had stopped hours earlier.

Black banners bearing the crowned serpent of House Darkheart hung motionless from the battlements. The surrounding forests had fallen silent. Even the wolves that prowled the northern hills had ceased their howling, leaving the darkness beyond the walls unnaturally empty.

Inside the royal chamber, the kingdom’s finest physicians and witches surrounded Aurelia’s bed.

Moisture covered the queen’s brow. Her dark hair clung to her face, and her fingers tightened around the sheets as another contraction tore through her body. She had endured a labor lasting nearly an entire day, but the child showed no sign of weakness.

If anything, the pressure within the chamber continued to increase.

King Victor Darkheart stood beside her.

He had removed his crown but not his sword. The weapon remained fastened at his side, an old habit born from years of border wars and palace betrayals. His black ceremonial armor had been replaced by a simple dark tunic, yet he looked no less imposing. He held Aurelia’s hand with both of his, his expression controlled even as fear tightened behind his eyes.

“Look at me,” he said.

Aurelia forced her eyes open.

Victor leaned closer. “You are not dying tonight.”

Despite her pain, she managed a weak laugh. “Was that an order?”

“Yes.”

Another contraction seized her before she could answer.

Aurelia cried out and crushed Victor’s fingers in her grip. He did not pull away.

The royal witches raised their hands.

Soft violet mana gathered around their palms. Threads of blue healing magic moved over Aurelia’s body, easing torn muscles and strengthening her heartbeat. The eldest among them murmured an old birthing prayer while the physicians prepared linen, silver instruments, and bowls of heated water.

Then the witch’s voice faltered.

The violet light around her hands flickered.

She frowned and reached deeper.

Nothing answered.

Her magic remained within her. She could feel it behind her ribs, woven through her blood and spirit as it had been since childhood.

Yet she could not grasp it.

It was as though she stood at the bottom of a dark sea, reaching toward a distant surface while an impossible weight pressed down from above.

The healing threads around Aurelia vanished.

A younger witch gasped.

“My spell—”

Her blue mana collapsed before it formed.

One after another, the witches lost control of their magic. Pale green wards dissolved from the walls. Protective symbols dimmed. The sacred flames in the bronze braziers narrowed until only thin points of light remained.

Victor released Aurelia’s hand and turned.

“What happened?”

The eldest witch tried again. Sweat formed across her brow as she strained for the power she knew was still there.

“I can feel my magic, Your Majesty.”

“Then use it.”

“I cannot reach it.”

Another witch stared at her trembling hands. “Something is drowning it.”

The chamber grew colder.

Aurelia gritted her teeth as the pressure inside her changed.

The child moved.

Not with the weak, desperate struggle of an infant fighting to enter the world.

With force.

A pulse rolled through the chamber.

Every candle went out.

Victor drew his sword before darkness had fully settled.

Steel rang through the room.

“Light.”

No spell answered.

A physician hurried toward the brazier with flint in hand, but before he reached it, crimson illumination seeped through the chamber.

It came from Aurelia.

No.

From within her.

A deep red glow passed beneath the skin of her stomach, pulsing in time with a heartbeat that did not belong to the queen.

Once.

Twice.

The third beat shook the castle.

Stone dust drifted from the ceiling.

Outside the chamber, guards stumbled as the floor moved beneath their boots. Horses screamed within the royal stables. Bells suspended in the western tower began ringing without hands or wind.

Aurelia stared down at the crimson light beneath her skin.

“Victor.”

He returned to her side, sword still in hand.

“I am here.”

“What is happening to our child?”

Victor had no answer.

Beyond Castle Darkheart, the first drop fell.

It struck the helmet of a sentry standing upon the northern wall.

The young soldier wiped the warm liquid from his cheek and looked at his fingers.

Red covered them.

He lifted his gaze toward the sky.

A second drop landed on the stone beside him.

Then another.

Within moments, blood began falling from the heavens.

It struck battlements and rooftops in heavy drops. It washed over the stone faces of ancient gargoyles. It soaked banners, armor, fields, and roads until the kingdom beneath Castle Darkheart appeared drowned beneath a crimson storm.

The sentry backed away from the wall.

“Sound the alarm.”

No one moved.

“Sound it!”

The warning horn cried across the fortress.

In the villages below, people rushed from their homes only to recoil beneath the bleeding sky. Mothers pulled children into doorways. Farmers abandoned livestock. Priests fell to their knees in flooded roads while blood streamed across their faces.

The storm did not remain over House Darkheart.

It spread.

Across the western kingdoms, blood struck palace windows and temple roofs. It ran down the marble towers of rival courts. It stained rivers and turned snowfields red. It fell upon battle camps where soldiers from enemy nations stopped killing one another long enough to stare upward.

No ruler understood it.

No priest could name it.

The ancient world watched the heavens bleed.

In the northern forests, the wolves went mad.

The first alpha collapsed mid-howl.

His bones shifted beneath his skin. His claws tore trenches through the frozen earth as his eyes darkened with a terror he could not comprehend. The other wolves backed away from him, whining, until the same madness seized them.

Pack law shattered.

Mates attacked one another.

Young wolves fled into the trees.

Alphas tore at their own kin as if every instinct within them had become tangled and violent. The madness passed from forest to forest, crossing borders no human army could traverse in a single night.

Some wolves ran toward Castle Darkheart.

Others fled from it.

None knew why.

Far beneath the eastern mountains, ancient vampires awakened.

Stone lids slid from coffins that had not opened for centuries. Dust-covered eyes stared into darkness. Deep within the blood of every vampire, an unfamiliar heartbeat sounded.

One beat.

Then another.

It was not their own.

It did not belong to prey.

It did not resemble the pulse of any witch, wolf, mortal, or vampire they had ever hunted.

A young vampire fell from his knees and clutched his chest.

“What is that?”

The elder beside him listened.

He had lived long enough to remember civilizations whose names no longer existed, yet no memory answered him.

The heartbeat passed through their blood one final time.

Then disappeared.

Across the world, vampires remained awake.

Listening.

Afraid.

Within Castle Darkheart, Aurelia screamed.

The Crimson Mana surrounding her burst outward.

Physicians were thrown against the walls. Witches collapsed to their knees. Victor drove his sword into the floor and used it to remain standing as the chamber filled with red light.

The pressure became unbearable.

The witches’ magic had not vanished.

It remained buried beneath the overwhelming presence entering the world.

Aurelia’s final cry ended abruptly.

Then came silence.

The infant was born.

The midwife caught him with shaking hands and nearly dropped him when his eyes opened.

They were crimson.

Not bloodshot.

Not reflecting the light.

Crimson from edge to edge.

Small fangs rested behind his lips. His tiny fingers opened and closed while Crimson Mana leaked naturally from his body in slow, living ribbons. Beneath his newborn skin, his heartbeat carried a predatory rhythm no human child should possess. A low sound rumbled in his chest—not quite a growl, but enough to make the nearest wolf-blooded guard outside the chamber recoil.

The child did not cry.

He looked at the world.

The Blood Rain stopped in midair.

For one suspended moment, every crimson drop hung between the sky and earth.

The wolves froze.

The vampires felt the impossible heartbeat settle.

The pressure inside the chamber eased.

The midwife placed the newborn against Aurelia’s chest.

Aurelia stared at him through tears.

“My son.”

The infant turned toward her voice.

Her hand trembled as she touched his cheek.

“Zee.”

The name left her softly.

“Zee Darkheart.”

Crimson Mana curled around Aurelia’s wrist but did not harm her. It felt warm against her skin, almost curious, before returning to the child.

Victor released his sword.

He stared at his son.

The fangs.

The crimson eyes.

The strange mana.

The low, instinctive sound within the child’s breathing.

Every sign should have driven him away.

Instead, Victor stepped forward.

Zee turned his head toward him.

The king’s expression changed.

For the first time that night, he was not looking at an omen.

He was looking at his child.

His heir.

Victor reached down and offered one finger.

Zee’s tiny hand closed around it.

The strength in the newborn’s grip surprised him.

A faint smile touched Victor’s face.

Then the air split.

Far beyond House Darkheart, inside a mountain kingdom built around rivers of molten stone, a crimson dragon egg cracked open.

Dragon attendants gathered around it.

The egg belonged to the royal clutch, guarded since the first sign of life appeared beneath its shell. Teal-and-gold fire burned within the ceremonial braziers while the Dragon King and Queen watched from the obsidian platform above.

The shell broke.

A newborn crimson hatchling pushed free.

His scales gleamed dark red beneath the cavern light. Small wings unfolded against his wet body. Teal-and-gold mana moved over him in intertwined currents, distinct colors flowing together without becoming one.

The Dragon Queen stepped forward.

The hatchling lifted his head.

Then vanished.

There was no spell.

No portal.

No burst of flame.

One moment, he stood among the fragments of his shell.

The next, the royal nest was empty.

The Dragon Queen’s roar shook the mountain.

At Castle Darkheart, the crimson hatchling appeared upon Aurelia’s bed.

The royal guards drew their weapons.

Witches raised hands, their magic still difficult to reach beneath the lingering pressure.

The hatchling ignored them.

His unsteady legs carried him across the blanket toward Zee.

Victor moved between the creature and his family.

“Stay back.”

The hatchling stopped.

Teal-and-gold mana shimmered faintly around his scales.

He did not attack.

He looked past Victor toward the newborn prince.

Zee stirred.

A simple feeling passed between the two infants.

Recognition.

Not knowledge.

Not memory.

Only the instinctive certainty that neither was alone.

The hatchling continued forward.

Victor tightened his grip on his sword but did not strike.

The tiny dragon reached Zee, circled once, and curled against the child’s side. Zee’s hand settled against the hatchling’s neck.

The tension inside both newborns eased.

Safe.

Aurelia looked from one child to the other.

“What is he?”

The eldest witch had recovered enough to stand.

She studied the hatchling’s crimson scales and strange mixed mana.

“I do not know.”

“Where did he come from?”

“I do not know that either.”

No one inside Castle Darkheart recognized him.

No one knew that a kingdom beyond the mountains had lost its newborn crown prince at the exact moment Zee entered the world.

The suspended blood resumed falling.

The pressure around Zee weakened until the royal witches could finally touch their power again. Violet light returned to the eldest witch’s hands. Another restored the ward around the chamber. A third began healing Aurelia’s injuries.

The younger witch stared at her own palms.

“It was never gone.”

The eldest looked toward Zee.

“No.”

“Then why could we not reach it?”

The elder had lived for more than a century.

She had no answer.

Before she could offer even a theory, the chamber doors opened.

A scout entered drenched in blood.

He dropped to one knee, chest heaving from the force of his run.

“My King.”

Victor turned.

“Report.”

“Messages have begun arriving from every border. The blood fell beyond our lands. The wolves have attacked settlements throughout the north. Foreign courts are demanding answers.”

“We have none.”

“They do not believe that.”

Victor’s face hardened.

The scout looked toward Zee.

Rumor had already outrun the truth.

Servants had seen the crimson light.

Guards had heard the newborn’s strange heartbeat.

Physicians had witnessed fangs in the mouth of a royal child born to an ancient Witch House. Beyond the walls, wolf-blooded soldiers claimed they felt something awaken inside them when Zee took his first breath.

The scout lowered his eyes.

“Several kingdoms are calling the child unnatural.”

Aurelia tightened her hold around Zee.

Victor stepped between the scout and the bed.

“He is the heir of House Darkheart.”

“My King, they are already sending riders.”

“For what purpose?”

“To learn what was born here.”

Victor looked toward the blood-streaked windows.

Across the ancient world, rulers were gathering witnesses. Witches argued over the moment their magic became unreachable. Vampires searched their memories for the source of the heartbeat. Hunters entered forests filled with maddened wolves and found entire packs moving toward the same distant kingdom.

No one understood Zee.

That did not prevent them from fearing him.

By dawn, the first royal messenger would leave a neighboring capital carrying a demand for the newborn’s death.

By sunrise, eleven more would follow.

The impossible had been born.

And the world had already begun to move against him.

Chapter Two

The King’s Fear

Castle Darkheart did not sleep.

The Blood Rain ended before dawn, but crimson water continued to run from the roofs and battlements. It gathered in the mouths of stone beasts, flowed through the courtyards, and spilled down the mountain in narrow red streams. Servants scrubbed the floors without making them clean. Priests burned incense in every hall. Soldiers stood along the walls with bows strung and swords loosened in their sheaths.

No enemy had reached the kingdom.

Fear had entered first.

Inside the royal chamber, the physicians completed their work around Queen Aurelia while the witches tested their recovered magic.

Violet light moved across torn flesh and eased the queen’s pain. Blue sigils appeared above bowls of water, purifying the blood from their surfaces. Pale green wards settled across the doors and windows.

Every spell answered normally.

That frightened the witches almost as much as their earlier helplessness.

The eldest royal witch stood near the window, watching the last traces of blood drip from the glass.

“My power was inside me the entire time,” she said.

The younger witch beside her nodded. “I could feel it. I simply could not make it answer.”

“Nor could I.”

“Was it the child?”

The elder looked toward Zee.

He slept against Aurelia’s chest. The crimson hatchling remained pressed along his side, its tail curled protectively around the blanket. Their breathing had fallen into the same slow rhythm.

“I do not know.”

“You felt the pressure.”

“I felt many things tonight. Certainty was not among them.”

The younger witch lowered her voice. “He has the blood hunger.”

The elder’s eyes narrowed.

“You have no proof of hunger.”

“He has fangs.”

“So do creatures that have never tasted blood.”

“And the sound inside him?”

The elder glanced toward the door, ensuring Victor remained too distant to hear.

“The royal wolf guard heard it.”

“He said the prince carried the scent of wolf blood.”

“A frightened man said many things.”

“Do you believe he was wrong?”

The elder did not answer.

House Darkheart had ruled as an ancient Witch Kingdom for generations. Its royal line was known for powerful witches, long-lived blood, and rulers whose magic had broken enemy armies.

No Darkheart child had ever been born with vampire fangs.

No newborn prince had ever carried the scent of a wolf.

No witch had ever produced mana like the crimson force surrounding Zee.

The younger woman whispered, “Three natures.”

“Do not name what you do not understand.”

“Witch. Vampire. Wolf.”

The elder’s gaze sharpened.

“Enough.”

But the words had already entered the room.

Three natures.

A trinity of blood no kingdom had ever witnessed.

A First Tribrid.

The name would not remain inside Castle Darkheart for long.

Near the bed, Victor watched Zee sleep.

He had dismissed most of the attendants and refused every request to remove the dragon hatchling. Twice, guards offered to place the creature inside an iron cage. Twice, Zee’s Crimson Mana surged before any hand reached it.

Victor had ordered them to stop trying.

He told himself the command protected Aurelia from another disturbance.

The truth was more difficult.

The hatchling had not threatened Zee.

It had calmed him.

Each time the child stirred, the dragon moved closer. Each time the hatchling made a weak sound of hunger or discomfort, Zee’s tiny fingers found its scales.

Victor understood nothing about the connection.

He could still see the way Zee had held his finger.

His son’s grip had been too strong for a newborn, yet the memory did not frighten him as much as it should have.

Not yet.

Aurelia opened her eyes.

“You are staring.”

Victor looked at her. “You should sleep.”

“So should you.”

“I have a kingdom to command.”

“You have a son.”

The words stopped him.

Aurelia shifted Zee carefully into her arms and held him toward Victor.

“Take him.”

Victor did not move.

The crimson hatchling lifted its head.

“It watches me,” Victor said.

“It watches everyone.”

“It does not watch you that way.”

“Perhaps it has good judgment.”

Despite the night’s horror, Victor almost smiled.

Aurelia extended Zee farther.

“Hold your son.”

Victor sheathed his sword and approached.

He slid one hand beneath Zee’s head and the other beneath his body. The child felt impossibly small against him.

Zee opened his crimson eyes.

Victor’s breath caught.

No infant should have looked so still.

So aware.

Yet there was no ancient intelligence inside the child’s gaze. No hidden message. Zee was only a newborn trying to understand warmth, sound, hunger, and the unfamiliar shape of the world around him.

His tiny fangs showed when his mouth opened.

Victor waited for a cry.

None came.

Instead, Zee settled against his chest.

Crimson Mana touched Victor’s hands.

It did not burn.

The king looked down at the heir he had waited years to meet.

“My son,” he said quietly.

Aurelia watched him.

For that moment, the blood outside did not matter.

The foreign riders did not matter.

The maddened wolves, waking vampires, and frightened witches seemed far beyond the chamber.

Victor held his child.

Then the first war horn sounded.

It came from the eastern tower.

A second answered from the southern wall.

The hatchling sprang upright, releasing a sharp cry as teal-and-gold mana flickered across its scales. Zee startled in Victor’s arms. A pulse of Crimson Mana struck the room, rattling every window.

Victor handed the child back to Aurelia and reached for his sword.

The chamber doors opened.

Captain Edric Vale, commander of the Darkheart Guard, entered with blood still staining the lower edge of his cloak.

“My King.”

“What has reached us?”

“Messengers. Not soldiers.”

“Then why sound the war horns?”

“Because there are twelve of them.”

Victor’s expression hardened.

“From whom?”

“Twelve crowns.”

Silence followed.

Aurelia held Zee closer.

Captain Vale continued. “They arrived separately, but each carries the same demand.”

Victor stepped toward him.

“Speak it.”

The captain hesitated.

“They want the child surrendered before nightfall.”

The crimson hatchling growled.

It was a weak, newborn sound, but the intention behind it was unmistakable.

Victor’s face darkened.

“On whose authority?”

“Theirs.”

“They believe twelve seals make them rulers of my house?”

“No, Your Majesty.”

“What do they threaten?”

“War.”

Aurelia looked toward Victor. “They would invade over a child born less than a night ago?”

“They are not invading over a child,” Victor said.

The words left him more harshly than he intended.

“They are invading because they believe fear gives them the right.”

He turned to Captain Vale.

“Send the messengers to the great hall. Feed them. Do not harm them.”

“And our answer?”

Victor looked back at Zee.

His child rested beneath Aurelia’s hand while the crimson hatchling remained beside him, watching the armed men.

“No foreign king decides what happens to the heir of House Darkheart.”

Captain Vale struck his fist to his chest.

“Yes, Your Majesty.”

When he departed, Aurelia’s shoulders eased.

“You will defend him.”

Victor looked toward the windows.

“I will defend this kingdom.”

The difference escaped her.

It did not escape him.

By midday, the twelve messengers stood beneath the vaulted ceiling of the great hall.

Each wore the colors of a different kingdom.

Some came from nations that had fought House Darkheart for generations. Others represented crowns bound to Victor through trade, marriage, or uneasy peace. Two served kings who had been at war with one another less than a week earlier.

Fear had made allies where diplomacy failed.

Victor sat upon the black throne.

The iron crown of House Darkheart rested upon his head. Generals and court witches stood along the walls. Captain Vale remained at the foot of the dais.

The first messenger stepped forward.

“My sovereign offers peace if the unnatural child is surrendered.”

Victor’s hand tightened around the throne.

The second spoke. “Our northern villages were destroyed by wolves at the exact hour of his birth.”

A third added, “Every witch in our capital became helpless.”

“Temporarily,” one of the Darkheart witches said. “Their magic was never gone.”

The messenger ignored her.

“A heartbeat entered the blood of every vampire beneath our mountains.”

Another voice rose from the line. “A child with witch mana, vampire fangs, and the scent of a wolf cannot be permitted to live.”

Victor stood.

The hall fell silent.

“You entered my kingdom beneath banners of peace,” he said. “You were fed at my table and permitted to stand within my throne room. Do not mistake restraint for weakness.”

The first messenger held his ground. “Then you refuse?”

“I refuse to surrender my son to frightened rulers who have not seen him.”

“They have seen the sky.”

“So have I.”

“They have buried those killed by the wolves.”

“So will I.”

“The child caused it.”

“You do not know that.”

“Neither do you.”

The words struck harder than Victor expected.

He descended one step from the throne.

The messenger continued. “Kill him yourself, and the armies will turn back.”

Aurelia’s voice came from the entrance.

“No.”

Everyone turned.

The queen entered carrying Zee. She should not have left the royal chamber, but there was no weakness in her posture. The crimson hatchling moved beside her in the arms of a nervous servant, struggling until it was placed near Zee again.

Aurelia stopped before the gathered envoys.

“You crossed our borders and entered my home to demand the murder of my newborn son.”

The first messenger lowered his head, though not in apology.

“My queen, we demand survival.”

“You demand obedience.”

The hatchling pressed against Zee, its teal-and-gold mana barely visible beneath its crimson scales.

One messenger stared at them.

“There are reports from the Dragon Kingdom.”

Victor looked toward him.

“What reports?”

“A royal egg hatched during the Blood Rain. The hatchling vanished from a sealed mountain chamber.”

Every eye shifted toward the small dragon beside Zee.

The creature buried its head against the infant.

The messenger whispered, “That may be what was taken.”

“No one here took him,” Aurelia said.

“Yet he came to the child.”

Another murmur moved through the hall.

Fear gained shape with every unanswered question.

Victor raised one hand.

“You have my answer. Leave Castle Darkheart before sunset.”

The first messenger did not move.

“Our armies are already gathering.”

“Then gather them farther from my walls.”

“If we return without the child, they will march.”

Victor’s voice lowered.

“Then they will die.”

The messengers were escorted from the hall.

Aurelia remained beside the throne after the doors closed.

“You meant it.”

Victor looked at the empty space where the envoys had stood.

“They threatened House Darkheart.”

“They threatened Zee.”

“They threatened both.”

She studied him.

“Does that distinction matter?”

Victor turned toward his son.

Zee’s crimson eyes were open again. The child reached toward him.

Victor did not take his hand this time.

Before Aurelia could question him, an old servant entered through a side door carrying a narrow wooden box.

He was blind in one eye and walked with the aid of an iron staff. Victor recognized him as the keeper of the royal burial vaults, a man who had served Victor’s father before Victor wore the crown.

The servant knelt.

“Forgive me, Your Majesty.”

“What is it?”

“Something opened beneath the castle.”

Victor’s attention sharpened.

“What opened?”

“A sealed chamber beneath the oldest crypt.”

“By whose command?”

“No living command.”

The servant raised the wooden box.

“This was inside.”

The object was carved from black wood and bound with rusted iron. No royal crest marked it. No witch sigil protected it. A strip of human skin had been wrapped around its center and tied with a knot darkened by age.

Aurelia recoiled.

“Remove that from my son.”

The servant remained kneeling.

“My Queen, the chamber opened when the prince was born.”

Victor looked toward Captain Vale. “Take Aurelia back to the nursery.”

“I am not leaving.”

“Aurelia.”

She heard the command in his voice.

For the first time since Zee’s birth, she saw something colder beneath Victor’s expression.

Not hatred.

Not yet.

Fear searching for an answer.

Aurelia held Zee more tightly.

“You will tell me what is inside that box.”

“When I know.”

She wanted to argue.

Then Zee stirred, and the crimson hatchling released a restless sound.

Aurelia finally turned away.

Victor watched her leave with their son.

The great hall doors closed.

“Open it,” he ordered.

The burial keeper placed the box upon the stone floor.

Captain Vale stood near Victor with one hand on his sword.

The old man cut through the strip of skin.

The knot loosened by itself.

A smell of earth, ash, and old blood entered the hall.

Inside the box rested no ancient book.

No record of a previous Tribrid.

No explanation of the child.

There was only a narrow piece of bone etched with words that looked freshly carved.

Victor crouched beside it.

“Who wrote this?”

“No one living,” the keeper whispered.

“That is not an answer.”

“It is the only one I possess.”

Victor lifted the bone.

The writing darkened beneath his touch.

A voice entered the silent hall.

Not spoken by the burial keeper.

Not spoken by Captain Vale.

It came from the bone itself, thin and broken, as though carried through the throat of something long dead.

“When blood falls upward and beasts forget their names, a child of crown and hunger shall open his eyes beneath the blackened throne.”

Victor’s grip tightened.

The voice continued.

“Three lives shall breathe within one flesh, and every blade raised against him shall sharpen what it seeks to destroy.”

Captain Vale stepped backward.

The burial keeper began praying.

Victor could not move.

“He shall not inherit the world as it was given.”

The final words emerged slowly.

“The world shall break before it teaches him how to die.”

The bone split in Victor’s hand.

Silence returned.

No name had been spoken.

No future victory revealed.

No explanation given for Zee’s Crimson Mana, the Blood Rain, or the child’s impossible nature.

Yet Victor saw his son in every word.

Blood falling from the heavens.

Wolves losing themselves.

Three lives inside one body.

Every blade making him harder to destroy.

Victor stared at the fragments in his palm.

“Who knew this prophecy?”

The burial keeper shook his head.

“No one, Your Majesty. The chamber had no door yesterday.”

“Who placed the box there?”

“I do not know.”

“Was it my father?”

“No.”

“My grandfather?”

“No record names it.”

Victor rose.

The king who had threatened twelve kingdoms only moments earlier was gone.

In his place stood a father who had been handed a reason to fear his own child.

“Leave us,” he said.

The burial keeper bowed and retreated.

Captain Vale remained.

“My King—”

“Leave.”

The captain obeyed.

Victor stood alone in the great hall.

Outside, ravens carried reports across the ancient world.

Twelve kingdoms called their banners.

Wolves still wandered without reason through blood-soaked forests.

Vampires hunted for the source of the heartbeat that had entered their blood.

Witches whispered about the newborn whose presence had buried their magic beneath impossible pressure.

Inside the royal nursery, Aurelia laid Zee in his cradle.

The crimson hatchling curled beside him.

Zee reached through the simple bond between them.

Unease.

The hatchling lifted his head and stared toward the distant throne room.

Victor remained there until the final light disappeared from the windows.

When he eventually returned to the nursery, Aurelia looked up with relief.

“You found your answer?”

Victor stood in the doorway.

His eyes settled upon Zee.

The child smiled at the sight of him.

Victor remembered holding him.

He remembered the tiny hand around his finger.

Then the prophecy whispered again inside his mind.

Every blade raised against him shall sharpen what it seeks to destroy.

Victor did not approach the cradle.

“No,” he said.

Aurelia frowned. “No?”

“I found something worse.”

That night, the armies began marching toward House Darkheart.

And for the first time since Zee’s birth, his father looked at him and felt afraid to love him.

================================================================================
Chapter Three

Fear Becomes Judgment

By sunrise, the roads surrounding House Darkheart were no longer empty.

Scouts returned mud-soaked and sleepless, carrying reports from every direction. Columns of soldiers had been sighted beyond the eastern ridge. Siege wagons moved through the southern valleys. Northern banners had crossed the river before dawn, and riders from the west had begun seizing villages to establish supply lines.

Twelve kingdoms had not yet formed a true alliance.

They did not trust one another enough for that.

But fear had given them something almost as dangerous.

A shared destination.

Castle Darkheart.

The fortress woke beneath the sound of preparation.

Blacksmiths worked without rest. Arrowheads piled beside the walls. Witches renewed ancient defenses carved into stone generations earlier. Soldiers dragged barrels of oil toward murder holes and reinforced gates already thick enough to survive rams. Messengers rode through the inner city calling every reserve banner back to the capital.

House Darkheart had survived wars before.

This felt different.

No one could say whether the armies came for conquest, survival, religious terror, or simple panic.

Most did not care.

They were coming.

That was enough.

King Victor Darkheart stood over the war table in silence.

Wooden markers surrounded the carved representation of his kingdom.

Too many.

Captain Vale remained across from him while generals argued over roads, troop strength, and which kingdom would likely strike first.

Victor barely heard them.

The prophecy remained inside his head.

Not all of it.

One line.

Every blade raised against him shall sharpen what it seeks to destroy.

He had repeated it so many times through the night that the words no longer sounded like language.

They had become fear.

“Your Majesty?”

Victor looked up.

The High Marshal was waiting.

“Say it again.”

“The southern coalition is moving fastest. If they continue at their current pace, their advance force reaches our border settlements by tomorrow night.”

“And the east?”

“Two days.”

“The north?”

“Difficult terrain. Perhaps three.”

Victor nodded.

“Evacuate the villages closest to the border.”

The marshal hesitated. “Into the capital?”

“Into the fortified interior. Leave nothing useful behind.”

“Food stores?”

“Take what we can. Burn what we cannot.”

Several generals exchanged looks.

Victor saw them.

“Do you have a better way to feed an invading army?”

“No, Your Majesty.”

“Then carry out the order.”

The marshal bowed.

Victor placed both hands upon the table.

“Every gate closes by sundown. No foreign traveler enters after that. No merchant leaves with military information. Double the watch around the western tunnels and place witches at every old passage beneath the castle.”

Captain Vale glanced toward him.

“The nursery as well?”

The room went quiet.

Victor’s eyes moved to him.

“Especially the nursery.”

One of the generals shifted uneasily.

“Protection for the prince?”

Victor answered too slowly.

“Yes.”

The word came without warmth.

Captain Vale heard it.

No one else challenged the king.

The orders continued.

But the nursery remained in Victor’s thoughts.

Not because he feared someone would reach Zee before House Darkheart could protect him.

Because he had begun to fear what would happen if no one ever could.

—

Queen Aurelia refused to remain in bed.

The physicians protested.

She ignored them.

By midday, she sat in the royal nursery wrapped in a heavy black robe, Zee cradled against her chest while the crimson hatchling slept near her feet.

The newborn dragon had eaten poorly.

No one knew what to feed him.

The kitchens tried raw meat, cooked meat, milk, blood, fish, and even crushed gemstone offered by a terrified servant who claimed dragons ate treasure.

The hatchling rejected nearly everything until Zee began crying from hunger.

The sound changed him.

His little head lifted.

A simple feeling moved across the strange connection between them.

Hunger.

Not his.

Zee’s.

The hatchling climbed clumsily toward the queen and nudged her arm.

Aurelia stared.

“You know.”

The hatchling chirped.

She did not understand the bond.

She only understood what she saw.

He knew Zee needed something.

Aurelia fed her son.

The hatchling settled again.

When Zee relaxed, so did he.

Aurelia smiled faintly.

“There is more sense between the two of you than in half the royal court.”

The door opened.

Victor entered.

He had not changed clothes since the previous night.

Aurelia’s smile faded.

“You look terrible.”

“I have twelve kingdoms marching toward my walls.”

“You had twelve kingdoms marching toward your walls yesterday.”

“Yesterday they were threatening.”

“And now?”

“They are moving siege equipment.”

Aurelia looked down at Zee.

The child slept peacefully.

“Because of him.”

Victor said nothing.

Aurelia studied his face.

Something had changed.

Not suddenly.

But undeniably.

“You have not touched him since last night.”

Victor looked toward the cradle.

The hatchling opened its eyes.

A low warning sound rolled from its tiny chest.

Victor’s jaw tightened.

“That creature does that every time I enter.”

“It does it when armed men enter.”

“I am always armed.”

“Perhaps that is the problem.”

Victor nearly smiled.

He did not.

Aurelia noticed.

“What did you find beneath the castle?”

He remained silent.

“Victor.”

“The burial keeper found something that should not have been there.”

“What?”

“A prophecy.”

Aurelia’s expression hardened.

“No.”

“You have not heard it.”

“I do not need to hear it.”

Victor stepped closer.

“It spoke of the Blood Rain.”

Aurelia’s fingers tightened around Zee.

“It spoke of wolves losing themselves.”

“Stop.”

“It spoke of three lives within one body.”

“Stop.”

Victor did.

The room fell silent.

Aurelia looked at him with anger now.

“Do not bring old bones into my child’s cradle and call them truth.”

“You think I want this?”

“I think you are frightened.”

“I am.”

“Then say that.”

Victor looked at Zee.

The child stirred.

“Every army outside these walls is frightened too.”

“They do not know him.”

“Neither do we.”

“He is our son.”

“That does not answer what he is.”

Aurelia stood too quickly and winced.

Victor instinctively reached toward her.

She stepped back.

“Do not.”

His hand lowered.

“You held him yesterday,” she said. “You looked at him and saw your child.”

“I still see my child.”

“No. You are trying not to.”

Victor’s expression hardened.

“The prophecy says—”

“The prophecy does not feed him.”

“Aurelia.”

“It does not know how he sleeps. It does not know the sound he makes when he is hungry. It does not know that he reaches for you.”

Victor looked away.

That hurt more than she intended.

She continued anyway.

“You want something ancient to tell you who your son is because you are afraid to learn for yourself.”

Victor’s voice lowered.

“You did not hear the final line.”

“I do not care.”

“I do.”

Aurelia’s eyes flashed.

“That is what frightens me.”

The hatchling rose between them.

Teal-and-gold mana shimmered along his crimson scales.

He did not understand the argument.

He understood fear.

Zee felt it through him.

The newborn’s Crimson Mana stirred.

The lamps flickered.

Victor stepped back.

Not because the mana threatened him.

Because the movement confirmed something inside him.

Even as an infant, Zee responded.

Adapted.

Reacted.

The prophecy whispered again.

Every blade raised against him shall sharpen what it seeks to destroy.

Victor looked at the crimson glow around his son.

For the first time, he wondered whether love itself might be another blade.

And whether mercy could become the cruelty that doomed them all.

—

That evening, the first foreign campfires became visible from Castle Darkheart.

Hundreds at first.

Then thousands.

They burned along the distant plains like a second constellation beneath the horizon.

Citizens gathered along the inner walls to watch.

No one celebrated.

No one panicked openly either.

House Darkheart had survived too much for that.

But fear moved through the capital in quiet ways.

Shops closed early.

Parents kept children indoors.

Shrines filled with offerings.

Old swords were pulled from family chests.

Witches prepared healing rooms in temples and military halls.

Rumors multiplied faster than soldiers.

Some said the prince had been born drinking blood.

Others claimed he had transformed into a wolf before his first breath.

One story insisted the dragon hatchling had bowed to him.

Another said every vampire in the east now carried Zee’s heartbeat.

None were true.

That did not matter.

Fear rarely waited for truth.

Within the war chamber, Victor listened as Captain Vale read the newest demands.

“Three kingdoms still request surrender.”

“Request?”

“Demand.”

“Then call it what it is.”

Captain Vale continued.

“Four demand execution witnessed by neutral envoys.”

Victor’s face did not change.

“Neutral.”

“Yes.”

“There are no neutral crowns left.”

“No, Your Majesty.”

“And the others?”

“Two demand the queen and child be removed from the royal line.”

Victor’s hand tightened.

“On what authority?”

“None that House Darkheart recognizes.”

“The remaining three?”

Captain Vale paused.

“They have stopped sending demands.”

Victor looked up.

“Why?”

“They are preparing to attack.”

The council went silent.

Victor walked toward the window.

From there he could see faint fires beyond the hills.

“Twelve kingdoms,” he said.

Captain Vale nodded.

“Against one newborn.”

“No.”

Victor turned.

“Against House Darkheart.”

Several nobles exchanged relieved looks.

It sounded like pride.

Sovereignty.

Defiance.

The king they understood.

Then Victor added, “And they will not decide his fate.”

The room changed.

Captain Vale heard the difference immediately.

Victor no longer said they would not kill Zee.

He said they would not decide.

That distinction was becoming larger every hour.

—

Later that night, Victor returned alone to the burial chamber.

The broken bone remained where it had split.

He had ordered no one to touch it.

The chamber smelled colder now.

He knelt and gathered the pieces.

No voice spoke.

No new words appeared.

The prophecy had given what it intended to give.

Nothing more.

Victor stared at the fragments.

“What are you?”

Silence.

“What does he become?”

Nothing answered.

Victor laughed once.

There was no humor in it.

“You tell me enough to fear him and not enough to know why.”

He looked toward the ceiling as though he could see through stone into the nursery above.

“My son.”

The words nearly broke him.

He closed his eyes.

He remembered Zee’s hand around his finger.

The small weight against his chest.

Aurelia’s smile.

Then he imagined the armies outside the walls multiplied a hundred times.

A thousand.

He imagined every kingdom someday falling.

Not because the prophecy promised it.

Because Victor’s fear supplied the rest.

That was how the prophecy began winning.

Not by revealing the future.

By forcing a frightened man to imagine one.

Victor opened his eyes.

“If they attack him…”

The line returned.

Every blade raised against him shall sharpen what it seeks to destroy.

His breathing slowed.

The problem was no longer only that Zee might survive an attempt on his life.

The problem was what survival might do to him.

Victor began to think like a king confronting an enemy.

Quietly.

Methodically.

Terribly.

He could not allow foreign rulers to test the prophecy.

He could not allow witches, vampires, wolves, or armies to discover whether hurting Zee truly made him harder to destroy.

He could not allow anyone else to control the experiment.

The thought arrived so naturally that Victor did not recognize how far he had fallen until it was already complete.

If the prophecy must be tested…

His stomach turned.

He stood abruptly.

“No.”

The word echoed through the chamber.

For several breaths, he fought himself.

Then he whispered,

“Not yet.”

That was worse.

—

In the nursery above, Zee woke.

No sound had reached him.

No spell touched the room.

Yet discomfort spread through his small body.

The crimson hatchling opened his eyes at the same moment.

Danger.

Not a place.

Not a face.

Only the instinctive feeling of something wrong.

The hatchling crawled closer.

Zee’s tiny hand found his scales.

Safe.

The feeling passed between them.

Small.

Simple.

Desperate.

Outside the nursery, two additional guards arrived under direct royal order.

Then two more.

By midnight, no one could enter the corridor without Victor’s permission.

Aurelia believed the king had increased protection because foreign armies were approaching.

She slept beside her son without knowing the truth.

Victor was not only keeping the world away from Zee.

He was beginning to keep Zee where he could control him.

By the end of the night, the child in Victor’s mind had become two things at once.

His son.

And the prophecy wearing his son’s face.

Chapter Four

The First Decision

The first arrow landed before dawn.

It struck the outer wall of Castle Darkheart and shattered against stone.

No soldier died.

No gate broke.

But the message tied beneath the arrow survived.

Captain Vale carried it personally to the throne room.

King Victor read it once.

Then again.

Queen Aurelia stood several paces away, Zee in her arms.

The crimson hatchling rested against her side beneath the folds of a heavy cloak, hidden from the growing number of foreign eyes beyond the walls.

Victor handed the message to no one.

Aurelia watched his face.

“What does it say?”

He folded the parchment.

“Nothing new.”

“Then read it.”

Victor looked at her.

Aurelia did not move.

Finally he spoke.

“They demand Zee be brought beyond the eastern gate before midday.”

“And if we refuse?”

“They begin the siege.”

The queen’s expression turned cold.

“Then let them begin.”

Several ministers shifted uneasily.

Victor said nothing.

Aurelia looked toward the assembled council.

“You heard me.”

The High Marshal lowered his head.

“My Queen.”

“We do not surrender children to armies.”

“No,” Victor said.

Every eye turned toward him.

He stepped down from the throne.

“We do not.”

Aurelia studied him carefully.

For one moment, she heard the man from before the prophecy.

Then Victor continued.

“Not because they are wrong to fear him.”

The room chilled.

Aurelia’s face hardened.

“Victor.”

“But because no foreign crown decides what happens inside House Darkheart.”

The distinction was unmistakable now.

The council heard it.

Captain Vale heard it.

Aurelia heard it most of all.

“You speak of our son as though he were property.”

“I speak as a king.”

“You used to speak as his father.”

Victor’s jaw tightened.

“This is not the place.”

“No. The place was our nursery, and you stopped speaking there too.”

The hatchling stirred beneath her cloak.

Zee’s Crimson Mana brightened faintly.

Victor noticed.

Of course he noticed.

Now he noticed everything.

Every flicker.

Every change in Zee’s breathing.

Every strange movement of the dragon beside him.

He collected details as if building a case against his own child.

Aurelia saw that too.

Fear turned slowly into anger.

“You will not touch him.”

The council went completely silent.

Victor’s eyes met hers.

“I have not said I would.”

“You no longer need to.”

Before he could answer, the fortress shook.

A deep impact thundered against the eastern wall.

Then another.

Siege stones.

The war had begun.

—

The first assault lasted three hours.

House Darkheart’s witches stood upon the battlements and cast through carved defensive channels built into the ancient walls. Violet force struck ladders from stone. Blue-white frost from enchanted siege wards froze ropes and shattered wooden towers. Green fire spilled across an advancing ram.

None of it carried Crimson Mana.

That belonged to Zee alone.

Darkheart soldiers filled the air with arrows.

Boiling oil rained from murder holes.

Foreign troops screamed beneath the walls while their kings remained safely beyond range.

The castle held.

But House Darkheart paid for it.

By midday, bodies filled the eastern courtyard.

Some belonged to invaders.

Many did not.

A healer died with both hands inside a soldier’s open abdomen.

A tower collapsed after repeated strikes and buried seventeen archers.

A captain Victor had known since boyhood bled out against the inner gate.

War did what fear always promised.

It made everything simpler by making everything worse.

Victor walked among the dead.

Blood covered his boots.

A young soldier grabbed his cloak.

“My King.”

Victor crouched.

The soldier could not have been older than eighteen.

“Did we hold?”

“Yes.”

The boy smiled.

Then died.

Victor remained there for several seconds.

Behind him, another siege stone struck the wall.

The prophecy whispered.

The world shall break before it teaches him how to die.

Victor looked toward the castle tower where Zee slept.

For the first time, resentment entered his fear.

Not hatred of the child.

Hatred of what followed him.

That distinction would not survive forever.

—

In the nursery, Aurelia heard the war through stone.

Every impact made dust fall from the ceiling.

Every horn sent the crimson hatchling into alert stillness.

Zee had begun crying.

Not loudly.

But enough to make Aurelia’s heart ache.

She held him close.

“I know.”

Another strike shook the room.

“I know.”

The hatchling crawled into her lap and pressed his head against Zee.

Fear moved between them.

Then comfort.

Their strange link did not give either child knowledge.

Only presence.

Neither was alone.

The eldest royal witch entered with blood across her sleeve.

Aurelia looked up.

“Are the walls holding?”

“For now.”

“How many dead?”

The witch hesitated.

“Too many.”

Aurelia closed her eyes.

The woman approached Zee.

Crimson Mana drifted around him more strongly than before.

“His power responds when the castle is struck.”

Aurelia’s eyes opened.

“Do not call it power as if he commands it.”

“I know he does not.”

“Then say what you mean.”

The witch nodded.

“His mana becomes more active when he is distressed.”

Aurelia looked down at him.

“Like any child.”

“Perhaps.”

The uncertainty mattered.

The witch did not pretend to understand.

She had learned better.

Aurelia asked, “What happened to your magic during his birth?”

The woman considered carefully.

“It remained inside me.”

“But?”

“I could not reach it.”

“Because of Zee?”

“I do not know.”

“You felt his mana.”

“Yes.”

“Was it stronger?”

The witch looked toward the infant.

“Overwhelming.”

“That is not the same answer.”

“No.”

Aurelia appreciated the honesty.

The witch continued.

“I have spent my life learning the shape of my own magic. That night, I knew it was still there. I simply could not hear myself beneath him.”

“Beneath my newborn son.”

“Yes.”

Aurelia looked toward the window.

Outside, men were killing one another because everyone believed observation had already become understanding.

It had not.

No one knew what Zee was capable of.

No one knew what he would become.

No one knew whether the Blood Rain had been caused by him, announced him, reacted to him, or merely occurred beside him.

Yet armies had come anyway.

Fear had filled every unanswered question with the worst possible answer.

Aurelia whispered, “Victor is doing the same thing.”

The witch did not respond.

She did not need to.

—

That evening, a second message came beneath a white flag.

The foreign coalition requested a single representative.

Victor allowed one envoy inside the outer gate.

The man entered without armor.

He was elderly, gray-bearded, and exhausted.

Victor met him in the lower audience hall rather than the throne room.

“You have lost thousands today,” the envoy said.

“So have you.”

“We can lose more.”

“So can we.”

The man looked at Victor for a long moment.

“Is that what you want?”

“No.”

“Then end it.”

Victor’s expression hardened.

“You know our terms.”

“You have no terms. You have a demand.”

“We have terror.”

“That is not law.”

“No. It is stronger.”

Victor almost drew his sword.

The envoy raised both hands.

“I am not your enemy, Victor.”

“You arrived with an army.”

“I arrived because my king watched blood fall from the sky.”

“So did mine.”

“Wolves slaughtered villages.”

“I know.”

“Witches became helpless.”

“They recovered.”

“Vampires screamed about a heartbeat that was not theirs.”

Victor said nothing.

The envoy stepped closer.

“And every report leads here.”

“To a child.”

“To something no one understands.”

Victor’s eyes sharpened.

“Then perhaps none of you should pretend you know enough to kill him.”

The envoy nodded slowly.

“Perhaps.”

Victor had not expected agreement.

“But perhaps you do not know enough to let him live.”

That landed.

The man saw it.

“You are his father.”

Victor’s jaw tightened.

“You think I cannot see it?”

The envoy lowered his voice.

“I think you are more frightened than any king outside these walls.”

Victor stared at him.

“Leave.”

“Victor—”

“Leave before your white flag becomes your burial cloth.”

The envoy bowed.

At the door, he stopped.

“If you refuse us, the assault resumes at dawn.”

Victor did not turn.

The door closed.

He remained alone.

More frightened than any king outside these walls.

The insult should have angered him.

Instead, it felt true.

—

That night, Victor summoned Captain Vale.

No council.

No ministers.

No Aurelia.

Only the two of them inside the king’s private chamber.

Victor poured wine but did not drink it.

“How many guards outside the nursery?”

“Eight.”

“Double them.”

Captain Vale hesitated.

“Against what?”

Victor looked at him.

“Everyone.”

“Foreign assassins?”

“Yes.”

“Court factions?”

“Yes.”

Vale waited.

“And the queen?”

Victor said nothing.

The captain’s expression changed.

“My King.”

“No one removes Zee from that wing without my command.”

“Not even Queen Aurelia?”

Victor’s eyes hardened.

“I said no one.”

Vale breathed slowly.

“You understand what that order means.”

“Yes.”

“Do you?”

Victor stepped toward him.

“I will not have twelve kings tear apart my kingdom deciding what should happen to my son.”

“Then what will happen?”

“I decide.”

Vale stared at him.

For years, he had followed Victor through wars without hesitation.

This frightened him more than battle.

“You intend to kill the prince?”

Victor’s face tightened.

“No.”

The answer came immediately.

Too immediately.

Then he looked away.

“Not tonight.”

Captain Vale went still.

Victor heard his own words.

There was no taking them back.

The king walked toward the window.

Far beyond the walls, enemy fires covered the plain.

“If the prophecy is true, attacking him may make him worse.”

“May.”

“Yes.”

“And if it is false?”

Victor looked toward him.

“Then a child dies.”

The words nearly broke whatever remained of the father inside him.

Vale spoke carefully.

“That should matter.”

“It does.”

“Then stop.”

Victor closed his eyes.

He wanted to.

Aurelia’s voice echoed through his memory.

You held him yesterday.

He remembered Zee sleeping against him.

His son.

His heir.

Then another siege stone struck the outer wall.

The room trembled.

Victor opened his eyes.

“And if I stop and every kingdom burns because I was too weak to act?”

“You do not know that will happen.”

“I do not know that it will not.”

Vale shook his head.

“That is fear speaking.”

“Yes.”

Victor turned toward him.

“And kings who ignore fear bury kingdoms.”

He walked to a locked cabinet and removed a small iron key.

Captain Vale stared at it.

“What does that open?”

“The old execution chamber beneath the western tower.”

Vale’s face went pale.

Victor placed the key on the table between them.

“I am not ordering his death.”

“Then why prepare the chamber?”

Victor looked at the key.

“Because if I decide the prophecy leaves me no choice… I will not make that decision with twelve foreign armies watching.”

The captain said nothing.

Victor’s voice became colder.

“No foreign king will claim they killed a Darkheart prince.”

“No priest will parade his body.”

“No vampire will take his blood.”

“No witch will dissect what remains.”

“If Zee dies, it will happen inside these walls.”

Vale whispered, “By your hand.”

Victor did not answer.

That was answer enough.

—

Near midnight, Aurelia woke and found Victor standing beside the cradle.

She sat upright.

“What are you doing?”

Victor looked toward her.

“Watching him.”

The crimson hatchling was awake.

His body pressed against Zee.

Teal-and-gold mana trembled faintly across his scales.

Danger.

Zee shifted in his sleep.

Victor reached toward him.

The hatchling hissed.

Aurelia stood.

“Do not.”

Victor stopped.

The distance between his hand and his son was less than an inch.

For several heartbeats, no one moved.

Then Zee opened his crimson eyes.

He saw Victor.

His tiny hand lifted.

The same gesture as before.

An invitation without understanding.

Victor stared at it.

Every part of him that remained a father wanted to take that hand.

He almost did.

Then the prophecy returned.

The dead soldier in the courtyard.

The armies outside.

The Blood Rain.

The wolves.

The impossible heartbeat.

Victor lowered his hand.

Aurelia’s face changed.

She understood.

Not everything.

Enough.

“You decided.”

Victor looked at her.

“I decided nothing.”

“You prepared something.”

His silence betrayed him.

Aurelia moved between him and the cradle.

“If you ever come near him with death in your heart, you will have to go through me.”

Victor’s expression hardened.

“You are threatening your king.”

“I am warning my husband.”

The hatchling curled tighter around Zee.

Victor stared at his family.

His wife.

His son.

The impossible dragon who had appeared beside him.

For one brief moment, grief almost conquered fear.

Almost.

Then another war horn sounded beyond the walls.

Victor stepped backward.

“No foreign ruler determines what happens to Zee.”

Aurelia’s voice was quiet.

“And neither does a frightened father.”

Victor left without answering.

He walked through the sleeping castle until he reached the western tower.

Below it, servants had already begun clearing dust from the old execution chamber.

Iron chains were removed from the walls.

A stone table was washed.

Torches were lit.

Victor stood at the top of the stairs and watched.

He had not yet ordered Zee brought there.

He had not yet raised a weapon against him.

He had not yet crossed the final distance between fear and murder.

But he had prepared the place where he might.

Outside, twelve kingdoms waited for Castle Darkheart to surrender the First Tribrid.

Inside, Queen Aurelia held her son and understood that the walls protecting Zee had become another kind of danger.

And before any foreign king could reach the newborn prince, the first man to decide Zee might have to die had already been crowned long before Zee was born.

His father.

Chapter Five

The First Attempt

The siege began again before sunrise.

This time, the kingdoms did not test the walls.

They tried to break them.

Three siege engines released at once, hurling stones large enough to crush houses. They struck the eastern battlements with enough force to split ancient masonry and throw soldiers from the walls. Horns answered from every direction. Arrows darkened the pale morning sky. Witches on both sides raised barriers, curses, and counterspells while infantry advanced beneath layered shields.

Castle Darkheart answered with violence of its own.

The Witch Kingdom had been built for war.

Runes buried deep within the fortress stone awakened under the hands of Darkheart battle-witches. Entire sections of wall shimmered beneath defensive magic. Enemy ladders caught fire before touching stone. The ground beneath one advancing battalion cracked open and swallowed horses, soldiers, and siege shields alike.

None of it stopped the next wave.

There were too many kingdoms.

Too many soldiers.

Too much fear.

King Victor stood upon the eastern battlement as arrows struck the barrier before him and burst into splinters.

“Left tower!”

A commander shouted the warning.

Victor turned just as an enemy stone smashed through the upper section of the tower.

Black stone exploded outward.

Men screamed.

A witch vanished beneath falling masonry.

Victor raised one hand and unleashed a violent burst of dark violet force. The largest pieces stopped in midair long enough for several soldiers to escape before crashing into the courtyard below.

“Get the wounded inside!” he ordered.

The High Marshal rushed toward him.

“We cannot hold every wall at this rate.”

“We do not need every wall.”

“My King?”

Victor pointed toward the eastern approach.

“They are attacking where they believe we are strongest.”

The marshal followed his gaze.

Understanding came quickly.

“A distraction.”

“Exactly.”

Victor looked south.

“Send riders to the lower tunnels. If even one foreign soldier enters beneath this castle, collapse the passage with them inside.”

“Yes, Your Majesty.”

The marshal hurried away.

Victor remained on the wall.

Below him, thousands of men were dying.

For Zee.

Because of Zee.

The thought came before Victor could stop it.

He hated himself for thinking it.

Then another soldier beside him screamed as an arrow pierced his throat.

Victor caught the man before he fell.

Blood poured over the king’s hands.

The soldier looked at him desperately.

“My King…”

Victor pressed one hand against the wound and tried to slow the bleeding.

The man died before the nearest healer reached them.

Victor stared at the blood covering his palms.

The prophecy returned.

Every blade raised against him shall sharpen what it seeks to destroy.

Victor looked toward the tower where his son slept.

Something inside him hardened.

Not completely.

Not yet.

But enough.

—

Queen Aurelia had not slept.

She sat beside the nursery window with Zee wrapped tightly against her chest.

The crimson hatchling remained pressed against them both.

Each impact against the walls made the tiny dragon flinch.

Each time he flinched, Zee stirred.

Their link carried only the simplest things between them.

Fear.

Unease.

Warmth.

Near.

Safe.

The hatchling pushed his snout against Zee’s shoulder.

Zee’s fingers closed weakly around one of his small horns.

The dragon calmed.

Aurelia watched them in silence.

“They are trying to kill you,” she whispered.

Zee did not understand the words.

His crimson eyes opened briefly.

Aurelia stroked his cheek.

“And your father is deciding whether to help them.”

The admission hurt more once spoken aloud.

The eldest royal witch stood near the door.

She had volunteered to remain with Aurelia.

Not under Victor’s command.

Under her own.

“My Queen…”

Aurelia looked at her.

“If he orders you to take Zee from me, what will you do?”

The witch did not answer immediately.

That frightened Aurelia.

Finally, the woman said, “I serve House Darkheart.”

“So do I.”

“Yes.”

“And?”

The witch looked toward the child.

“I do not believe fear is enough reason to murder a newborn.”

Aurelia’s shoulders loosened slightly.

“Then you will help me.”

“If it comes to that.”

“It already has.”

The witch lowered her eyes.

Outside, another impact shook the castle.

Dust drifted from the ceiling.

The dragon hatchling growled.

Then every flame in the nursery bent toward Zee.

The witch looked up sharply.

Crimson Mana thickened around the child.

Not violently.

Not consciously.

It simply gathered.

Zee’s breathing changed.

His heartbeat deepened.

The witch took one step backward.

Aurelia noticed.

“What?”

“I do not know.”

“Do not begin guessing.”

“I wasn’t.”

The woman studied Zee carefully.

“Something about him is reacting.”

“To the siege?”

“Perhaps.”

“To fear?”

“Perhaps.”

“To the dragon?”

“Perhaps.”

Aurelia’s jaw tightened.

“You truly know nothing.”

The witch looked at her.

“No.”

Then, after a moment:

“And I am beginning to think that is the only honest answer anyone in this kingdom has.”

—

By midday, the first outer village burned.

Victor watched smoke rise from beyond the walls.

It belonged to farmers who had refused evacuation.

The enemy had taken the settlement without resistance.

Then burned it anyway.

The High Marshal approached.

“They are sending another envoy.”

Victor did not turn.

“Kill him.”

The marshal froze.

Victor closed his eyes.

“No.”

He exhaled.

“Bring him inside.”

The correction came quickly.

But the marshal had heard the first answer.

So had Victor.

The envoy entered the lower audience chamber less than an hour later.

This one was younger.

He wore no crown colors.

Only plain gray cloth and a silver chain marking him as a neutral herald.

Victor laughed when he saw it.

“There are no neutrals left.”

The envoy bowed.

“Then consider me useful instead.”

Victor remained standing.

“What do they want now?”

“The same thing.”

“My son.”

“Yes.”

“Alive?”

The envoy hesitated.

Victor’s expression darkened.

“Answer.”

“Not necessarily.”

Silence filled the chamber.

The envoy continued carefully.

“Some rulers would accept proof of death.”

“And the others?”

“Some want the body.”

Victor’s face changed.

The envoy saw the danger too late.

“Leave.”

“My King—”

“Leave.”

“I was sent to explain—”

Victor crossed the distance between them in three strides and seized the man by the throat.

The guards moved instinctively.

No one interfered.

Victor lifted the envoy from the floor.

“If one foreign hand touches my son’s corpse…”

The words caught in his throat.

His son’s corpse.

He nearly released the man.

Then fear returned.

“If anyone attempts to claim his body as a trophy, relic, weapon, specimen, sacrifice, or prize…”

Victor tightened his grip.

“I will tear apart every kingdom represented outside my walls.”

The envoy clawed weakly at Victor’s hand.

Victor dropped him.

The man collapsed, coughing.

“Tell them no.”

The envoy looked up.

Victor’s voice lowered.

“And tell them something else.”

The room seemed colder.

“Zee Darkheart belongs to House Darkheart.”

The envoy stared at him.

Victor heard the words after saying them.

Belongs.

Not lives.

Not is protected by.

Belongs.

The envoy slowly stood.

“Then you intend to decide his fate yourself.”

Victor did not answer.

The man bowed.

“I think that is what they feared.”

He left.

Victor remained alone.

For a long time.

—

That evening, the castle changed around Zee.

The guards outside the nursery doubled again.

No one entered without being searched.

Windows were sealed.

Servants were replaced by soldiers personally selected by Victor.

Aurelia noticed every change.

So did the royal witch beside her.

“This is no longer protection,” Aurelia said.

The witch remained silent.

Aurelia stood.

“Pack what Zee needs.”

“My Queen?”

“Clothes. Blankets. Food.”

“For where?”

Aurelia looked toward the sealed window.

“Anywhere my husband cannot reach him.”

The witch’s face tightened.

“You are speaking of fleeing Castle Darkheart during a siege.”

“I am speaking of keeping my son alive.”

“The roads are surrounded.”

“Then we do not use roads.”

The witch looked toward the nursery door.

“There are old passages.”

Aurelia nodded.

“Exactly.”

The crimson hatchling lifted his head.

A simple feeling passed through the Link.

Move.

Zee stirred.

Aurelia looked down.

“Even he knows.”

The witch began gathering supplies.

Neither woman heard the footsteps approaching.

The door opened.

Victor entered.

Alone.

Aurelia stopped.

The witch did not.

She continued folding linen into a travel satchel.

Victor noticed.

“Where are you going?”

Aurelia answered without hesitation.

“With my son.”

“Where?”

“Away from you.”

Victor’s expression tightened.

“Aurelia.”

“You prepared an execution chamber.”

He went still.

The witch stopped packing.

Silence swallowed the room.

Victor looked at her.

“How do you know?”

“Do you think stone servants do not speak?”

“I gave no order to execute him.”

“You prepared for it.”

“That is not the same.”

“It is when the child is two days old.”

Victor stepped closer.

Aurelia moved between him and Zee.

The hatchling rose.

Teal-and-gold mana flickered around his crimson scales.

Victor saw it.

“Move.”

Aurelia did not.

“You are frightening him.”

“He is a newborn.”

“He knows fear.”

Victor looked toward Zee.

The infant stared back with crimson eyes.

No accusation.

No understanding.

Just recognition.

Father.

That simple truth almost undid everything.

Victor’s face softened.

For one moment.

Aurelia saw it.

“Victor…”

His eyes remained on Zee.

“He held my finger.”

Aurelia said nothing.

“He trusted me.”

“He still does.”

Victor swallowed.

“That is the problem.”

“No.”

Aurelia’s voice hardened.

“That is the only thing left worth saving.”

Victor looked at her.

“You heard what the prophecy says.”

“I heard what you told me it says.”

“Every attack may make him harder to kill.”

“You do not know that.”

“He was born under Blood Rain.”

“That is not an answer.”

“Wolves lost control.”

“Not an answer.”

“Vampires felt him in their blood.”

“Still not an answer.”

“The witches—”

“Still.”

“Not.”

“An answer.”

Each word struck harder than the last.

Victor’s voice rose.

“What would satisfy you?”

“Knowing who our son becomes by allowing him to become someone.”

The room fell silent.

Even the hatchling stopped growling.

Aurelia stepped closer.

“You are condemning him for surviving a future that has not happened.”

Victor’s breathing slowed.

“And if I am right?”

“And if you are wrong?”

He had no answer.

Another siege stone struck the castle.

The entire nursery shook.

A crack appeared across one wall.

The hatchling cried out.

Zee startled.

Crimson Mana erupted from him.

Not as an attack.

As instinct.

A wave of red force passed through the nursery.

The falling stones stopped before reaching the cradle.

For one impossible moment, fragments of ceiling hung in the air.

Victor stared.

Aurelia stared.

The witch stared.

Then the stones dropped harmlessly around the room.

Zee began crying.

A true newborn cry.

Small.

Frightened.

Human enough to make Aurelia’s heart break.

She gathered him into her arms immediately.

The hatchling pressed close.

Victor did not move.

His eyes remained on the fallen stone.

The prophecy returned.

Every blade raised against him shall sharpen what it seeks to destroy.

The castle had been struck.

Zee had responded.

Victor saw confirmation.

Aurelia saw a terrified child.

That difference destroyed the last fragile bridge between them.

Victor whispered, “It has started.”

Aurelia looked at him.

“No.”

He backed away.

“You saw it.”

“I saw my son survive falling stone.”

“He stopped it.”

“He was afraid.”

“Exactly.”

Victor’s fear crystallized.

Every danger would teach Zee.

Every attack would reveal more.

Every survival would become something else.

He no longer saw possibility.

He saw escalation.

Aurelia saw the change happen in his face.

“Victor.”

He turned toward the door.

“Lock the nursery.”

The guards outside stiffened.

Aurelia’s expression went cold.

“You will not imprison me.”

“This is not about you.”

“It is now.”

Victor looked toward the royal witch.

“You remain.”

The witch hesitated.

A dangerous mistake.

Victor noticed.

“Is there a problem?”

“No, Your Majesty.”

“Good.”

He stepped into the corridor.

Aurelia called after him.

“What are you going to do?”

Victor stopped.

For several breaths, he faced away from her.

Then he answered.

“What a king must.”

The doors closed.

Locks turned from the outside.

Aurelia rushed forward.

“Victor!”

No answer came.

Only retreating footsteps.

The crimson hatchling pressed against Zee.

Danger.

The feeling crossed the Link more strongly than ever before.

Zee cried harder.

—

Victor descended beneath the western tower.

Alone.

No guards.

No council.

No witnesses.

The execution chamber had been restored.

The stone table stood clean beneath iron chains.

A brazier burned in each corner.

Weapons once used against traitors and enemy kings rested along the wall.

Axes.

Blades.

Hooks.

Iron spikes.

Victor ignored them.

He walked toward the center of the chamber.

There, on a smaller table, sat something newly brought from the royal armory.

A dagger.

Nothing mystical.

Nothing ancient.

Nothing tied to prophecy.

Simple steel.

Victor had chosen it for exactly that reason.

No magic.

No ritual.

No spectacle.

If Zee was only a strange child born beneath terrible omens…

The blade would prove it.

If the prophecy was true…

Victor did not allow himself to finish the thought.

He picked up the dagger.

His hand trembled.

“No foreign king.”

His voice echoed through the chamber.

“No frightened mob.”

“No vampire.”

“No witch.”

“No wolf.”

He stared at the blade.

“If this must be done…”

His breathing became uneven.

“I decide.”

For a moment, he almost dropped it.

Then he remembered the soldier dying in his arms.

The villages burning.

The twelve armies.

The falling stone freezing above the cradle.

Fear won.

Not completely.

Enough.

Victor slipped the dagger beneath his cloak.

Above him, Aurelia pounded against the locked nursery doors.

The royal witch whispered hurriedly over an old hidden passage beneath the floor.

The crimson hatchling stood over Zee, tiny wings spread as wide as his newborn body allowed.

And beneath Castle Darkheart, King Victor Darkheart began walking toward the first murder attempt of Zee’s life.

Not as a foreign invader.

Not as a monster.

As his father.
