Chapter Six

The First Death

The hidden passage beneath the nursery had not been opened in eighty-three years.

Dust filled the narrow stairwell. Ancient roots had pushed between the stones, twisting through the walls like petrified veins. The royal witch knelt beside the concealed entrance with both hands pressed against a faded seal while Queen Aurelia held Zee against her chest.

The crimson hatchling refused to leave him.

He clung to Aurelia’s shoulder with tiny claws, his tail wrapped around the cloth covering Zee. Teal-and-gold mana trembled across his scales whenever footsteps passed beyond the locked nursery doors.

Danger.

The feeling moved through the Dragon Link without words.

Zee felt it.

His crying had stopped.

That frightened Aurelia more.

He simply stared toward the door with wide crimson eyes.

“Can you open it?” she whispered.

The witch gritted her teeth.

“This passage was sealed by one of your husband’s ancestors.”

“Then break it.”

“I am trying.”

Purple mana spread through cracks in the floor. The old seal resisted, not because it possessed greater power, but because it had been woven into the foundations of Castle Darkheart.

Another impact from the siege shook the tower.

Dust fell.

The hatchling hissed.

Aurelia looked toward the nursery door.

“How long?”

“Minutes.”

“We do not have minutes.”

A sound came from the corridor.

Metal sliding against metal.

The locks.

Someone was opening them.

The witch looked over her shoulder.

“My Queen.”

Aurelia knew.

“Keep working.”

The first lock turned.

Then the second.

Then the third.

The witch increased the pressure of her spell.

The floor seal cracked.

Aurelia stepped backward until the cradle pressed against her legs.

The nursery doors opened.

King Victor stood beyond them.

Alone.

His cloak hung over one shoulder.

His face was pale.

His right hand remained hidden beneath the folds of fabric.

Aurelia’s eyes went immediately to it.

“No.”

Victor entered.

The guards outside remained motionless.

“Leave us.”

No one obeyed.

Captain Vale had arrived behind Victor.

He looked from the king to the queen and understood enough.

“My King…”

Victor did not turn.

“I said leave us.”

Vale’s hand rested on his sword.

“Your Majesty, perhaps—”

“Leave.”

The command struck the corridor.

Vale’s jaw tightened.

He bowed.

The guards withdrew with him.

Victor closed the doors himself.

Aurelia stared at him.

“You brought no witnesses.”

“I did not want witnesses.”

The hatchling climbed down from Aurelia’s shoulder and placed himself between Victor and Zee.

He was absurdly small.

His wings barely reached the width of Aurelia’s forearm.

His growl sounded more like a broken purr than a threat.

Victor looked at him anyway.

The Dragon Link flooded with simple instinct.

Protect.

Zee’s Crimson Mana stirred.

Aurelia saw it.

So did Victor.

“Do not,” she whispered.

“I have not done anything.”

“You came here with a weapon.”

Victor froze.

Aurelia’s voice broke.

“I know you.”

His hand emerged from beneath the cloak.

The dagger caught the firelight.

The witch stopped working on the passage.

For several seconds, no one breathed.

Then Aurelia laughed.

Not because anything was funny.

Because grief had become too large for silence.

“You actually brought it.”

Victor looked down at the weapon as though seeing it for the first time.

“Aurelia.”

“You held him.”

“I know.”

“He trusted you.”

“I know.”

“You called him your son.”

“He is my son.”

“Then put the dagger down.”

Victor’s fingers tightened around the hilt.

“I cannot.”

The queen’s face changed.

Whatever remained between husband and wife began dying in that moment.

“You mean you will not.”

Victor swallowed.

“There is a difference between fear and cowardice.”

“You are about to murder a newborn because a piece of bone frightened you.”

“I am about to prevent something none of us may survive.”

“You do not know that.”

“The prophecy—”

“Does not know him.”

“It knew enough.”

“Enough for you to finish the rest yourself.”

Victor stared at her.

She stepped closer.

“You imagined kingdoms burning.”

His face hardened.

“You imagined Zee destroying everything.”

“Aurelia—”

“You imagined him becoming a monster.”

“Stop.”

“And then you decided your imagination was evidence.”

“Stop.”

“You became afraid of what our son might become, so now you are trying to become worse first.”

Victor’s expression broke.

For one heartbeat, the king disappeared.

The father returned.

He looked at Zee.

The infant watched him.

No hatred.

No understanding.

Only recognition.

Victor’s hand began to lower.

Then another siege stone hit the castle.

The wall behind Aurelia split.

The hatchling cried out.

Zee startled.

Crimson Mana erupted.

This time, the force was stronger.

The cracked wall stopped moving.

Falling stone hung motionless for a breath.

Then every fragment shifted away from Aurelia and Zee, striking the opposite side of the room.

The witch stared.

Victor stared.

Zee began crying.

And Victor’s fear returned greater than before.

“You see?”

Aurelia looked at him in disbelief.

“He protected himself.”

“He is two days old.”

“He is terrified.”

“He is two days old!”

Victor shouted it now.

The chamber went still.

“No witch child does that.”

“No vampire child does that.”

“No wolf child does that.”

Aurelia’s voice lowered.

“He is not any one of them.”

Victor flinched.

The words confirmed what everyone already feared.

Three natures.

One child.

The First Tribrid.

Victor looked at the dagger.

Then at Zee.

The prophecy whispered inside his mind.

Every blade raised against him shall sharpen what it seeks to destroy.

He had spent the night fearing that line.

Now he made the cruelest possible decision.

He decided to test it.

Victor stepped forward.

The hatchling lunged.

Tiny teeth sank into Victor’s wrist.

He cursed and ripped his arm back.

Teal-and-gold mana flashed.

Not enough to seriously injure him.

Enough to draw blood.

Victor stared at the hatchling.

The creature stood over Zee.

Protect.

The feeling crossed the Link.

Zee’s crying stopped.

Aurelia saw Victor raise the dagger.

She moved before thought.

Her hand struck his wrist.

The blade missed Zee and sliced across Aurelia’s forearm.

Blood sprayed across the blankets.

Victor froze.

Aurelia did not.

She slapped him.

The sound cracked through the room.

“You cut me.”

Victor stared at the blood.

“I did not mean—”

“No.”

Her voice trembled with rage.

“You meant worse.”

The witch rushed forward.

Victor turned toward her.

“Stay back.”

She stopped.

Not from fear.

From calculation.

Aurelia held Zee tighter.

“You will have to kill me first.”

Victor looked at his wife.

Then his son.

Then the hatchling.

Something inside him shattered.

He hated what he was about to do.

That did not stop him.

“Aurelia…”

Tears filled his eyes.

“Forgive me.”

He struck her with magic.

A dark violet force hit Aurelia across the chest and threw her onto the bed.

Zee slipped from her arms.

The witch screamed.

The hatchling leaped.

Victor caught Zee before he hit the floor.

For one terrible moment…

Father held son again.

Zee stared up at him.

Crimson eyes.

Tiny fangs.

Small hands.

Victor remembered the first time.

He remembered saying my son.

Then Aurelia screamed his name.

“VICTOR!”

He closed his eyes.

And drove the dagger into Zee’s chest.

Silence.

The entire world seemed to stop.

The hatchling shrieked.

A sound too large for his tiny body tore from him as teal-and-gold mana exploded through the nursery.

Aurelia crawled from the bed.

“No.”

Victor opened his eyes.

The dagger remained inside Zee.

Blood spread across the infant’s clothes.

Crimson.

Ordinary-looking.

Terrible.

Zee’s mouth opened.

No cry came.

His heartbeat stumbled.

Once.

Twice.

Then stopped.

Aurelia reached him.

Victor did not resist when she tore Zee from his arms.

She fell to the floor holding her child.

“No.”

Her fingers pressed against the wound.

“Zee.”

Nothing.

The royal witch dropped beside her.

Magic flooded her hands.

Purple light entered the wound.

Nothing happened.

“Again!”

“I am trying!”

“Again!”

The hatchling pushed himself against Zee’s side.

Fear became panic through the Dragon Link.

Where?

Gone?

Come back.

The simple emotions struck something that no newborn should have known how to answer.

But Zee did not move.

Victor stood above them.

Blood covered his hand.

His son’s blood.

He had done it.

The room blurred.

“I…”

Aurelia looked up.

The grief in her face became hatred.

“You killed him.”

Victor’s lips parted.

No words came.

Outside…

The siege stopped.

Not gradually.

All at once.

Every wolf across the northern forests collapsed.

Vampires across the world clutched their chests as the impossible heartbeat disappeared completely.

Witches everywhere felt a pressure vanish that they had not realized still lingered since Zee’s birth.

The blood-soaked clouds above Castle Darkheart turned black.

The world did not know what had happened.

It only felt the absence.

Inside the nursery, the hatchling pressed his forehead against Zee’s.

His entire body shook.

Teal-and-gold mana wrapped helplessly around the dead infant.

Aurelia sobbed.

The witch continued healing a heart that no longer beat.

Victor stared at the prophecy fulfilled by his own hand.

Or so he believed.

Then Zee’s blood moved.

One drop crawled backward across his skin.

The witch stopped.

Aurelia did not notice.

Another drop rose from the blanket.

Then another.

Victor’s face drained of color.

The blood gathered around the dagger wound.

Not flowing outward.

Returning.

The torn flesh began closing.

Slowly.

Wrongly.

Beautifully.

Zee’s tiny fingers twitched.

The crimson hatchling froze.

A feeling crossed the Link.

There.

Aurelia gasped.

“Zee?”

The infant inhaled.

The breath came violently.

His back arched.

Crimson Mana exploded through the nursery with enough force to throw every adult backward.

Victor struck the wall.

The witch crashed into the floor.

Aurelia held onto Zee with everything she had.

The dagger tore free from his chest by itself and clattered across the stone.

Zee screamed.

This time the cry was not quiet.

It rolled through Castle Darkheart.

Across the walls.

Across the battlefield.

Across forests and mountains and buried vampire halls.

His heartbeat returned.

Once.

The vampires felt it.

Twice.

The wolves lifted their heads.

Three times.

Every witch inside Castle Darkheart felt their magic shudder beneath the sudden pressure.

Zee’s wound vanished.

Completely.

No scar remained.

But something had changed.

His Crimson Mana was denser now.

Not vastly stronger.

Not transformed into some understood new state.

Simply different.

As though his body had encountered death…

And refused to remember how to remain dead.

Victor stared from the floor.

The prophecy whispered again.

Every blade raised against him shall sharpen what it seeks to destroy.

He finally understood the horror of his mistake.

He had not prevented the prophecy.

He had become the first blade.

Aurelia rose with Zee in her arms.

The hatchling climbed against him immediately.

His tiny body pressed around Zee as though he could physically prevent death from returning.

Zee’s crying softened.

The Dragon Link carried one feeling between them.

Safe.

Victor slowly stood.

Aurelia looked at him.

“Do not come closer.”

He stopped.

The king’s face had become ash.

“I killed him.”

“Yes.”

“He came back.”

“Yes.”

Victor stared at Zee.

Fear unlike anything he had ever known entered his eyes.

Not because Zee had attacked him.

Not because Zee had threatened the kingdom.

Because Victor had just killed his own newborn son…

And death had failed to keep him.

The witch whispered,

“What is he?”

Aurelia looked at her sharply.

“No.”

The woman fell silent.

No one would answer that question tonight.

No one possessed the right.

No one possessed the knowledge.

Outside, foreign soldiers stared toward Castle Darkheart as the infant’s scream faded through the air.

The armies did not know what had happened inside.

They only knew that for several moments, the impossible presence they had feared had vanished.

Then returned.

Stronger.

And inside the nursery, King Victor Darkheart looked at the blood on his hands and realized that the first person to kill Zee…

Had also become the first person to teach his body how to survive death.

Chapter Seven

The Child Who Returned

No one moved for several heartbeats.

Queen Aurelia stood in the center of the ruined nursery with Zee clutched against her chest. The crimson hatchling pressed against the child as though his tiny body alone could keep death away. The eldest royal witch remained on one knee, staring at the place where the dagger wound had been.

There was no wound now.

No scar.

Only clean newborn skin beneath torn fabric and fresh blood.

King Victor Darkheart looked at his hands.

They would not stop shaking.

He had killed his son.

He knew exactly what he had felt when the dagger entered Zee’s chest. The resistance of bone. The terrible softness beyond it. The warmth of blood running across his fingers.

He had watched the child’s heartbeat stop.

And then he had watched death lose him.

Victor took one step forward.

Aurelia backed away immediately.

“Do not.”

Her voice was quiet.

That made it worse.

Victor stopped.

“Aurelia…”

“You do not get to say my name like nothing happened.”

“I know.”

“No. You do not.”

Zee stirred against her.

His crimson eyes remained open.

No golden light had entered them. No transformation announced what had happened. He was still visibly the same newborn child who had existed moments earlier.

But Aurelia could feel the difference.

His breathing had steadied far too quickly.

His heartbeat had returned stronger than before.

And his Crimson Mana now clung closer to his body, less like random leakage and more like something that had learned where danger came from.

The royal witch noticed too.

She opened her mouth.

Then remembered what had happened when everyone tried to explain Zee.

She said nothing.

Victor looked at his son.

“Is he hurt?”

Aurelia laughed once.

It was hollow.

“You are asking me if the child you stabbed is hurt?”

Victor flinched.

The hatchling hissed.

Teal-and-gold mana shimmered over his crimson scales.

Danger.

The feeling passed through the Dragon Link.

Zee responded with simple unease.

Aurelia felt him tense.

The hatchling moved closer.

Safe.

The answer came without words.

Zee relaxed.

Victor watched it happen.

Even now, part of him searched for meaning.

He hated that part.

He hated that the prophecy had taught him to look at every movement and wonder whether it proved something.

The witch finally stood.

“My Queen, we need to move.”

Aurelia looked toward her.

“The passage?”

“Opened.”

Victor’s eyes sharpened.

“What passage?”

No one answered.

He understood anyway.

“You planned to flee.”

Aurelia’s expression hardened.

“I planned to survive you.”

The words cut deeper than any blade.

Victor looked toward the broken nursery wall.

Beyond it came the distant thunder of the siege.

For several seconds, he appeared almost exhausted enough to collapse.

Then the king returned.

“You cannot leave the castle.”

Aurelia stared at him.

“Watch me.”

“There are armies outside every road.”

“Then I will find another road.”

“You do not understand what waits beyond these walls.”

“I understand exactly what waits inside them.”

Victor’s face tightened.

“Aurelia, listen to me.”

“No.”

“This is larger than us.”

“You made it larger than us when you put a dagger in our son.”

“I was trying to prevent—”

“You were trying to control what you feared.”

Victor fell silent.

Because she was right.

Aurelia adjusted Zee against her chest and moved toward the hidden passage.

Victor stepped into her path.

The crimson hatchling growled immediately.

Zee’s mana pulsed.

Victor saw it.

Then, slowly, he moved aside.

Aurelia stopped.

She had expected a fight.

Victor looked at Zee one last time.

“I do not know what to do with this.”

Aurelia’s voice softened only slightly.

“Then do nothing.”

His eyes lifted to hers.

“For once, do nothing.”

She entered the hidden passage.

The witch followed.

The hatchling remained with Zee.

Victor stood alone in the nursery.

A few moments later, the stone floor slid back into place.

His family was gone.

He had never felt more like a king.

He had never felt less like a father.

⸻

Outside Castle Darkheart, the battlefield had changed.

The attacking armies had heard Zee’s scream.

Not all of them recognized it as a child.

Some thought the fortress had unleashed a weapon.

Others claimed a demon had awakened.

Still others swore the earth itself had cried out.

The truth reached no one.

Only rumor did.

A line of soldiers from the southern kingdoms refused to advance.

Their commander rode before them.

“Forward!”

No one moved.

The commander drew his sword.

“I said forward!”

One soldier pointed toward Castle Darkheart.

“We felt it stop.”

The commander’s expression hardened.

“What?”

“The thing.”

Another soldier whispered, “Whatever was born there.”

The men around him nodded.

“For a moment it was gone.”

“And then it came back.”

The commander looked toward the castle.

He had felt it too.

He refused to admit that.

“Fear is not permission to abandon formation.”

A soldier near the front crossed himself.

“That was not fear.”

The commander raised his sword.

“It was an order.”

An arrow came from the walls.

It struck him through the neck.

The formation broke.

Not into retreat.

Into chaos.

The kingdoms had marched together because they feared the same newborn.

Now they could not agree on what the newborn had become.

⸻

Deep beneath the eastern mountains, vampires gathered in silence.

The impossible heartbeat had vanished.

Then returned.

That disturbed them more than anything before it.

One ancient vampire paced the edge of the blood chamber.

“It died.”

Another shook his head.

“You do not know that.”

“I felt it disappear.”

“And now?”

The first vampire stopped.

The heartbeat remained distant.

Steady.

Unfamiliar.

Present.

He whispered, “Now it is back.”

No one spoke.

An elder seated in the shadows finally said, “Then we have learned nothing.”

A younger vampire looked toward him.

“Nothing?”

“Nothing except that whatever happened in Castle Darkheart has become more dangerous to misunderstand.”

That was the closest anyone came to wisdom.

⸻

In the northern forests, the wolves changed direction.

Not all of them.

Not together.

But enough for hunters to notice.

Some packs that had spent the night tearing through villages suddenly retreated into the wilderness. Others began circling paths leading toward Darkheart territory. A few simply lay down and refused to move.

No alpha could explain it.

No shaman could interpret it.

The madness remained.

But beneath it, instinct had begun searching for something.

⸻

Beneath Castle Darkheart, Aurelia moved through darkness.

The hidden passage was narrow enough that her shoulders brushed the walls. The witch walked ahead with a small blue flame floating above her palm, guiding them deeper through forgotten stone.

Zee slept again.

Aurelia could not understand how.

She had watched him die.

Every time she closed her eyes, she saw the dagger.

Every time she opened them, he was alive.

Her mind could not reconcile the two truths.

The crimson hatchling remained awake.

He had not looked away from Zee since the resurrection.

His fear had changed too.

He now reacted to every footstep, every shift in the stone, every breath from the witch.

The Dragon Link carried the same simple intention again and again.

Stay.

Stay.

Stay.

Zee responded with warmth.

Near.

The hatchling relaxed only slightly.

The witch glanced back.

“My Queen.”

“What?”

“There is something ahead.”

Aurelia stopped.

The passage opened into an older tunnel.

Not a royal corridor.

Something beneath that.

The walls were rough.

Unworked.

Ancient roots had cracked through the stone.

Cold air moved from somewhere deeper underground.

The witch raised her flame.

A figure stood at the far end of the tunnel.

Aurelia’s body went rigid.

The hatchling growled.

The figure lifted both hands slowly.

“I am not armed.”

The voice belonged to a man.

Aurelia narrowed her eyes.

“Who are you?”

He stepped into the blue light.

Dark travel clothes.

Gray hair.

A scar beneath one eye.

No royal crest.

No obvious weapon.

He looked first at Aurelia.

Then at Zee.

His expression changed.

Not recognition.

Shock.

Fear.

Exactly what everyone else felt.

“Is that him?”

Aurelia stepped back.

“You have one chance to answer me.”

The man lowered his eyes.

“My name is Ser Caldrin Marr.”

The witch stiffened.

Aurelia noticed.

“You know him?”

“By reputation.”

“That is rarely good.”

Caldrin gave a humorless smile.

“No.”

He looked toward the passage behind them.

“You cannot continue east.”

“Why?”

“Foreign scouts found the old drainage tunnels hours ago.”

Aurelia’s grip tightened around Zee.

“How do you know?”

“Because I killed the three men who found them.”

Silence.

The hatchling watched him.

Caldrin looked toward Zee again.

He did not kneel.

He did not praise him.

He did not pretend to understand him.

“What happened up there?”

Aurelia’s expression hardened.

“Nothing you need to know.”

Caldrin studied the blood on her clothes.

Then the torn fabric around Zee’s chest.

He understood enough.

“The king?”

Aurelia said nothing.

That was answer enough.

Caldrin exhaled.

“Then Castle Darkheart has two enemies now.”

The witch looked toward him.

“What do you want?”

“To survive the siege.”

“And helping us does that?”

“No.”

“Then why?”

Caldrin’s gaze shifted toward Zee.

“Because I have seen kings kill children for less.”

Aurelia held his stare.

He continued.

“And I have buried enough of them.”

The tunnel shook from another impact above.

Dust fell.

Caldrin looked toward the ceiling.

“You have minutes before the eastern passages become unusable.”

Aurelia made a decision.

“Show us another way.”

The witch looked at her.

“My Queen—”

“If he wanted Zee dead, he had opportunity before announcing himself.”

Caldrin nodded once.

“There is a route beneath the old burial vaults.”

Aurelia’s face hardened.

“Victor uses those.”

“Not the oldest ones.”

He turned.

“Follow me.”

They moved deeper beneath the castle.

⸻

Victor did not discover the empty nursery for long.

He had remained there after Aurelia fled, staring at the blood-covered dagger on the floor.

Eventually Captain Vale entered.

The captain stopped upon seeing the room.

Blood.

Broken stone.

No queen.

No prince.

No dragon.

His eyes went to Victor.

“What happened?”

Victor did not answer.

Vale looked at the dagger.

Then at the blood on Victor’s sleeve.

Understanding came slowly.

His expression changed from confusion to horror.

“You did it.”

Victor looked up.

Vale’s voice lowered.

“You actually did it.”

“He survived.”

The captain stared.

Victor repeated it.

“He survived.”

Vale looked toward the empty cradle.

“You stabbed him?”

“Yes.”

“And he survived?”

“He died.”

Silence.

Victor’s voice cracked.

“Then he came back.”

Captain Vale took one step away from his king.

For the first time in all their years together, the movement was not tactical.

It was fear.

Not of Zee.

Of Victor.

“You killed your own son.”

Victor’s jaw tightened.

“I know.”

“No.”

Vale shook his head.

“You keep saying that as if knowledge is punishment enough.”

Victor stepped toward him.

“Careful.”

The captain laughed.

It was bitter.

“There it is.”

“What?”

“The king.”

Victor’s eyes narrowed.

“You hide behind him whenever the father cannot survive what he has done.”

The words struck.

Vale did not stop.

“Twelve kingdoms came here to murder your child.”

“I know.”

“And you decided to beat them to it.”

“That is not what happened.”

“That is exactly what happened.”

Victor’s voice rose.

“You did not hear the prophecy.”

“No.”

“You did not watch him stop falling stone.”

“No.”

“You did not feel the world change when he was born.”

Vale stared at him.

“Neither did you understand any of it.”

Victor froze.

Vale continued.

“You feared what you could not explain.”

“And now?”

“Now your wife has fled with your heir.”

Victor’s face hardened.

“Find her.”

Vale did not move.

“Captain.”

“You want me to bring them back?”

“Yes.”

“For protection?”

Victor said nothing.

Vale laughed again.

“I thought so.”

The king stepped closer.

“You will obey.”

The captain held his gaze.

“For House Darkheart?”

“Yes.”

Vale’s expression changed.

“Then I will find the queen.”

Victor relaxed slightly.

Vale continued.

“But I will not deliver that child to your execution chamber.”

The room went still.

Victor’s voice became cold.

“You are refusing your king.”

“I am serving my kingdom.”

“You do not decide what that means.”

“Neither do prophecies carved into dead bone.”

Victor’s hand went to his sword.

Vale’s did not.

For several seconds, the two men stood facing one another.

Then the eastern tower shook violently.

A horn screamed from outside.

A soldier rushed into the nursery.

“My King!”

Victor turned.

“The eastern wall has been breached.”

Everything changed.

Kingdom before family.

War before fear.

Victor drew his sword.

“How large?”

“Not enough for cavalry. Infantry are forcing through.”

Victor looked toward Vale.

“Find Aurelia.”

Then he ran for the walls.

Vale watched him go.

He waited until the footsteps disappeared.

Then he looked at the hidden passage.

“Find the queen.”

The soldier beside him waited.

“Sir?”

Vale’s eyes hardened.

“We are going to.”

He moved toward the passage.

“But not for the king.”

⸻

The breach became a slaughter.

Foreign soldiers poured through a gap barely wide enough for three men at once.

Darkheart defenders met them with spears.

Bodies piled until the dead became part of the barricade.

Victor entered the fighting without hesitation.

His sword cut through the first invader’s shoulder.

Dark violet magic blasted another into broken stone.

A third reached him with an axe.

Victor ducked and drove his blade beneath the man’s ribs.

Blood covered the king.

Again.

Different blood.

That mattered less than it should have.

The High Marshal shouted from above.

“They are widening the breach!”

“Collapse the upper wall!”

“Our men are beneath it!”

“Move them!”

“There is no time!”

Victor looked toward the breach.

More enemy soldiers were coming.

If they entered the inner courtyard, the siege would become street fighting.

Thousands of civilians waited beyond the second gate.

Victor made the decision.

“Collapse it.”

The marshal stared.

“My King—”

“Do it!”

Darkheart witches raised their hands.

Purple and blue mana struck the damaged tower supports.

Stone cracked.

Defenders realized what was happening.

Some escaped.

Many did not.

The eastern wall collapsed.

The breach vanished beneath thousands of tons of black stone.

Enemy soldiers screamed beneath it.

So did Darkheart men.

Then silence.

Victor stood in the dust.

The castle held.

At terrible cost.

His generals looked at him.

Some with loyalty.

Some with fear.

Victor understood something then.

A king survived by making choices other men could not.

He had always believed that.

The danger was how easily that belief could excuse anything.

He looked toward the tower where his son had been.

Empty now.

For one moment, the prophecy became distant.

He saw only Aurelia’s face.

You are condemning him for surviving a future that has not happened.

Victor closed his eyes.

Then a scout approached.

“My King.”

Victor turned.

“What?”

“We found blood in the lower passages.”

His heart stopped.

“Whose?”

“We do not know.”

Victor began moving before the scout finished.

“Take me there.”

⸻

Deep below, Caldrin led Aurelia through a narrow burial tunnel.

The air had grown colder.

The witch’s blue flame flickered.

Behind them, distant footsteps echoed.

Someone was following.

Caldrin stopped.

“Give me the child.”

Aurelia’s eyes turned murderous.

“No.”

“So I can fight.”

“I said no.”

The hatchling growled.

Caldrin looked at him.

“I am beginning to understand why everyone likes you.”

The dragon hissed.

The witch whispered, “They are closer.”

Caldrin drew a short sword from beneath his cloak.

Aurelia looked at him.

“You said you were unarmed.”

“I said it when I needed you not to stab me.”

Despite everything, she almost laughed.

Almost.

The footsteps approached.

Caldrin moved forward.

Then a familiar voice echoed through the tunnel.

“My Queen.”

Aurelia froze.

Captain Vale stepped into the blue light.

Three guards stood behind him.

Caldrin raised his sword.

Vale drew his own.

Aurelia moved between them.

“Stop.”

Vale looked toward Zee.

Relief crossed his face.

“He is alive.”

Aurelia’s expression darkened.

“You know.”

“The king told me.”

The hatchling growled.

Vale lowered his sword.

“I am not here for him.”

Aurelia studied him.

“Then why are you here?”

“To get you out.”

She said nothing.

Vale continued.

“The eastern wall nearly fell. Victor is occupied.”

“For now.”

“Yes.”

“And afterward?”

Vale looked toward Zee.

“Afterward, the king will search every stone in this kingdom.”

Caldrin frowned.

“Then we need to leave Darkheart territory.”

Vale shook his head.

“Impossible tonight.”

“Then what?”

“There is one place Victor will not search immediately.”

Aurelia’s eyes narrowed.

“Where?”

Vale looked deeper into the tunnel.

“The old enemy crypts.”

The witch’s expression changed.

“Those were sealed after the Black Winter.”

“Exactly.”

Caldrin looked between them.

“What is inside?”

Vale answered quietly.

“Things House Darkheart preferred buried.”

Aurelia looked down at Zee.

The child slept.

Alive.

For now.

She had a kingdom outside trying to kill him.

A husband inside who already had.

And beneath her feet waited something the Darkhearts themselves had once feared enough to seal away.

Aurelia looked up.

“Take us there.”

The witch stared at her.

“My Queen.”

“We are out of safe choices.”

Vale nodded.

They moved.

Behind them, far through the passage, another set of footsteps entered the tunnels.

Victor had found the blood trail.

And this time, he was not carrying a dagger.

He was carrying a sword.

Chapter Eight

The World Comes Below

The old enemy crypts had not been opened since the Black Winter.

Captain Vale broke the first seal with the pommel of his sword.

The sound echoed through the buried corridor like a hammer striking a coffin.

Dust poured from the archway.

Queen Aurelia stood behind him with Zee held tightly against her chest while the crimson hatchling pressed along her shoulder, his small claws tangled in the queen’s cloak. The royal witch kept one hand raised, blue-violet mana trembling around her fingers as she listened for movement beyond the stone.

Ser Caldrin Marr watched the darkness.

“Why were these sealed?”

Vale pushed against the ancient door.

“Because House Darkheart won the war.”

Caldrin glanced at him. “That does not answer the question.”

“No.”

The stone groaned.

Vale shoved harder.

“Because what we defeated refused to stay defeated.”

The door opened.

Cold air rushed over them.

The hatchling lifted his head immediately.

Fear passed through the Dragon Link.

Not the sharp terror he had felt when Zee disappeared.

Something older.

Something waiting.

Zee stirred against Aurelia.

His crimson eyes opened.

The queen looked down.

“It is all right.”

She no longer believed those words when she said them.

But Zee recognized her voice.

That was enough.

For now.

They entered.

The crypt was enormous.

Far larger than anything that should have existed beneath Castle Darkheart.

Columns disappeared into darkness overhead. Broken statues lined a sunken avenue, each depicting warriors whose faces had been deliberately carved away. Rusted chains hung from walls covered in dead runes. In the distance, black water reflected the witch’s spell-light without revealing how deep it went.

Caldrin stopped.

“This is not a crypt.”

Vale looked ahead.

“No.”

“What is it?”

“A prison.”

Aurelia’s eyes hardened.

“You brought my son into a prison?”

“I brought him somewhere Victor would hesitate to enter.”

“That is not the same as safe.”

“There is no safe.”

The answer silenced them.

That truth had followed Zee since the sky began bleeding.

A sound came from somewhere beyond the columns.

Stone scraping stone.

The hatchling growled.

Vale raised his sword.

Caldrin drew his own.

The royal witch strengthened her light.

Aurelia held Zee closer.

“Move.”

They continued deeper.

Behind them, far above, Castle Darkheart remained at war.

And beneath it…

Something had begun waking.

⸻

King Victor reached the lower passage minutes later.

He found blood first.

Aurelia’s.

Drops marked the old stones where the wound on her arm had reopened during the escape.

Victor crouched beside one.

His expression tightened.

Captain Vale had betrayed him.

Aurelia had fled.

His son had been taken into the oldest foundations of the castle.

Every part of him wanted to pursue.

Then he remembered the dagger.

The stillness after Zee’s heartbeat stopped.

The impossible breath that followed.

Victor’s hand closed around the hilt of his sword.

He would not do that again.

That certainty had formed the moment Zee returned.

Not from mercy alone.

Fear had changed shape.

Victor no longer feared only what Zee might become if allowed to live.

He now feared what trying to kill him might create.

The prophecy had warned him.

He had tested it.

Once.

That mistake would not be repeated.

But he would not allow Aurelia to disappear with something that could bring twelve kingdoms down upon House Darkheart either.

Victor rose.

“Seal every tunnel leading beyond the castle.”

The soldiers behind him exchanged glances.

“My King?”

“You heard me.”

“What about the queen?”

“She remains within Darkheart territory.”

“And the prince?”

Victor’s face hardened.

“Especially the prince.”

The commander bowed.

Victor looked into the darkness ahead.

“Send men through the southern passages.”

“How many?”

Victor considered.

Then stopped himself.

Not an army.

Not near Zee.

“Six.”

The commander looked surprised.

“Only six?”

“I said six.”

Victor stared into the tunnel.

“Do not attack the child.”

The soldiers went still.

Victor’s next words came colder.

“Do not provoke him.”

That order spread through the castle before sunset.

The king who had been the first person to kill Zee now became the first ruler to warn his own soldiers against attempting it again.

Not because he had accepted his son.

Because he had learned to fear the result.

⸻

Outside Castle Darkheart, the foreign armies learned something else.

The siege was failing.

Not because House Darkheart was stronger.

Because the coalition was beginning to fracture.

The twelve kingdoms had agreed that the child needed to die.

They had not agreed on who should control what remained afterward.

Some wanted the body burned.

Others wanted it studied.

One vampire-backed kingdom demanded the blood.

A northern wolf king wanted proof that the newborn’s existence had caused the madness among his packs.

Three witch courts wanted the child alive long enough to examine the strange mana witnessed during the birth.

The moment survival became politics…

Unity began dying.

Inside the largest command tent, King Orsik of Dunmere slammed his gauntlet onto a wooden table.

“We breach the western wall tonight.”

A foreign general shook his head.

“And lose another two thousand men.”

“Then lose them.”

“They are not your soldiers.”

“They will be dead either way if that creature grows.”

Across the table, Lady Maevra of the Ash Coven watched them with visible contempt.

“You continue calling him a creature because it makes your fear sound noble.”

Orsik glared at her.

“You lost your magic when he was born.”

“No.”

The witch’s expression sharpened.

“I could not reach it.”

“That distinction will comfort the dead?”

“It comforts truth.”

“Truth is that something happened.”

“Yes.”

“And the child was at its center.”

“Perhaps.”

Orsik laughed.

“You witches hide cowardice behind uncertainty.”

Maevra leaned forward.

“And kings hide stupidity behind certainty.”

Hands moved toward weapons.

A vampire envoy seated near the rear of the tent smiled.

This was more familiar.

Fear dividing prey.

King Orsik noticed.

“You find this amusing?”

The vampire’s smile faded.

“No.”

“You people felt him.”

The tent grew quieter.

The vampire looked toward Castle Darkheart.

“Yes.”

“What did you feel?”

He considered lying.

Instead, he said, “A heartbeat that did not belong inside my blood.”

“Whose?”

“I do not know.”

“Was it the child?”

“I do not know.”

Orsik struck the table again.

“Does anyone know anything?”

No one answered.

That was the truth none of them wanted.

They had marched thousands of soldiers across kingdoms to destroy something they did not understand.

Then a runner entered.

“My lords.”

Orsik turned.

“What?”

“Movement beneath the eastern ridge.”

“How many?”

“We do not know.”

“Darkheart troops?”

The runner hesitated.

“No.”

The vampire envoy stood.

“What did you see?”

The soldier swallowed.

“Something came out of the ground.”

⸻

In the enemy crypts, Aurelia heard the first scream.

It came from ahead.

Human.

Short.

Then silence.

Vale stopped walking.

“That was not one of ours.”

Caldrin looked back. “You sound disappointed.”

“It means someone else found another entrance.”

The witch dimmed her light.

“How?”

“Siege damage,” Vale said. “Or the foreigners knew more about the old tunnels than we thought.”

Aurelia looked down at Zee.

The child remained awake.

Too awake.

His crimson eyes moved slowly through the darkness.

The hatchling’s body had gone rigid.

Danger.

Closer now.

Not one thing.

Many.

Vale whispered, “Stay behind me.”

Aurelia almost laughed.

“Everyone keeps saying that.”

This time, she obeyed.

They entered a wider chamber.

Bodies covered the floor.

Foreign scouts.

Six, perhaps seven.

All dead.

No visible wounds.

Their faces were frozen in expressions of terror.

Caldrin crouched beside one.

“No blood.”

The witch stepped closer.

“What killed them?”

Caldrin turned the body.

Nothing.

No cuts.

No broken bones.

No burns.

Vale looked toward the far side of the chamber.

An ancient door stood open.

Black mist crawled beneath it.

“That.”

Aurelia’s voice lowered.

“What was imprisoned here?”

Vale did not answer.

She looked at him.

“Captain.”

“My grandfather called them Hollow Men.”

Caldrin stood.

“That sounds comforting.”

“They are not men.”

The mist thickened.

The royal witch raised both hands.

Violet mana gathered around her.

“What are they?”

Vale’s grip tightened around his sword.

“Things that learned how to wear people.”

The first one stepped through the doorway.

It wore the body of a dead soldier.

Almost.

Its joints bent incorrectly.

Its smile stretched too far.

Its eyes were empty black pits.

The hatchling screamed.

Zee’s Crimson Mana surged.

The Hollow thing stopped.

For the first time, it looked uncertain.

Then more shapes emerged behind it.

Three.

Five.

Nine.

Caldrin whispered, “How many did your ancestors bury?”

Vale answered without taking his eyes off them.

“Enough.”

The first creature rushed forward.

Vale met it with steel.

His sword passed through its chest.

The body folded around the blade as though empty.

Then one black hand closed around his throat.

Caldrin struck from the side.

The creature twisted toward him.

The royal witch released a blast of violet force.

The Hollow thing flew backward and struck a column.

It stood immediately.

“Magic works,” she said.

“Not well enough,” Vale choked.

The others came.

Aurelia backed toward the wall.

The hatchling spread his tiny wings.

Teal-and-gold mana flashed violently around him.

One Hollow creature turned toward Zee.

Everything changed.

The thing ignored the adults.

It moved toward the child.

Aurelia felt the shift instantly.

“No.”

The witch stepped between them and cast.

A binding spell wrapped around the creature’s limbs.

It tore through the spell.

Caldrin intercepted it.

Its hand struck his chest and threw him across the chamber.

Vale cut through another.

Two more replaced it.

The Hollow creature kept coming.

Zee watched.

He did not understand monsters.

He understood Aurelia’s fear.

He understood the hatchling’s panic.

He understood something approaching.

Danger.

His heartbeat accelerated.

Crimson Mana thickened around him.

The creature reached.

The hatchling lunged first.

Newborn claws struck its face.

Teal-and-gold Dragon Mana burst against black flesh.

For the first time…

The Hollow creature screamed.

Not from pain.

From recognition.

The sound stopped everyone.

The creature recoiled from the hatchling.

Then looked at Zee again.

Something in its stolen face changed.

Hunger.

Aurelia saw it.

“Get away from him!”

The Hollow thing attacked.

Zee’s Crimson Mana erupted.

Not outward.

Inward.

Across his skin.

The creature’s hand touched him.

Then froze.

Blackness spread across Zee’s blanket.

Aurelia screamed.

The witch reached for the creature.

“Do not touch it!”

Too late.

The Hollow thing began draining something from Zee.

Not blood.

Not mana alone.

Warmth.

Life.

The child’s body went cold against Aurelia.

The Dragon Link exploded with terror.

Gone?

No.

No.

Stay.

The hatchling bit into the Hollow creature’s wrist.

Teal-and-gold mana flooded through the contact.

The creature shrieked again.

Zee reacted.

Instinct met threat.

His vampire nature reached first.

Tiny fangs extended.

Aurelia felt him turn.

Before she could understand what he was doing, Zee bit down into the Hollow creature’s hand.

The chamber went silent.

The creature convulsed.

Black essence flowed toward Zee.

Not willingly.

The Hollow thing tried to pull away.

It could not.

Crimson Mana wrapped around its arm.

The essence entered Zee.

His body seized.

Aurelia nearly dropped him.

“Zee!”

The creature collapsed.

Its stolen human shape withered inward until nothing remained but black ash.

Everyone stared.

Zee released the dead hand.

His crimson eyes remained open.

Something dark moved briefly beneath his skin.

Then Crimson Mana consumed it.

The blackness vanished.

Zee inhaled sharply.

Warmth returned to his body.

The witch stared in horror.

“What did he just—”

“Do not,” Aurelia snapped.

No explanations.

Not now.

The remaining Hollow creatures stopped attacking.

Every one of them looked toward Zee.

Then they retreated.

Not from the adults.

From him.

Vale watched them disappear beyond the ancient doorway.

Caldrin pushed himself upright, one hand pressed against his ribs.

“That seems bad.”

Aurelia looked down at her son.

Zee was breathing normally again.

Yet his Crimson Mana had changed.

Only slightly.

A thin black-red edge now appeared whenever it moved across his skin.

Gone within seconds.

Present long enough to be real.

The hatchling pressed his forehead against Zee.

Safe?

Zee’s tiny hand found him.

Safe.

For the moment.

The royal witch approached carefully.

“My Queen.”

“No theories.”

“I was going to say we need to leave.”

Aurelia looked toward the open doorway.

The Hollow creatures had vanished.

Vale wiped blood from his mouth.

“They will come back.”

Caldrin frowned. “Why?”

Vale looked at Zee.

“Because everything does.”

⸻

By nightfall, the story escaped the crypts.

Not the truth.

Never the truth.

A wounded foreign scout reached the coalition camp babbling about dead men walking beneath Castle Darkheart.

Another claimed a crimson-eyed infant had devoured a shadow.

A third insisted the dragon hatchling breathed gold fire.

None of them had seen the same thing.

None of them agreed.

That did not stop the rumors.

The child had survived death.

The child commanded monsters.

The child ate souls.

The child had awakened something under the castle.

Every retelling became worse.

Kingdoms that had marched to destroy Zee became more determined.

Others became afraid to approach him at all.

The first bounty appeared that night.

Not from a king.

From merchants.

Ten thousand silver crowns for proof of Zee Darkheart’s death.

Twenty thousand if the body remained intact.

By morning, assassins would hear.

By the end of the week, hunters would come.

Not armies.

Individuals.

Patient people.

Cruel people.

People who did not care about prophecies or kingdoms.

Only payment.

The world had learned something from the siege.

Armies were too loud.

Fear would become clever next.

⸻

Aurelia emerged from the lower crypts shortly before dawn.

Not into Castle Darkheart.

Into the forest beyond the western cliffs.

Captain Vale had known one forgotten exit.

The tunnel opened behind a waterfall half a mile from the fortress walls.

Cold dawn air struck Aurelia’s face.

She stopped.

For the first time since Zee was born, there was no ceiling above him.

No castle.

No nursery.

No execution chamber.

Only sky.

The hatchling looked upward.

He had never seen open sky either.

His tiny wings spread instinctively.

Teal-and-gold mana shimmered around him.

Zee followed his movement.

The Dragon Link carried something new.

Wonder.

Aurelia felt tears rise unexpectedly.

Caldrin emerged behind them.

“We cannot remain here.”

She knew.

The armies were east.

Darkheart patrols were everywhere.

Assassins would come soon.

Victor would search.

The world would keep moving.

Aurelia looked toward Castle Darkheart in the distance.

Smoke rose from its broken towers.

Her kingdom.

Her husband.

Her home.

All behind her.

She looked down at Zee.

His crimson eyes stared up at the bleeding colors of sunrise.

He had lived three days.

In those three days, the heavens had rained blood.

The world had marched against him.

His father had killed him.

He had returned.

And something buried beneath House Darkheart had already tried to consume him.

Aurelia tightened the blanket around him.

“Your life will not always be this.”

Vale looked away.

Caldrin said nothing.

Even Aurelia knew it was a lie.

The hatchling curled against Zee.

The Dragon Link carried a simple feeling between them.

Go.

Aurelia looked west.

Beyond the mountains lay kingdoms that had not yet chosen whether to fear Zee.

Among them…

One kingdom had refused to send soldiers to Castle Darkheart.

House Vesper.

Aurelia did not know whether that meant safety.

She had stopped believing in safety.

But it meant a direction.

“West,” she said.

Vale nodded.

Caldrin adjusted his sword.

The witch pulled up her hood.

Behind them, Castle Darkheart continued burning beneath siege fire.

Ahead, the ancient world waited.

And for the first time, Zee Darkheart left the kingdom of his birth.

Not as a prince beginning a royal journey.

As a hunted child.

The world had tried an army.

It had failed.

Now it would begin sending everything else.

Chapter Nine

The Road of Teeth

The western road had been abandoned before Aurelia ever reached it.

That was the first thing Captain Vale noticed.

No merchants.

No pilgrims.

No wagons.

No patrols from nearby villages.

Only wheel ruts hardened in old mud and a line of overturned carts left beneath a stand of black pines.

Caldrin crouched beside one of them.

“Too clean.”

Aurelia shifted Zee higher against her shoulder.

“What does that mean?”

“No bodies.”

The royal witch scanned the tree line.

“Maybe whoever attacked them took the dead.”

Caldrin stood.

“Maybe.”

The crimson hatchling pressed against Zee beneath Aurelia’s cloak.

The two had grown quieter since leaving Castle Darkheart.

Not calmer.

More aware.

The Dragon Link had begun carrying new flashes between them.

Not words.

Shapes.

Cold.

Movement.

The direction of fear.

Zee turned his head toward the forest.

The hatchling did the same.

Vale saw it.

“You both felt something?”

The hatchling’s scales tightened along his spine.

Zee’s Crimson Mana stirred.

Caldrin drew his sword.

That was answer enough.

Something moved between the trees.

Fast.

Low.

Then another shape crossed behind it.

Aurelia stopped.

“How many?”

Vale whispered, “Pack.”

The first wolf stepped onto the road.

It was enormous.

Larger than any natural wolf.

Its fur was gray-black and soaked with old blood. One ear had been torn away. Its yellow eyes fixed on Zee before moving to the dragon hatchling.

Then came the second.

Third.

Sixth.

Tenth.

The pack spread across the road and tree line until retreat vanished.

The royal witch raised both hands.

Violet mana gathered around her wrists.

“Werewolves?”

Vale studied them.

“No.”

Caldrin frowned.

“Then what?”

Vale’s expression darkened.

“Wildbloods.”

The alpha growled.

A sound answered from deeper in the forest.

Dozens more.

Aurelia tightened her hold around Zee.

“Explain quickly.”

“Wolves born too close to old magic,” Vale said. “Not shifters. Not beasts anymore either.”

The alpha took one step forward.

Then stopped.

Its nostrils flared.

It smelled Zee.

Something passed through the entire pack.

Confusion.

Hunger.

Fear.

The wolves lowered their bodies.

Not submission.

Preparation.

The attack came all at once.

Vale met the first wolf with his sword.

Steel cut across its shoulder.

The wound barely slowed it.

Caldrin drove his blade through another’s jaw.

The witch released a violet shockwave that threw three wolves into the trees.

More replaced them.

Aurelia backed toward the overturned carts.

The hatchling climbed from beneath her cloak.

“No.”

He ignored her.

Tiny crimson wings spread.

Teal-and-gold mana crawled along his scales.

Zee felt the intention.

Protect.

He reached toward the hatchling.

The Dragon Link answered with something simple.

Together.

A wolf leaped.

The hatchling screamed.

Teal-and-gold fire burst from his mouth.

Not large.

Not controlled.

But hot enough to strike the wolf across the face.

It crashed into the road, smoking.

The pack recoiled.

For one moment.

Then the alpha charged.

Vale moved to intercept.

Too slow.

The wolf hit him like a battering ram and threw him into a tree.

Aurelia turned.

The alpha came for Zee.

Zee stared at it.

His crimson eyes widened.

The wolf scent entered him.

Predator.

Pack.

Territory.

Threat.

His own wolf nature answered.

Not with transformation.

With instinct.

A low growl came from the newborn’s chest.

Every Wildblood stopped.

The sound was too small to matter.

Yet it did.

The alpha’s ears flattened.

Zee growled again.

His Crimson Mana spread into the air.

The pack began whining.

Aurelia stared.

The alpha fought whatever instinct had seized it.

Then lunged anyway.

The hatchling attacked first.

He slammed into the wolf’s muzzle and bit down.

The alpha shook violently.

The hatchling flew sideways.

Zee screamed.

The Dragon Link flooded with pain.

The world around him narrowed.

He could feel the hatchling’s fear.

His anger answered before thought.

Crimson Mana erupted from Zee’s body.

Not as a wave.

As pressure.

The alpha collapsed mid-step.

Every wolf on the road dropped with it.

No bones broke.

No blood spilled.

They simply flattened against the earth as though the air itself had become too heavy to resist.

The witch stared.

Vale pushed himself upright.

Caldrin stopped fighting.

Aurelia looked down at her son.

Zee was crying now.

Furious.

The hatchling crawled back toward him.

The moment their bodies touched, the pressure vanished.

The wolves gasped.

Several immediately fled.

Others limped backward.

The alpha remained.

Its eyes fixed on Zee.

Not hunger anymore.

Recognition.

Something in the newborn’s scent had changed.

Or perhaps the wolf had simply noticed what it had ignored before.

Zee was not prey.

The alpha lowered its head.

Then turned away.

The rest of the pack followed.

Within moments, the road was empty again.

Caldrin stared after them.

“I preferred the dead men in the crypt.”

Vale coughed.

“You say that now.”

Aurelia ignored both of them.

She looked at Zee.

“What did you do?”

The child hiccuped.

The hatchling nudged his cheek.

Safe.

Zee relaxed.

The royal witch approached carefully.

“My Queen…”

Aurelia glanced at her.

The woman corrected herself immediately.

“I do not know.”

“Good.”

The witch almost smiled.

Almost.

Vale walked toward the place where the alpha had fallen.

He crouched and touched the earth.

No spell mark.

No scorch.

Nothing.

Only deep impressions where claws had dug into the road.

“He did not cast.”

Caldrin looked at Zee.

“No.”

Vale stood.

“He commanded.”

Aurelia’s expression hardened.

“You do not know that either.”

“No.”

Vale sheathed his sword.

“But the wolves believed he did.”

That mattered.

Perhaps too much.

⸻

The road grew worse by afternoon.

They left it.

Caldrin led them into the foothills where ancient hunting paths wound between dark trees and limestone ridges.

Aurelia’s body began failing before sunset.

She refused to admit it.

The royal witch noticed anyway.

“You need rest.”

“We need distance.”

“You gave birth days ago.”

“I remember.”

“You were wounded.”

“I remember that too.”

“You cannot keep walking.”

Aurelia stopped.

Her eyes hardened.

“Then carry me when I fall.”

The witch said nothing after that.

Zee slept.

The hatchling did not.

He rode against Aurelia’s shoulder, staring constantly into the woods.

Something had changed after the Wildblood attack.

His protectiveness had become sharper.

More deliberate.

He had felt Zee die once.

Now every danger seemed to carry the memory of absence.

The Dragon Link repeated one instinct again and again.

Stay close.

Zee answered even while sleeping.

Warmth.

Near.

The bond quieted.

Caldrin stopped suddenly.

Everyone froze.

Vale whispered, “What?”

Caldrin pointed toward the ground.

A footprint.

Human.

Then another.

Fresh.

Vale followed the trail with his eyes.

“Not ours.”

The witch lowered her voice.

“Soldiers?”

Caldrin shook his head.

“Too light.”

“Scouts?”

“No armor marks.”

Aurelia looked toward the trees.

“Assassins.”

Caldrin smiled without humor.

“Probably.”

The first arrow came from above.

It struck the witch’s barrier.

Violet light flashed.

“Down!”

Vale pulled Aurelia behind a rock.

Three more arrows hit the barrier.

The fourth passed through.

Not because the shield failed.

Because the arrowhead carried a seal etched into black metal.

It disrupted the spell on contact.

The witch stared.

“Anti-magic iron.”

Caldrin cursed.

Figures appeared along the ridge.

Six.

No banners.

No armor.

Mercenaries.

One raised a crossbow.

“Alive if possible!”

Another called back.

“The queen too?”

“Not required!”

Aurelia’s face went cold.

The bounty had already traveled.

Faster than expected.

Vale drew his sword.

“They are not soldiers.”

Caldrin unsheathed both blades.

“That makes them worse.”

The mercenaries descended.

They knew what they were doing.

One targeted the witch.

Two went for Vale.

Two spread wide to cut off Caldrin.

The last stayed behind with the crossbow.

No one charged Aurelia directly.

Not yet.

They wanted the defenders separated first.

The witch cast.

Violet force struck one mercenary.

He threw a black metal disk into the ground.

Her spell collapsed around it.

Caldrin saw.

“Runes!”

“They prepared for witches!”

“Of course they did.”

The world was already learning.

That frightened Aurelia more than the attack itself.

These men had heard reports.

They had adapted.

The next hunters would know even more.

Vale blocked a sword strike.

Caldrin buried a blade beneath another mercenary’s ribs.

The witch tried a different spell.

The black disk disrupted that too.

The crossbowman aimed.

At Zee.

Aurelia saw it.

“No!”

The bolt fired.

The hatchling reacted.

Teal-and-gold mana flashed.

He spread his wings in front of Zee.

The bolt struck him.

The tiny dragon screamed.

Aurelia screamed with him.

The projectile had pierced one wing.

The Dragon Link flooded Zee with pain.

Sharp.

Hot.

Wrong.

Zee woke instantly.

His crimson eyes opened.

The hatchling fell from Aurelia’s shoulder.

Blood stained his crimson scales.

Zee stared.

The mercenary reloaded.

Something inside Zee shifted.

Not power arriving from nowhere.

Instinct finding a path.

His vampire senses sharpened.

He heard the crossbow string tighten.

He heard the man’s heartbeat.

He smelled blood from the wound in Zareth’s wing.

He smelled every living body around him.

Six rhythms.

Five.

Four.

His perception narrowed until the forest seemed suddenly too slow.

Crimson Mana gathered around his eyes.

The crossbowman fired again.

Zee turned his head.

The bolt stopped inches from his face.

Not suspended by force this time.

Caught.

Aurelia stared.

Zee’s tiny hand was wrapped around the shaft.

No newborn should have possessed the reflexes.

No newborn should have possessed the grip.

The mercenary stared too.

That hesitation killed him.

Caldrin’s throwing knife struck his throat.

He fell.

The remaining mercenaries broke.

One ran.

Vale caught him.

Another surrendered.

Caldrin did not care.

The witch turned toward the hatchling.

“Let me see him.”

Zee began crying.

The sound was different.

Not fear.

Rage.

The hatchling’s blood touched Zee’s hand.

Crimson Mana reacted immediately.

It crawled toward the wound.

The witch stopped.

“My Queen.”

Aurelia looked.

Teal-and-gold Dragon Mana flickered around the damaged wing.

Zee’s Crimson Mana touched it.

For a moment, the two powers met.

They did not merge.

They did not become the same.

The teal-and-gold remained Zareth’s.

The crimson remained Zee’s.

But Zee reacted to what he felt through the Link.

Pain.

Torn flesh.

Heal.

His mana tightened around his own fingers.

Something inside his blood seemed to study the injury without understanding it.

Then the hatchling’s wound began closing faster.

Not instantly.

Not completely.

But faster than before.

The witch stared.

Aurelia looked at Zee.

He had not healed Zareth.

Not exactly.

Something about their bond had pushed his own dragon vitality harder.

The hatchling’s breathing steadied.

Zee stopped crying.

Safe?

The hatchling nudged his hand.

Safe.

Caldrin approached with blood on both swords.

“You should see this.”

Aurelia looked toward him.

One mercenary remained alive.

Vale held him on his knees.

The man was young.

Younger than Aurelia expected.

Terrified.

Caldrin pulled a folded parchment from his coat.

A bounty notice.

A rough sketch of Zee covered the center.

Crimson eyes.

Fangs.

A dragon beside him.

Below it:

THE DARKHEART TRIBRID

TWENTY THOUSAND SILVER CROWNS ALIVE

TEN THOUSAND DEAD

ADDITIONAL PAYMENT FOR BLOOD, TEETH, OR CONFIRMED MAGICAL REMAINS

Aurelia stopped breathing.

Vale read over her shoulder.

His face changed.

“Who issued this?”

The mercenary spat blood.

“Does it matter?”

Caldrin pressed a blade beneath his chin.

“Yes.”

The man laughed nervously.

“Half the continent will issue one by winter.”

Aurelia stepped forward.

“Who paid you?”

The mercenary looked at Zee.

Fear crossed his face.

Not because Zee threatened him.

Because the child existed.

“A broker in Red Hollow.”

“Working for whom?”

“I do not know.”

Caldrin increased pressure.

“You expect us to believe that?”

“I swear.”

The man swallowed.

“Contracts are being sold everywhere.”

“Kings?”

“Some.”

“Witches?”

“Yes.”

“Vampires?”

“Yes.”

“Wolves?”

The mercenary hesitated.

“Some packs are paying for information.”

Vale’s expression darkened.

Aurelia looked at the parchment again.

Three days old.

Zee was three days old.

And the world had already turned his body into currency.

She tore the bounty in half.

Then again.

And again.

The pieces fell into the dirt.

“Let him go.”

Caldrin looked at her.

“My Queen?”

“Let him go.”

Vale frowned.

“He knows our direction.”

“Exactly.”

Aurelia stepped toward the mercenary.

The man recoiled.

She looked down at him.

“You will go back.”

“To whom?”

“Everyone.”

Her voice remained calm.

“You will tell every broker, king, witch, vampire, hunter, and bastard who thinks my son is worth silver that they failed.”

The mercenary stared.

Aurelia continued.

“And tell them something else.”

Her eyes hardened.

“The price is too low.”

Caldrin smiled.

Vale released the man.

He ran.

No one stopped him.

The story would travel.

Not accurately.

Stories never did.

But it would travel.

The Tribrid lived.

The dragon lived.

The first bounty had failed.

And whoever came next would come prepared for what the mercenaries had learned.

⸻

That night, they made camp inside the ruins of an abandoned shrine.

No fire.

No songs.

No guards standing openly.

Only darkness.

The witch slept first.

Vale watched the eastern approach.

Caldrin watched the west.

Aurelia sat against a broken statue with Zee in her arms and the hatchling curled across her lap.

The injury in his wing had nearly closed.

Too quickly.

Aurelia touched the repaired membrane gently.

The hatchling opened one eye.

“You almost died for him.”

The tiny dragon blinked.

“You are both insane.”

He chirped.

Zee stirred.

Aurelia smiled despite herself.

For a few breaths, there was peace.

Then Zee’s eyes opened.

He looked toward the darkness outside the shrine.

His vampire hearing caught something distant.

A heartbeat.

Then another.

Then another.

Not human.

Too slow.

Too deep.

He did not understand what he heard.

But the wolf inside him recognized the scent carried by the wind.

Predator.

The hatchling lifted his head.

The Dragon Link tightened.

Danger.

Aurelia saw both infants react.

Her smile vanished.

“Vale.”

The captain stood immediately.

“What?”

Caldrin rose too.

The royal witch woke.

Aurelia looked toward the tree line.

“We are not alone.”

A growl answered from the darkness.

Not wolf.

Not Wildblood.

Something larger.

Two pale eyes opened between the trees.

Then four more.

Then eight.

Caldrin drew his sword.

“I suppose sleeping was too ambitious.”

Vale stepped in front of Aurelia.

The creatures began moving toward the shrine.

Zee watched them come.

Three days old.

Already hunted by kingdoms.

Already hunted by mercenaries.

Now hunted by something with no interest in money at all.

And beneath his skin, the First Natural Tribrid remembered every danger that had touched him.

The world had learned to hunt differently.

So had Zee.
