Chapter Fifty

Where Kingdom Maps End

The trees stopped growing in a straight line three miles before the border stone.

Zee noticed first.

Not because the others were distracted.

Because the forest offended every predatory sense he possessed.

Pines twisted east while their roots pushed west. Moss grew on both sides of trunks. Snow clung beneath branches but not above them. One dead tree stood upside down in the earth, roots reaching toward the sky while blackened branches disappeared beneath frozen ground.

Zee slowed.

Rez noticed immediately.

“What?”

Zee looked around.

“I do not like this forest.”

Ner glanced toward the upside-down tree.

“That is unusually reasonable.”

Zareth circled overhead.

The Dragon Link pressed against Zee with a sensation he had rarely felt from the Crown Prince of Drakonis.

Uncertainty.

Not fear.

Not yet.

Zee looked up.

“What do you feel?”

The Link answered with fractured impressions.

Old stone beneath mountains.

Dragon elders refusing to fly farther west.

A childhood memory that did not belong to Zee: Zareth, smaller, listening while an elderly Drakonis warrior scratched a warning symbol into ash.

Then a concept.

Hungry land.

Zee frowned.

Rez heard.

“Hungry?”

“Something like that.”

Ner pulled one glove tighter.

“We are not calling a forest hungry until we know what that means.”

Zee looked at him.

“You object to everything interesting.”

“I object to terrible descriptions becoming facts.”

Rez smiled.

“He has a point.”

Zee sighed.

They continued.

No royal escort.

No Aurelia.

No Vesper soldiers.

This mission had started simply enough.

Three hunting parties had vanished near the western edge of wolf territory.

Not children.

Not merchants.

Experienced supernatural hunters.

The wolf clans had found abandoned weapons, intact supplies, and tracks ending in places where nothing should have been able to remove a body without leaving blood.

They had asked neighboring kingdoms for help.

Two refused.

One sent scouts.

The scouts did not return.

Then a wolf envoy reached Vesper carrying a piece of black antler that no one recognized.

Zee wanted to go before the envoy finished speaking.

Rez made them wait for the rest.

That had turned out to be useful.

Now the four of them followed the last recorded trail beyond the final maintained road.

The border stone appeared after noon.

It had once marked the end of a wolf kingdom.

Years of weather had erased most of the carved crest.

Beyond it lay no road.

No patrol markers.

No kingdom banners.

Nothing.

Rez stopped beside the stone.

“This is where their maps end.”

Ner examined the ground.

“No.”

Rez looked toward him.

Ner pointed.

“Their maps stop here.”

A thin line of pale residue cut across the soil.

Zee crouched.

“Magic?”

Ner did not answer immediately.

Pure Golden Mana gathered along two fingers.

He did not touch the line.

He brought his hand close.

The residue moved away.

Ner froze.

Zee leaned closer.

“It moved.”

“I saw.”

Rez crouched opposite them.

“Spell?”

“No.”

“You sound sure.”

“I am sure it did not respond like one.”

Ner shifted his hand left.

The pale line retreated right.

He moved upward.

It flattened into the soil.

Zee smiled.

“It does not like you.”

Ner stared.

“I refuse to take offense from dirt.”

Zareth landed beyond the border stone.

The ground trembled beneath his weight.

Teal-and-Gold Mana rolled once along his scales.

The pale line vanished completely.

All four noticed.

Zareth lowered his head.

The Dragon Link sharpened.

Below.

Zee touched the earth.

Nothing.

No heartbeat.

No blood.

No ordinary scent.

His Wolf nature found wet stone, old snow, dead leaves, animal trails.

Then something else.

Not scent exactly.

Absence.

A place where scent should have continued and did not.

Zee stood.

“There is something underground.”

Rez looked toward the trail ahead.

“Living?”

“I do not know.”

“Dead?”

“I do not know.”

Ner looked pleased.

Zee stared.

“Why are you smiling?”

“Because you finally understand how annoying that answer is.”

Zee almost shoved him.

Then the forest made a sound.

Not a roar.

Not a branch breaking.

A deep vibration moved through the trees.

Every bird went silent.

Zareth’s wings lifted.

The Link flashed.

Movement.

Many.

Not approaching.

Leaving.

Zee turned.

Deer burst through the undergrowth.

Seven.

Then wolves.

Wild ones.

Then animals Zee did not recognize at all—long-bodied gray things with six narrow legs and smooth faces where eyes should have been.

Rez drew his sword.

“Do we know those?”

“No,” Zee said.

Ner stared.

“Do not attack.”

One eyeless creature passed within ten feet of them.

It did not turn.

Did not react to Zee.

Did not react to Zareth.

It ran.

That frightened Zee more.

Whatever could make something unknown flee without even noticing a Dragon was worth respecting.

The ground vibrated again.

Harder.

Rez looked toward the fleeing animals.

“We move with them.”

Zee blinked.

“Back?”

“No.”

Rez pointed northwest.

“They are not running away from the whole region. They are angling around something.”

Ner understood.

“So we follow the edge.”

“Yes.”

Zee looked toward the deeper forest.

“I wanted to see what they were running from.”

Rez stared.

“I know.”

“That was almost insulting.”

“It was.”

Zareth’s amusement passed through the Link.

Zee sighed.

They moved northwest.

⸻

The first missing hunter was alive.

Barely.

They found him suspended six feet above the ground between two trees.

No rope.

No web.

No spell Zee could see.

His body simply hung horizontally in empty air.

Rez stopped everyone before they approached.

“Do not touch him.”

Zee looked toward the hunter’s chest.

Heartbeat.

Very slow.

“Alive.”

Ner stepped forward.

Golden Mana formed into a hair-thin line.

He passed it beneath the floating man.

Nothing.

Then above.

Nothing.

Around his left arm.

The Gold distorted.

Ner stopped.

“There.”

Zee saw nothing.

“What?”

“A boundary.”

Rez frowned.

“Shape?”

Ner extended more threads.

One disappeared.

Another bent.

A third reflected back toward him.

His expression changed.

“This is wrong.”

Zee smiled faintly.

“You say that often.”

“No.”

Ner looked at him.

“I mean the boundary does not have one side.”

Silence.

Rez lowered his sword slightly.

“Explain.”

“I cannot yet.”

“Try.”

Ner moved two fingers.

Golden threads mapped empty air.

Some lines bent around the suspended hunter.

Others passed through the same space from different angles.

One thread vanished entirely and reappeared three feet behind Ner.

He jerked backward.

Zee caught his arm.

Their hands stayed together a heartbeat too long.

Not now.

Ner pulled away.

“Thank you.”

Zee nodded.

Rez pretended not to see anything.

Poorly.

Ner looked back toward the hunter.

“It is not a cage.”

“What is it?” Zee asked.

“I do not know.”

Rez sighed.

Ner glared.

“You asked me not to lie.”

“I did.”

Zareth approached carefully.

The Dragon Link tightened around Zee’s senses.

Zareth smelled something.

Not through Zee.

His own Dragon senses.

A memory-impression passed through.

Hot caverns beneath Drakonis.

A mineral vein Dragons avoided because fire disappeared near it.

Then another.

Old Dragon word.

Not language Zee could hear.

Concept.

Fold.

Zee frowned.

“Zareth thinks the space is folded.”

Ner looked immediately toward the Dragon.

“Folded how?”

Zareth sent irritation.

If he knew, he would have sent more.

Rez walked around the suspended hunter.

“No blood.”

Zee nodded.

“No wound.”

“No binding marks.”

“No poison smell.”

“Nothing?”

Zee looked closer.

“One thing.”

A pale discoloration along the hunter’s forearm.

Not bruise.

Not frostbite.

The skin looked faded.

As though color itself had been removed.

Zee’s vampire senses sharpened.

The blood beneath that patch moved incorrectly.

Slow.

Then fast.

Then slow again.

He stepped closer.

Rez caught his shoulder.

“No.”

Zee looked over.

“I need to see.”

“See from here.”

“I cannot.”

“Then we learn another way.”

Zee’s jaw tightened.

He hated when Rez was right.

Ner pointed toward the hunter’s hand.

“His fingers.”

They were moving.

Not consciously.

One finger twitching in a pattern.

Three.

Pause.

Two.

Pause.

Three.

Rez crouched.

“Signal?”

Zee listened to the hunter’s heartbeat.

Each finger movement matched a change in pulse.

Three beats fast.

Two slow.

Three fast.

“He is trying to tell us something.”

Ner moved closer without crossing the invisible boundary.

“What?”

The hunter’s eyes opened.

Wild.

Terrified.

His mouth moved.

No sound came out.

Then Zee heard something.

Not with hearing.

Not thought.

A pressure against his fangs.

Against his bones.

Against the Dragon ridges beneath his shoulder blades.

One word that was not a word.

Below.

Zee staggered.

Ner grabbed him.

Rez’s sword came up.

Zareth roared.

The suspended hunter dropped.

Rez caught him before he hit the ground.

The invisible boundary vanished.

Ner immediately moved in.

Golden Mana checked the hunter’s body.

Zee grabbed a tree for balance.

“What was that?”

No one answered.

Because the ground opened.

Not cracked.

Opened.

A circle of forest floor six feet across folded downward without breaking soil or roots.

Zee stared.

There was no hole beneath it.

There was sky.

Dark violet sky filled with unfamiliar stars.

For one impossible second another place existed beneath their feet.

Then something looked up.

One enormous eye.

Pale.

Horizontal pupil.

Too large to belong to anything that should fit below the forest.

The opening snapped shut.

Earth returned.

Roots unbroken.

Snow undisturbed.

Silence.

No one moved.

Rez looked down.

Then at Zee.

“We are leaving the normal rules behind.”

Ner stared at the ground.

“That was not teleportation.”

Zee looked toward him.

“You know that?”

“Yes.”

“How?”

“Because nothing moved.”

Ner swallowed.

“The distance changed.”

Zareth’s Link exploded with Dragon instinct.

Danger.

Territory.

Not predator.

Not exactly.

Older.

Zee’s Crimson scales spread involuntarily along his ribs.

The Dragon ridges beneath his shoulders tightened.

Crimson energy moved through his blood.

Not awakening.

Reaction.

Recognition without knowledge.

Zee looked toward the unconscious hunter.

Then the silent forest.

Then the border stone far behind them.

For fifteen years he had believed kingdoms were large because wars could take months to cross them.

Now an eye had looked at him from a sky beneath the ground.

The known world suddenly felt very small.

And for the first time in years, Zee Darkheart smiled because he was afraid.

Not because fear felt good.

Because fear meant they had finally found something none of them understood.

Chapter Fifty-One

The Place Beneath Places

The rescued hunter woke screaming.

Not because of pain.

Because he saw the sky.

He sat upright in Rez’s arms, clawed at the frozen ground, and shouted:

“Do not let it turn!”

Rez grabbed both shoulders.

“Look at me.”

The hunter did not.

His eyes stayed fixed on the forest floor.

“Do not let it turn!”

Ner knelt beside him.

“What turns?”

“The land.”

“What does that mean?”

The hunter looked at him as though language had become useless.

Then he saw Zareth.

He froze.

“A Dragon.”

Zareth lowered his head.

The man started laughing.

Not relief.

Despair.

“Oh, gods.”

Rez’s expression hardened.

“Stay with us.”

The hunter looked toward him.

“You crossed the stone.”

“Yes.”

“Why?”

“Looking for you.”

The hunter stared.

Something like guilt entered his face.

“You should not have.”

Zee crouched across from him.

“What happened to the others?”

The hunter’s eyes found Zee.

Recognition came slowly.

“The Darkheart boy.”

“Zee.”

The man swallowed.

“We found animals.”

“The eyeless six-legged things?”

His face changed.

“You saw them?”

“Yes.”

“Then it is moving.”

Rez looked toward Ner.

Ner frowned.

“What is moving?”

The hunter shook his head.

“We thought they were monsters.”

Zee smiled faintly.

“Were they?”

“No.”

The answer came instantly.

“They were running.”

Just as Zee had thought.

The hunter continued.

“We followed them.”

“Found a valley that wasn’t on our maps.”

“A river running uphill.”

“Trees growing beneath the ground.”

“One of my men stepped across a shadow.”

Zee frowned.

“A shadow?”

“He never came back.”

No blood.

No body.

No sound.

The hunter’s hands shook.

“Then the world turned.”

Rez’s eyes narrowed.

“Describe that.”

“I cannot.”

“Try.”

The man stared toward the trees.

“The mountain was above us.”

“Then beside us.”

“Then inside the river.”

“One moment I was standing.”

“The next I was falling without moving.”

Ner went still.

That matched his boundary.

Distance changing without movement.

The hunter continued.

“Something found us.”

Zee leaned forward.

“The eye?”

The man stopped breathing for a moment.

“You saw it.”

“Yes.”

“Then it saw you.”

Zareth growled.

The hunter flinched.

Zee asked, “What is it?”

“I do not know.”

Good.

Terrible.

Good.

The hunter looked toward the unconscious forest.

“We never saw a body.”

“Only pieces.”

“An eye.”

“Something like antlers.”

“A mouth inside water.”

“Tracks that started on tree trunks.”

Rez glanced toward Zee.

“Not one creature?”

The hunter shook his head.

“Maybe.”

Ner’s expression changed.

“Or one thing appearing through different boundaries.”

The hunter stared.

Zee looked toward Ner.

“Can something do that?”

Ner gave him a flat look.

“We just saw a sky under dirt.”

Fair.

Rez stood.

“We take him back to the border stone.”

Zee looked up.

“And then?”

“Then we return.”

The hunter shouted, “No!”

Everyone turned.

He grabbed Rez’s coat.

“If you cross back now, you might not reach the same side.”

Silence.

Rez slowly looked toward the distant direction of the border.

“What?”

The hunter’s face had gone pale.

“It changes after it notices you.”

Ner stood.

“What changes?”

“The paths.”

Of course.

Zee smiled.

Rez glared.

“Why are you smiling?”

“This is terrible.”

“That was not an answer.”

“I know.”

The forest vibrated.

Closer now.

The hunter screamed.

“Move!”

This time no one argued.

⸻

Rez took command before they had run fifty yards.

“Zareth, air.”

The Dragon launched.

“Ner, watch boundaries.”

Gold gathered around Ner’s hands.

“Zee, track living things.”

Zee listened.

“Most are moving northeast.”

“Then we move northeast too.”

Zee frowned.

“Toward what?”

“Not what is making everything run southwest.”

Good point.

They ran.

The forest began changing around them.

Not dramatically at first.

A tree appeared twice.

Same split trunk.

Same patch of white fungus.

Zee passed it once.

Then again thirty seconds later.

“Ner.”

“I saw.”

Rez looked back.

“We turned?”

“No.”

Ner fired a Golden line behind them.

It stretched straight through the trees.

Then curved upward.

Then vanished into empty air.

His face hardened.

“The path is folding.”

Rez shouted, “Do not follow sight.”

Zee understood first.

“Scent?”

“Anything stable.”

Zee inhaled.

Bad idea.

The scents layered.

Wolf.

Snow.

Hunter blood.

Zareth.

Ner.

Rez.

Then all of them again from three different directions.

“Not scent.”

Rez adjusted immediately.

“Sound.”

Zee listened.

Same problem.

Footsteps repeated ahead before they made them.

“Not sound.”

Ner shouted, “Mana!”

He threw a Golden marker against a tree.

It stayed.

They passed it.

Thirty seconds later another tree carried the same marker.

Rez cursed.

“Not Mana.”

Zee looked upward.

Zareth.

The Link.

Unique.

Not a path in the forest.

Not magic anchored to terrain.

Bond.

“Zareth!”

The Link struck back.

Sky.

Three versions of the forest below.

One real?

No.

All real.

Zareth was seeing overlapping landscapes.

Mountains where trees should be.

A silver lake suspended vertically.

A herd of massive pale animals walking through air hundreds of feet above Zee’s current position.

Zee stumbled under the sensory flood.

Rez caught him.

“What?”

“Zareth sees more than one land.”

Ner looked upward.

“Simultaneously?”

“I think.”

“Ask him where we are.”

Zee sent the concept.

Us.

Position.

Zareth answered with frustration.

Four Zees.

Four groups.

All moving differently.

Zee went cold.

“There are copies.”

Rez’s face changed.

“Copies of us?”

“Not sure.”

Ner looked around.

“Do not interact with anything that looks like us.”

Zee smiled.

“That is very specific.”

“Because you would.”

Zee opened his mouth.

Then closed it.

Fair.

A voice called from ahead.

“Zee!”

Rez stopped dead.

It was Aurelia.

Zee’s entire body reacted.

Heart.

Blood.

Wolf instinct.

Everything.

“Mother?”

Rez grabbed him.

“No.”

The voice came again.

“Zee!”

Exactly her voice.

Warm.

Afraid.

Close.

Zee’s feet moved before his mind did.

Ner stepped in front of him.

“No.”

“That is her.”

“No.”

“I know her voice.”

Ner looked directly at him.

“So do I.”

The voice changed.

Closer.

“Baby, come here.”

Zee froze.

Aurelia had called him that when he was little.

Not often now.

Almost never where others heard.

His chest tightened.

Ner grabbed both his hands.

Zee looked down.

Golden light flickered between their fingers.

Not spellwork.

Ner’s Mana reacting to his own fear.

“Your mother is in Vesper.”

Zee looked at him.

“I know.”

“Then choose what you know.”

The words cut through instinct.

Zee breathed.

The false Aurelia called again.

He closed his eyes.

Listened past sound.

Heartbeat?

None.

Blood?

None.

Scent?

Only forest.

Dragon Link?

Zareth sent disgust.

Wrong.

Zee opened his eyes.

“Not her.”

Ner did not release his hands immediately.

Neither noticed until Rez said:

“Wonderful. Move.”

They separated.

Zee’s face warmed.

Ner looked away.

Even here?

Apparently.

The voice behind them stopped.

Then laughed.

Not Aurelia anymore.

Something wet and enormous moved between the trees.

They never saw the whole body.

Only antlers.

Too many.

White structures taller than houses passed between trunks without disturbing branches.

Then an eye opened in the bark of a nearby tree.

Same horizontal pupil.

Zee moved.

The eye followed.

Zareth dove from above.

Teal-and-Gold Dragonfire struck the tree.

The flame hit bark.

Then disappeared.

Not extinguished.

Gone.

Zareth pulled upward violently.

The Link carried shock.

Zee shouted, “Do not attack!”

Too late.

The forest answered.

Every tree opened an eye.

Hundreds.

Rez stopped.

“New plan.”

“Good,” Ner said.

“What?”

“Do not make it angry.”

Zee looked around.

“You think it is angry?”

A branch bent toward him.

The tip opened into a mouth.

Zee stepped back.

“Yes.”

Rez grabbed the wounded hunter.

“Run.”

They ran.

⸻

The first direct strike came from the ground.

A pale antler burst upward beneath Rez.

Zee saw it.

Moved.

Crimson Mana hit Rez sideways.

Rez flew clear.

The antler impaled Zee through the lower abdomen.

Pain erased everything.

Ner shouted.

Zareth roared.

Zee looked down.

White bone through his body.

Blood soaked his coat.

He did not die.

Could not.

That did not make it pleasant.

The antler lifted.

Zee screamed as his feet left the ground.

Rez regained his footing.

“Do not cut it!”

Ner stopped mid-cast.

“Why?”

“We do not know what that does!”

Good.

Zee hated him.

Good.

The antler began pulling Zee downward.

Not into soil.

Into somewhere else.

The ground beneath him turned transparent.

Violet sky.

Stars.

The enormous eye.

Closer.

Zee’s Dragon nature exploded.

Crimson scales covered his abdomen around the wound.

His horns burned.

The ridges beneath his shoulder blades pushed violently outward without becoming wings.

Crimson Dragon energy surged into the antler.

Not an attack he understood.

Reaction.

The white structure shuddered.

For the first time, the eye below changed.

Its pupil narrowed.

Recognition?

Pain?

Zee did not know.

His blood touched the antler.

Something strange passed through him.

Cold without temperature.

Distance without movement.

A sense of edges existing where none should.

His body reacted.

Not copying.

Adapting.

Crimson Mana changed texture around his hands.

Thinner.

Sharper.

It began outlining something invisible.

Zee saw lines.

Not with his eyes.

Boundaries.

Folds.

The places where the world bent.

“Ner!”

Ner looked toward him.

Zee pointed with one shaking hand.

“There!”

Nothing visible.

Ner trusted him anyway.

Golden Mana struck the point Zee indicated.

The world flashed.

The antler released him.

Zee fell.

Rez caught one arm.

Ner caught the other.

They dragged him away as the transparent ground snapped shut.

Zee collapsed.

Blood everywhere.

His body already repairing.

Slowly.

Painfully.

Ner knelt.

“Can you move?”

“Yes.”

“That sounded false.”

“Mostly.”

Rez looked at the wound.

“It went through.”

“I noticed.”

Zareth landed beside them in a fury.

The Link hit Zee like a storm.

Pain.

Rage.

Protect.

Destroy.

Zee grabbed his snout.

“No.”

Zareth’s Mana flared.

“No fire.”

The Dragon snarled.

Zee pushed a concept back.

Not enemy?

Maybe territory.

Unknown.

Zareth hated the uncertainty.

So did Zee.

Ner looked at Zee’s hands.

Crimson lines still shimmered faintly between his fingers.

“What is that?”

“I do not know.”

He smiled through pain.

Ner glared.

“This is not funny.”

“I know.”

Rez crouched.

“You saw the fold.”

Zee looked toward him.

“Yes.”

“How?”

“The antler touched my blood.”

Ner stiffened.

“You absorbed something?”

“No.”

Important.

Zee knew the difference.

Nothing foreign sat inside him waiting to become a copied power.

His body had encountered something impossible and changed how it perceived danger.

Adaptation.

Not theft.

Zee lifted one hand.

Crimson lines appeared again.

The forest suddenly looked different.

Not normal.

Layered.

He could see where paths bent against one another.

Where one tree existed in two positions.

Where a patch of snow opened toward violet sky.

Not clearly.

Enough.

“Rez.”

“What?”

“I can see where not to walk.”

Rez smiled.

“There is our route.”

Ner immediately said, “Maybe.”

Zee looked at him.

Ner continued.

“We test it first.”

Good.

Always annoying.

Good.

Ner formed a tiny Golden sphere and threw it toward the nearest Crimson-outlined fold.

The sphere vanished.

Reappeared twenty feet above them.

Then fell.

Rez stepped aside.

It struck the ground.

Ner looked at Zee.

“Accurate.”

Zee smiled.

“Thank you.”

“Do not get arrogant. You were impaled thirty seconds ago.”

“Forty.”

“That is worse.”

Zareth’s amusement slipped through rage.

The hunter stared at all four.

“You are insane.”

Rez stood.

“Yes.”

Then pointed.

“Zee leads.”

“Ner verifies.”

“Zareth stays above and warns us when the landscape overlaps.”

“I manage movement.”

Zee looked at him.

“And the hunter?”

Rez glanced down.

“Stays alive.”

The man looked touched.

Rez added:

“Because I refuse to explain losing the person we came here to rescue.”

Zee laughed.

There he was.

They moved.

⸻

The deeper forest stopped pretending to obey ordinary geography.

They passed a waterfall flowing sideways through open air.

A field of black flowers turned their petals away from Zee’s blood.

A herd of eyeless six-legged creatures watched from a cliff that had not existed a minute earlier.

None attacked.

That mattered.

Zee began understanding.

“This place is not hunting us.”

Rez looked toward him.

“What?”

“It attacked after Zareth burned the tree.”

Zareth sent offense.

Ner thought.

“The antler came after the fire.”

“And the false Aurelia?” Rez asked.

Ner frowned.

“Maybe defensive behavior.”

Zee looked toward the eyes opening in distant bark.

“Or curiosity.”

The wounded hunter shook his head.

“It killed my people.”

“Did they attack first?” Zee asked.

Silence.

The man looked away.

Rez noticed.

“What did your group do?”

The hunter swallowed.

“We found one of the six-legged animals.”

Zee’s face hardened.

“And?”

“We killed it.”

Of course.

Ner closed his eyes.

“Why?”

“We thought it was dangerous.”

“Did it attack?”

“No.”

Zee’s darkness stirred.

Not enough to act.

Enough to judge.

The hunter continued quickly.

“Then we cut it open.”

Zareth growled.

The Link filled with disgust.

Rez’s expression went cold.

“You crossed into unknown territory, killed an animal that did not threaten you, and dissected it.”

The hunter looked ashamed.

“We needed to know what it was.”

Ner stared.

“That is not how asking works.”

Zee almost smiled.

Not because it was funny.

Because the world had once used the same logic on him.

Unknown.

Dangerous.

Cut it open.

Find out afterward.

He understood this place a little better now.

Maybe.

“Where did you kill it?”

The hunter pointed uncertainly.

“No idea.”

Zee looked at the Crimson folds.

“I do.”

His new perception pulled faintly toward something.

Blood.

Not ordinary blood.

The creature’s blood had touched one of the folds and left a pattern.

Zee followed.

Rez did not question.

Ner tested every turn.

Zareth mapped from above.

For once, the strange place allowed them through.

Or they stopped fighting it enough to move correctly.

Both were possible.

They found the dead creature near sunset.

Its body had not rotted.

Six legs folded beneath it.

Smooth eyeless face turned toward the ground.

A long wound opened across its abdomen.

Hunter tools lay nearby.

The forest around it was silent.

Zee approached slowly.

No threat.

No touch.

He crouched.

“I am sorry.”

Rez looked at him.

The hunter bowed his head.

Something moved beneath the earth.

The enormous eye opened again.

Not under Zee.

Ten yards away.

Watching.

Zareth lowered himself but did not attack.

Ner kept his Mana quiet.

Rez lowered his sword.

The eye remained.

Zee looked toward the hunter.

“Your weapon.”

The man hesitated.

Then handed over his hunting knife.

Zee placed it beside the dead creature.

Then the man’s specimen pouch.

Inside were pieces of pale tissue taken from the animal.

Ner saw.

His face tightened.

Zee placed them beside the body too.

The forest shifted.

Not violently.

Trees straightened a fraction.

The sideways waterfall slowed.

The eye blinked.

Zee’s new Crimson perception saw a fold opening nearby.

Different.

Stable.

A path.

Rez saw Zee’s face.

“Exit?”

“I think.”

Ner threw a Golden sphere.

It crossed the fold.

Did not vanish.

Rolled normally through the snow beyond.

Zee smiled.

“Yes.”

The hunter started crying.

Quietly.

No one mocked him.

They crossed one by one.

Rez took the hunter first.

Ner next.

Zee waited.

Zareth remained behind him.

The Dragon Link carried a question.

The eye still watched.

Zee looked back at it.

“What are you?”

No answer.

Good.

He did not expect one.

The world did not owe him explanations simply because he survived meeting it.

Something passed through the Link from Zareth.

Old Dragon concept.

Not name.

Not certainty.

A category.

Deep wild.

Places older than borders.

Regions Dragons remembered only enough to avoid.

Not evil.

Not safe.

Zee nodded.

Then crossed.

Zareth followed.

The fold closed.

The forest behind them became ordinary trees.

Mostly.

The border stone stood less than a hundred yards away.

Impossible.

They had traveled for hours.

Ner looked back.

“No.”

Rez smiled tiredly.

“Do not start.”

Ner pointed.

“We were miles inside.”

“Yes.”

“That is impossible.”

Zee looked at his hands.

Crimson lines flickered once around his fingers.

Then disappeared.

“Apparently not.”

The hunter sat in the snow.

Alive.

The core four stood around him.

Bloodied.

Exhausted.

Different.

They had entered expecting a monster.

Found an ecosystem.

Provoked a territory.

Learned that some supernatural things did not fit neatly into Witch, Vampire, Wolf, Dragon, demon, curse, spell, or kingdom.

And Zee carried a new scar through his abdomen that had already begun fading into something his body would remember.

Not a copied power.

Not victory.

A new way to see when the world folded wrong.

Ner looked toward him.

“Do not experiment with that.”

Zee frowned.

“I was not going to.”

Rez stared.

Zareth sent immediate disbelief.

Zee looked offended.

“Fine.”

Ner smiled.

The wounded hunter laughed weakly.

For the first time since they crossed the border stone, the sound did not feel inappropriate.

Rez looked back toward the unknown forest.

“We tell the wolf clans to mark this entire region.”

“As forbidden?” Zee asked.

Rez thought.

“No.”

Ner looked toward him.

Rez continued.

“As inhabited.”

That was better.

Much better.

Zee looked at the forest one last time.

Kingdom maps had called the land empty.

It was not.

They simply had not understood what lived there.

The known world had not expanded because Zee conquered something.

It expanded because, for once, he had survived something without needing to own it, kill it, or understand all of it.

Beyond the trees, deeper places waited.

Older species.

Stranger laws.

Things kingdoms had never named.

Zee’s Crimson eyes brightened.

Fear remained.

So did wonder.

And now that he knew how little of the world belonged to crowns—

he wanted to see all of it.

Chapter Fifty-Two

The Country Without Roads

The first problem with trying to warn people about a place that folded distance was deciding where the place actually was.

The wolf clans wanted coordinates.

Rez wanted boundaries.

Ner wanted repeated measurements.

Zareth wanted everyone to stop pretending the land cared about their maps.

Zee wanted to go back.

That last opinion was unpopular.

They stood inside a long timber hall three days after escaping the deep wild, surrounded by wolf trackers, two witch surveyors, a Vesper cartographer, and one clan elder who had spent twenty minutes insisting that every region could be mapped if enough people survived measuring it.

Ner finally placed both hands on the table.

“No.”

The elder stared.

“No?”

“No.”

“You have been fifteen for exactly long enough to become disrespectful.”

Ner smiled.

“I was disrespectful before fifteen.”

Rez coughed.

Zee looked innocent.

The elder glared at all three.

Ner pointed toward the map.

“You keep asking where the boundary moved.”

“Yes.”

“We do not know.”

“You crossed it.”

“Yes.”

“You came back.”

“Yes.”

“Then mark the route.”

“We tried.”

Ner slid three pieces of parchment forward.

Each held a different version of the same journey.

On the first, the path curved six miles northwest.

On the second, the same landmarks appeared nearly fourteen miles apart.

On the third, the border stone sat less than a hundred yards from where the dead six-legged creature had been found.

The elder looked between them.

“That is impossible.”

Zee smiled.

“You are going to hear that a lot.”

Rez gave him a look.

Zee shrugged.

The Vesper cartographer leaned closer.

“What if the terrain physically moved?”

Ner shook his head.

“The trees changed position without moving through the space between positions.”

The witch surveyor frowned.

“How can you know?”

Ner lifted one hand.

Pure Golden Mana formed a thin line across the map.

“I anchored spell markers.”

“Some returned behind us.”

“Some appeared above us.”

“One remained exactly where I placed it while the path around it stopped leading to the same location.”

The hall went quiet.

The elder looked toward Zee.

“And you could see these… folds?”

“After one stabbed me.”

Several wolves looked toward his abdomen.

Zee frowned.

“It healed.”

“That was not the concern.”

“It usually is.”

Rez leaned against the table.

“What matters is this: do not call the region uninhabited.”

The elder’s expression hardened.

“We lost people there.”

“Yes.”

“To something dangerous.”

“Yes.”

“And you are telling me not to seal it?”

Rez shook his head.

“I am telling you that sealing and invading are different decisions.”

One wolf captain folded his arms.

“What would you call it?”

Rez looked toward Zee.

Zee thought about the eye beneath the ground.

The false Aurelia.

The eyeless animals.

The hunter confessing what his party had done first.

Then the path opening only after the stolen remains were returned.

“Inhabited.”

The elder frowned.

“By what?”

Zee looked toward Zareth.

The Dragon Prince had remained outside because the hall was too small, but his head rested beside an open wall section built for larger visitors.

The Link carried the same old Drakonis concept.

Deep wild.

Not a species.

Not a kingdom.

Not a name.

A warning category.

“Something that was there before us.”

“That tells me nothing.”

“Then write that.”

The elder stared.

Zee continued.

“Unknown inhabitants.”

“Unknown laws.”

“Do not kill anything unless it attacks first.”

“Do not cut pieces off things because you are curious.”

The surviving hunter from the expedition stood near the rear wall.

His face tightened.

Good.

He had chosen to testify publicly.

That mattered.

Zee looked toward him.

The man stepped forward.

“We caused what happened.”

A murmur moved through the wolves.

The hunter swallowed.

“We killed one of the creatures.”

“Unprovoked.”

“We opened it.”

“Took tissue.”

“And after that… the land changed.”

One clan warrior looked disgusted.

“You expect us to believe the forest judged you?”

The hunter shook his head.

“No.”

“I expect you to believe we did something stupid inside a place we did not understand.”

That answer was better.

The elder sat back.

“What do you recommend?”

Rez answered.

“Observation posts outside the last stable landmarks.”

“No patrols crossing the line without cause.”

“Nobody alone.”

“No hunters entering for trophies.”

Ner added, “No permanent magical anchors.”

The surveyors looked toward him.

“Why?”

“Because we do not know whether the region reads anchored magic as intrusion.”

Zee glanced at him.

“That is a guess.”

“Yes.”

“Good.”

Ner smiled.

The elder looked toward Zareth.

“And Drakonis?”

Zee opened the Link.

Question.

The answer came slowly.

Dragon history.

Old regions.

Avoidance.

Watching from high altitude.

No nesting nearby.

No claim.

Zee translated carefully.

“Drakonis will not claim it.”

The wolf elder raised an eyebrow.

“Zareth has that authority?”

The Dragon Prince’s Teal-and-Gold Mana flared outside the hall.

The elder looked toward the massive crimson head filling half the wall opening.

“Fair.”

Rez smiled.

Then the hall doors opened.

A young wolf messenger entered breathing hard.

“Elder.”

Everyone turned.

The messenger bowed.

“Something came out.”

Silence.

Zee straightened.

“From the deep wild?”

The messenger looked toward him.

“Yes.”

“What?”

“We do not know.”

Zee smiled.

Rez immediately said, “Stop smiling.”

“I am not.”

“You absolutely are.”

The elder stood.

“Where?”

“North watch.”

“Hostile?”

The messenger hesitated.

“No.”

That changed everything.

“What is it doing?” Ner asked.

The messenger looked deeply confused.

“Waiting.”

⸻

The thing waiting beyond the north watch had antlers.

That was where resemblance to any known animal ended.

It stood in a field of dead winter grass beneath a gray afternoon sky, nearly nine feet at the shoulder, with six narrow legs and a body covered in pale charcoal hide that seemed smooth from a distance and patterned with fine moving lines up close.

Its head was long.

Eyeless.

But unlike the smaller creatures from the deep wild, this one possessed a split crown of black antlers that curved backward and then inward as though framing empty space above its skull.

No mouth.

No visible nostrils.

No heartbeat Zee could detect.

No blood scent.

No obvious Mana.

Wolf warriors ringed the field at a distance.

None had attacked.

Good.

The creature stood perfectly still.

Zareth landed behind the group.

The animal reacted immediately.

Its antlers changed.

Not shape.

Position.

For a heartbeat Zee saw the crown in three places at once.

Then one again.

Zareth’s Link tightened.

Recognition?

No.

Caution.

Ner moved closer.

Rez caught his sleeve.

“Not yet.”

“I am not touching it.”

“That sentence has history.”

Ner glared.

Zee listened.

Nothing.

Then the strange Crimson perception in his blood stirred.

Faint lines appeared around the animal.

Not around its body.

Through it.

Several folds crossing the same space.

Zee inhaled.

“It is not fully here.”

Rez looked over.

“Meaning?”

“I do not know.”

Ner smiled faintly.

Zee frowned.

“Do not.”

Ner lifted one hand.

Pure Golden Mana formed a tiny sphere.

Not aimed at the creature.

He released it several feet to the left.

The sphere moved normally.

Then vanished when it crossed one of Zee’s perceived lines.

Ner’s expression sharpened.

“Again.”

He formed another.

This one he sent lower.

It passed.

Another higher.

Gone.

The creature finally moved.

One step.

Every wolf raised a weapon.

Rez raised one hand.

“Hold.”

The creature’s six legs folded oddly, each joint bending in different directions, yet the movement remained smooth.

It approached Zee.

Only Zee.

He did not move.

Aurelia was not here to tell him not to.

That made the choice more important.

Ner whispered, “Zee.”

“I know.”

Zareth’s Link filled with readiness.

Rez moved half a step closer.

The animal stopped six feet away.

Its antlers shifted again.

The air between them folded.

Zee saw a landscape.

Not around them.

Inside the space between the antlers.

Black grass.

Silver rain falling upward.

A distant mountain hanging upside down in a violet sky.

Then something moved across that landscape.

Hundreds of pale creatures.

Migrating.

Zee’s eyes widened.

Ner stepped closer despite Rez.

The image sharpened.

Not illusion.

A view.

Somewhere else.

The creature lowered its head.

One antler touched the ground.

The field beneath it changed.

Only a circle several feet across.

Winter grass became black.

For one heartbeat.

Then normal again.

Zee felt pressure against his bones.

Same impossible almost-language as before.

Not words.

Need.

Movement.

Blocked.

Danger.

Rez looked at Zee.

“You are getting something.”

“Not language.”

“What?”

Zee focused.

Images arrived.

A migration path.

Animals moving through deep wild folds.

Then a rupture.

Fire.

Not Dragonfire.

Different.

White-green.

A section of folded terrain collapsing.

Creatures scattering.

One route closed.

Then—

A thing Zee recognized.

Not species.

Structure.

A tower.

Human-made.

Built at the edge of unfamiliar land.

Ner saw only Zee’s face.

“What?”

“Someone built something.”

“Where?”

“I think inside.”

Rez frowned.

“Inside the region?”

Zee nodded slowly.

The antlered creature raised its head.

The view vanished.

Then it turned north.

Took three steps.

Stopped.

Looked back without eyes.

Zee stared.

Rez sighed.

“No.”

Zee smiled.

“It wants us to follow.”

“We do not know that.”

Ner looked toward the creature.

“Yes, we do.”

Rez turned.

“How?”

Ner pointed.

The animal had taken another three steps.

Stopped again.

Zareth’s Link supplied dry amusement.

Rez closed his eyes.

“Fine.”

The wolf elder, who had arrived with them, looked horrified.

“You are not going back in there.”

Zee turned.

“Probably.”

“That is not an answer.”

“It is the true one.”

The elder stared toward the creature.

“What if this is bait?”

Rez answered.

“Then we find out before sending anyone else.”

The elder looked toward him.

“You are all fifteen.”

Rez nodded.

“Yes.”

Nothing else.

The elder seemed to realize age was not going to win the argument.

Ner stepped toward the antlered creature.

It did not retreat.

“Whatever happened inside affected the migration.”

Zee nodded.

“And whatever caused it looks like something built.”

Rez’s expression darkened.

That was important.

The deep wild had not come looking for kingdoms.

Someone from the known world may have gone farther in.

Zareth lifted his wings.

Question through the Link.

Go?

Zee looked toward the others.

Rez sighed.

Ner smiled.

Of course.

Zee turned toward the wolf elder.

“Keep everyone outside.”

“You cannot order me.”

“No.”

Zee looked toward the strange creature.

“But if we are right, the thing inside may be dangerous because somebody already ignored the warning.”

The elder’s face tightened.

Then he nodded.

“Six hours.”

Rez frowned.

“What?”

“If you are not back in six hours, we do not send anyone after you.”

Zee smiled.

“Good.”

The elder blinked.

“You agree?”

“Yes.”

Rez looked toward him.

Zee continued.

“If this place folds people wrong, adding more bodies is stupid.”

Ner nodded.

“There is hope for you.”

Zee shoved him lightly.

The antlered creature started walking.

This time they followed.

The line between mapped kingdoms and everything beyond them opened without a door.

One step was winter field.

The next was black grass beneath silver rain.

No transition.

No warning.

No border stone.

Zee looked back.

The wolves were gone.

The sky had changed.

And the creature had already moved fifty yards ahead.

Rez drew his sword.

Ner’s Gold gathered around his hands.

Zareth spread enormous wings.

Zee’s Crimson lines returned around the world.

This time, they had not entered the deep wild because they were lost.

Something inside had asked for help.

Or something close enough to asking that Zee Darkheart was willing to find out.

And if someone from the kingdoms had brought fire into a place older than their maps—

then the monsters might not be the things with antlers.

Chapter Fifty-Three

The Men Who Built a Sun

Silver rain fell upward.

Zee hated it immediately.

Not because it was dangerous.

Because every drop that struck his skin rolled toward the sky instead of the ground.

His hair slowly became wetter from underneath.

“That is disgusting.”

Rez looked over while trying to keep his footing on black grass that leaned away from him.

“Of all the things here, that bothers you?”

“Yes.”

Ner tilted his head.

“It is actually fascinating.”

“You would say that.”

A droplet struck Ner’s chin and slid upward along his cheek.

He smiled.

Zee stared.

Then realized he was staring.

Then became irritated with himself because even impossible rain could apparently become a Ner problem.

Rez saw.

He said nothing.

That was worse.

Zareth moved overhead.

His crimson body crossed a violet sky where two mountain ranges hung at different angles, one below and one suspended sideways in the distance.

Through the Link came tactical impressions.

Antlered creature ahead.

Large herd farther east.

Fire-light beyond ridge.

Movement.

Human-sized.

Zee looked toward Rez.

“There are people.”

Rez’s expression sharpened.

“How many?”

Zareth sent scattered points.

Twelve.

Maybe more below ground.

Ner frowned.

“Human?”

Zee waited for the Link.

No certainty.

“Two legs.”

Rez sighed.

“Useful.”

They followed the antlered creature across a landscape that made direction meaningless.

The black grass ended at a cliff.

Except the cliff extended horizontally into open air.

The creature walked onto it.

Zee stopped.

“No.”

Ner looked toward him.

“You are scared of heights?”

“No.”

“You have Zareth as a best friend.”

“I am scared of walking on walls that think they are floors.”

Rez stepped beside him.

“Reasonable.”

The antlered creature continued.

Its six legs adhered to stone as if gravity agreed with it.

Zareth banked nearby.

The Link delivered an image of the same path from above.

Except from Zareth’s angle, the cliff was level ground.

Zee frowned.

“This place is rude.”

Ner smiled.

“Move.”

He stepped onto the vertical stone.

Nothing happened.

His body rotated without rotating.

One heartbeat Zee watched Ner standing sideways.

The next Zee’s mind accepted the surface as ground.

Ner looked back.

“Come on.”

Zee hated that Ner looked good while doing impossible things.

He stepped.

The world shifted.

Rez came next.

No comment.

His face suggested comment would happen later.

They crossed.

At the far end, the smell reached Zee.

Smoke.

Metal.

Blood.

Not much blood.

Oil.

Alchemy.

Witchcraft.

And something artificial burning too hot.

Zee stopped.

“I know that smell.”

Rez looked toward him.

“What?”

“Not the whole thing.”

He inhaled.

“Spell fuel.”

Ner’s expression sharpened.

“Human-made?”

“Witch-made.”

Zareth landed nearby.

The antlered guide finally stopped.

Ahead, black grass opened into a crater.

Someone had built a camp inside it.

Not tents.

Structures.

Metal supports drilled into pale stone.

Wooden platforms.

Ropes.

Crates.

Three portable ward pylons.

A central framework surrounded something bright.

Too bright.

White-green light burned inside an iron cage.

It resembled a tiny sun.

Zee’s Dragon nature recoiled.

Hard.

Crimson scales raced across his neck.

His shoulder ridges tightened.

Zareth snarled so violently the ground vibrated.

The Link hit Zee with pain.

Wrong-fire.

Dragon instinct hated it.

Ner stared.

“What is that?”

Rez looked toward the workers below.

“Whatever it is, they built it.”

The antlered creature lowered its head.

The black grass around its feet faded gray.

Zee understood.

“That is what damaged the route.”

Ner crouched.

Golden Mana formed along his fingertips.

He studied the distant framework without touching it.

His face changed.

“No.”

Rez looked toward him.

“What?”

“That is not producing energy.”

“What is it doing?”

Ner looked at the world around them.

“Taking structure.”

Zee frowned.

“Explain.”

“I am trying.”

Ner narrowed his eyes.

“Magic usually has an anchor.”

“Caster.”

“Object.”

“Place.”

“Blood.”

“Something.”

He pointed toward the white-green light.

“That thing is anchoring itself by forcing the surrounding space to become simpler.”

Rez looked toward the impossible mountain overhead.

“Which means?”

“It is making this place obey ordinary geometry.”

Silence.

Zee looked at the crater again.

Around the artificial light, the deep wild looked almost normal.

Ground stayed down.

Rain fell downward.

Trees grew upright.

Distances held.

A circle of kingdom logic carved into a place that did not share it.

Rez’s face hardened.

“They are not studying the region.”

“No,” Ner said.

“They are changing it.”

The antlered creature moved its head toward the eastern horizon.

Zee followed.

Far away, herds of pale animals crowded against folded terrain.

Their migration route severed by the artificial stable zone.

Zee’s darkness stirred.

This time not because he enjoyed violence.

Because someone had entered a place they did not understand and decided understanding was unnecessary if they could force it to behave.

He thought of Victor.

Different scale.

Same temptation.

Control what frightens you.

Call that safety.

Rez watched the camp.

“We need to know why.”

Zee looked at him.

“You already know enough?”

“No.”

Good.

Rez continued.

“Maybe they are preventing something worse.”

Ner nodded reluctantly.

“Possible.”

Zee did not like it.

That did not make it false.

Zareth’s Link pushed a memory.

Drakonis border engineers stabilizing volcanic ground before hatchling migrations.

Sometimes changing dangerous land saved lives.

Important distinction.

Zee exhaled.

“Fine.”

Rez smiled.

“You are learning patience.”

“Do not ruin it.”

⸻

They entered the camp openly.

That was Rez’s decision.

Zee hated it.

Sneaking would imply guilt if the camp was legitimate.

Attacking would be worse.

So four fifteen-year-olds and one enormous Dragon walked down the crater slope toward a group of researchers who reacted exactly as badly as expected.

Weapons came out.

Wards ignited.

Someone shouted:

“Dragon!”

Someone else shouted:

“Darkheart!”

Zee sighed.

“Of course they know me.”

Rez lifted empty hands.

“We are not attacking.”

A woman near the central framework stepped forward.

Forties.

Witch.

Dark green Mana.

Heavy coat.

Silver goggles.

Not a soldier.

Her first reaction to Zee was not fear.

It was annoyance.

“What are you doing here?”

Zee blinked.

That was new.

Rez answered.

“Investigating disappearances tied to this region.”

“You should not be here.”

Ner looked toward the artificial sun.

“That makes at least six people who should not be here.”

The woman’s eyes narrowed.

“Who are you?”

“Nereus Azrion.”

Her expression changed at the name.

Not greed.

Recognition.

Professional.

“Golden Mana.”

Ner’s face hardened.

“My name was first.”

The woman paused.

Then:

“Fair.”

She looked toward Rez.

“Prince Vesper.”

“Yes.”

Then Zareth.

She swallowed.

“Crown Prince Drakonis.”

Zareth stared.

Finally Zee.

“Zee Darkheart.”

Zee smiled.

“There.”

“What?”

“You used my name.”

The woman looked confused.

Rez covered his face briefly.

“My name is Doctor Maeven Oris.”

Zee frowned.

“Doctor?”

“Scholar.”

“That sounds safer.”

“It is not.”

Ner smiled faintly.

Rez asked, “What did you build?”

Maeven looked toward the caged light.

“A stabilization core.”

“Purpose?”

“To create a survivable research perimeter.”

Ner stared at her.

“You are rewriting local spatial behavior.”

Maeven’s expression sharpened.

“You understand it?”

“No.”

That surprised her.

Ner continued.

“I understand what it is doing.”

“Not why it works.”

Maeven looked at him differently now.

Respect.

Maybe.

“Neither do we.”

Zee laughed once.

Everyone looked at him.

“You built it anyway?”

Maeven’s face hardened.

“We lost eleven researchers before the first stable perimeter.”

Rez’s expression changed.

“Dead?”

“Missing.”

Important.

Maeven continued.

“We came here after finding evidence of rare spatial minerals beyond the western range.”

Zee looked toward the pale supports.

“Mining?”

“Research.”

Ner glanced at the crates.

Some were marked with ore weights.

Maeven saw.

“Research funds itself poorly.”

Ner’s mouth tightened.

There.

Less noble.

More complicated.

Rez asked, “Did you know you were blocking migration?”

Maeven frowned.

“What migration?”

Zee looked toward the antlered creature.

It had remained beyond the camp boundary.

Maeven saw it.

Her face went pale.

“That thing has been following us for weeks.”

“Did it attack?”

“No.”

“Did you attack it?”

Maeven hesitated.

Zee’s expression cooled.

“How many?”

“Two.”

Zareth growled.

Maeven looked toward the Dragon.

“They approached the perimeter.”

Ner stared.

“So?”

“We did not know what they were.”

Zee almost laughed at the familiarity of that sentence.

Rez spoke first.

“And what happened after?”

“The terrain became more hostile.”

Zee looked toward him.

Rez looked back.

There.

Pattern.

Maeven’s face changed.

“You think it is retaliating.”

Zee shook his head.

“I think you keep calling everything retaliation because you assume it is thinking about you.”

Maeven stared.

That landed.

Zee continued.

“Maybe you built your core across where they live.”

Ner stepped closer to the framework.

“Turn it off.”

Maeven immediately said, “No.”

“Why?”

“Because if we shut it down too quickly, every stabilized boundary may collapse at once.”

Ner stopped.

That mattered.

“How many?”

“Seven field anchors.”

“How far?”

“Four miles.”

Rez cursed quietly.

They had found one camp.

The damage was larger.

Zee looked toward the antlered creature.

The pressure in his bones intensified.

Images.

Herds trapped.

Folds compressed.

One section tearing.

Not anger.

Emergency.

Ner looked at Zee.

“It is showing you something.”

“Yes.”

“What?”

Zee described it.

Maeven went pale.

“That cannot happen.”

Ner rounded on her.

“You just said you do not understand how the region works.”

Maeven stared.

Then shut her mouth.

Good.

Rez stepped toward the camp map.

“Show us the seven anchors.”

Maeven hesitated.

Rez’s voice sharpened.

“Now.”

Future king.

No shouting needed.

Maeven unfolded a field chart.

Seven stabilization points formed a rough ring.

Ner stared.

Then his face changed.

“Oh, no.”

Zee hated that phrase from him.

“What?”

Ner traced the circle.

“These are not independent.”

Maeven nodded.

“They reinforce each other.”

“No.”

Ner looked at her.

“They are tightening.”

Maeven frowned.

“What?”

“Your anchors are not holding seven areas stable.”

Pure Golden Mana flickered over the map.

The geometry became visible.

Lines pulling inward.

“They are compressing everything unstable between them.”

Rez immediately understood.

“A trap.”

“For the land itself.”

The ground shuddered.

Hard.

Zareth spread his wings.

The artificial sun brightened.

Every impossible mountain in the distance shifted at once.

The antlered creature outside the perimeter collapsed onto its front legs.

Zee felt the pressure hit his Dragon nature like a hammer.

His horns burned.

Crimson lines exploded across his vision.

Folds everywhere.

Too many.

All being dragged toward the stabilization ring.

Ner grabbed his shoulder.

“What do you see?”

Zee could barely answer.

“Everything is folding inward.”

Rez looked toward Maeven.

“How long?”

She stared at her instruments.

“I do not know.”

“Guess.”

“Minutes.”

Zee smiled without humor.

“There goes diplomacy.”

Rez pointed toward the central core.

“No one destroys anything yet.”

Zee looked offended.

“I know.”

Ner was already studying the map.

“We have to release the anchors in sequence.”

Maeven stared.

“That will collapse the perimeter.”

“Yes.”

“And kill us.”

“Maybe.”

Maeven looked horrified.

Ner continued.

“If we leave them active, you may collapse whatever this place uses instead of geography.”

“That could be worse.”

Rez took command.

“Zareth.”

The Dragon Prince looked toward him.

“Aerial anchors.”

Zareth launched.

“Ner, sequence.”

“Working.”

“Maeven, evacuation.”

She hesitated.

Rez shouted for the first time.

“Move!”

She moved.

“Zee.”

Zee looked toward him.

Rez pointed toward the Crimson lines only Zee could see.

“You tell us where reality is safe enough to stand.”

Zee smiled.

“That is a terrible job.”

“You are uniquely qualified.”

“Rude.”

“Accurate.”

The camp erupted.

Researchers grabbed equipment.

Others abandoned it.

Crates were left.

Good.

Life before ore.

Zee moved through the crater seeing folds no one else could.

“Not left!”

A team changed direction.

The ground where they would have stepped opened into silver ocean.

“Right!”

Ner shouted from the central frame.

“Anchor six first!”

Zareth’s Link flashed.

Found.

Teal-and-Gold Mana struck not the anchor itself but the support braces around it.

Careful.

Independent judgment.

The first anchor tilted.

Ner released its magical connection remotely.

The world screamed.

There was no other word.

A vibration passed through Zee’s teeth.

The black grass outside the perimeter turned white.

Maeven shouted, “That made it worse!”

Ner ignored her.

“Anchor two!”

Zee saw the folds.

“No!”

Everyone stopped.

Ner looked at him.

Zee pointed to the map.

“If two releases now, that whole side overlaps.”

Ner stared.

Then recalculated.

“You are right.”

That scared Zee.

Ner rarely said it that quickly.

“Four.”

Rez relayed.

Zareth turned midair.

The Dragon Link carried understanding.

Anchor four fell.

A section of artificial normalcy vanished.

Gravity changed.

Three researchers lifted from the ground.

Zee jumped.

Caught one.

Rez grabbed another.

Ner threw a Golden plane beneath the third and rotated it until the woman dropped safely.

Maeven stared.

“This is impossible.”

Zee shouted, “Stop saying that!”

Another tremor.

The artificial sun cracked.

White-green fire leaked through the cage.

Zareth screamed through the Link.

Pain.

Zee’s Dragon nature answered.

The fire hurt Dragons.

Not ordinary flame.

Something about forced stability cut against what Dragon magic sensed in the deep wild.

Zee’s scales spread.

He looked at the core.

Darkness stirred.

Destroy it.

Easy.

No.

Not yet.

Rez saw him.

“Zee!”

“I know!”

“Good!”

Ner shouted:

“Three and seven together!”

Zee checked the folds.

“Yes!”

Zareth hit seven.

Zee ran toward three.

Maeven shouted, “What are you doing?”

“Helping!”

“There is a release lever!”

“Where?”

“Inside the frame!”

Zee smiled.

“Of course.”

He entered.

White-green fire struck his arm.

Pain tore through him.

His Crimson scales blackened.

Did not die.

Did not stop.

His body adapted enough to keep moving.

Not immunity.

Resistance growing second by second.

The fire bit differently each time.

His Crimson Mana changed around it.

Less like a shield.

More like a refusal to let the forced stability define his blood.

Unique.

His.

Zee reached the lever.

Pulled.

Anchor three released.

At the same instant, Zareth tore seven free.

The artificial sun imploded.

Not exploded.

Light collapsed inward.

The crater disappeared.

For one heartbeat Zee stood nowhere.

No ground.

No sky.

No sound.

Then Ner’s hand caught his.

Golden Mana.

Boundary.

Rez grabbed Ner.

Zareth’s Link hit Zee like a chain of instinct.

Together.

Four points.

Not enough to control the deep wild.

Enough not to lose one another.

The world returned.

Black grass.

Silver rain upward.

No camp.

No crater.

No artificial sun.

Researchers scattered across the field.

Alive.

Maeven lay twenty yards away staring at the sky.

All seven anchors were gone.

The deep wild settled.

Slowly.

The strange mountains returned to impossible positions.

The migrating herd began moving.

The antlered creature rose.

Zee lay on his back breathing hard.

Ner’s hand was still locked around his.

Neither released.

Rez sat nearby covered in black grass.

Zareth landed with enough force to shake silver rain from the sky.

The Link flooded Zee.

Alive.

Angry.

Relieved.

Zee laughed.

Ner looked at him.

“What?”

“We fixed it.”

Rez groaned.

“We survived fixing it.”

“Same thing.”

“No.”

The antlered creature approached.

Every researcher tensed.

Zee lifted one hand.

“Do not.”

They listened.

Good.

The creature stopped near Maeven.

She stared up at it.

No weapon.

No spell.

For the first time, perhaps, no assumption.

The creature lowered its antlers.

A fold opened between them.

Maeven saw another landscape.

A migration.

Broken paths reconnecting.

Then the view closed.

Maeven whispered:

“We were in the way.”

Zee sat up.

“Yes.”

She looked toward him.

Not angry.

Ashamed.

“We thought the instability was the danger.”

Ner finally released Zee’s hand.

“Sometimes the instability is just the rule.”

Maeven nodded.

That lesson hurt her.

Good.

Lessons should.

Rez stood.

“What happens to your research?”

Maeven looked toward the destroyed equipment.

“Over.”

One of her researchers protested.

“Doctor—”

“No.”

She looked toward the migrating herd.

“We entered without understanding enough to know what damage meant.”

Then toward the surviving staff.

“We leave.”

Zee watched her.

No villain defeated.

No execution.

No glorious victory.

Just a woman realizing curiosity had become entitlement somewhere along the way.

Zee understood that danger.

He felt it himself.

He wanted to know everything about the deep wild.

Wanted to touch the folds.

Test the Crimson perception.

See what else existed beyond kingdom maps.

But wanting knowledge did not make everything his to open.

That mattered.

The antlered creature turned.

Walked toward a fold.

Then stopped.

Looked back.

Not at the researchers.

At the four.

Zee felt one final concept.

Not invitation.

Not friendship.

Recognition.

Different.

Allowed.

For now.

Then it vanished.

No door.

No spectacle.

One step here.

Next step elsewhere.

Zareth watched.

The Link carried wonder.

Ner stared at the empty space.

Rez exhaled.

“Well.”

Zee smiled.

“What?”

Rez looked around at silver rain, impossible mountains, and a herd walking through the side of a hill.

“We need better maps.”

Ner laughed.

Zee did too.

The known world had become smaller again.

Not because they had conquered the deep wild.

Because they had discovered that something could exist beyond kingdoms without asking to become one.

And somewhere beyond those folding horizons, the world continued.

Older.

Stranger.

Alive.

Waiting for no prince.

Not even Zee Darkheart.
