Chapter Sixty

The Years That Made the King

Sixteen

One year after Aurelia died, Zee stopped visiting her grave every morning.

Not because he missed her less.

Because grief had changed shape.

At fifteen, he had woken expecting pain and found it waiting.

At sixteen, pain woke with him.

It had become part of the architecture.

He carried it into hunts.

Into meals.

Into sleep.

Into the spaces where laughter still occasionally found him and immediately made him remember the person whose laugh he wanted most.

He no longer spoke to Aurelia’s grave every day.

Sometimes he simply sat beside it.

Sometimes he brought blood on his mouth.

That would have bothered the boy he had been.

It no longer bothered the boy becoming a man.

Tonight, he arrived after killing three hunters who had spent months taking supernatural children from isolated villages and selling their locations to kingdoms that wanted rare bloodlines contained.

Zee had followed them for nine days.

Not because he could not catch them sooner.

Because he wanted everyone attached to the network.

Nanda Parbat had changed the way he hunted.

He did not attack the first man.

He followed him.

Learned where he slept.

Who he paid.

Who he feared.

Which hand reached for a knife.

Which tavern door lacked a guard during rain.

Which accomplice always checked behind himself twice and therefore never noticed the person already ahead.

The first hunter died without seeing Zee.

One knife beneath the ribs.

Upward.

Heart.

Silent.

The second realized what was happening only when Zee appeared inside his locked room.

The man reached for a bell.

Zee’s Vampire speed could have crossed the distance.

He did not need it.

He had already cut the bell cord.

The hunter looked toward the empty rope.

Then Zee.

Fear.

Zee liked that moment now.

The realization.

The mind trying to recalculate around a predator already inside the plan.

“Please.”

Zee studied him.

Blood scent.

Human.

No compulsion marks.

No magical coercion.

No evidence someone else had forced him into this.

“You knew what the children were for?”

The man swallowed.

“Yes.”

“Did you care?”

Silence.

Enough.

Zee killed him.

No speech.

No anger.

No guilt afterward.

The third hunter was a Wolf.

He ran.

That was a mistake.

Zee let him.

For nearly an hour.

Through wet forest.

Across a stream.

Up stone where the hunter deliberately cut his own palm and threw blood east to confuse a Vampire tracker.

Zee smiled when he found it.

Clever.

Not enough.

Wolf Zee took over.

The trail was not blood.

It was crushed fern.

Changed bird calls.

A fox refusing one patch of ground.

Mud compressed beneath one heel harder than the other.

The hunter had an old hip injury.

Zee knew which side he would favor when tired.

He reached the destination first.

Waited inside the abandoned watchtower.

The Wolf entered gasping.

Saw Zee sitting on the windowsill.

Stopped.

“You…”

Zee stood.

“No more running?”

The Wolf attacked.

Claws.

Strength.

Fury.

Zee met him without Witchcraft.

Wolf against Wolf.

His own claws extended.

His stance lowered.

His body read aggression before conscious thought.

Shoulder.

Hip.

Weight.

Predatory instinct.

The enemy lunged.

Zee slipped outside the attack, hooked one arm, drove his knee into the old hip, and broke the joint.

The Wolf screamed.

Zee caught his throat before he fell.

Fangs descended.

The Wolf smelled what was coming.

“No.”

Zee’s crimson eyes darkened.

“You sold children to people who cut them open.”

“I can tell you names.”

“I already have them.”

“Please.”

Zee thought about mercy.

Actually thought.

Then decided no.

He fed.

Wolf blood burned hotter than Human.

By sixteen, Zee could tell far more from supernatural blood than species.

Age.

Health.

Poison.

Recent spell exposure.

Foreign blood in the body.

Old curse residue.

The Wolf had traces of silver poisoning from years earlier.

His body had adapted around it imperfectly.

Zee drank.

His own Crimson blood processed everything differently.

Nothing copied.

Nothing stolen whole.

The silver history entered an organism that had already survived suppression, dragonbane, demonic essence, strange folded spaces, and the blood of six killers.

Hours later, silver touched Zee’s skin and burned less deeply than before.

Not immunity.

Accumulation.

Crimson adaptation.

One more thing that would have killed an ordinary predator becoming less effective against him.

Zee returned to Aurelia’s grave after midnight.

Rez was already there.

Of course.

He sat against the opposite side of the memorial stone with a cup in one hand.

“You smell terrible.”

Zee sat beside him.

“Wolf.”

“I guessed.”

“Then why comment?”

“Brotherly obligation.”

Zee took the cup.

“Mine?”

“It was.”

Zee drank.

Rez stared.

“You are unbelievable.”

“You gave it to me.”

“I set it down.”

“Near me.”

“That is not law.”

“It should be.”

For a moment they were sixteen-year-old idiots beside a grave.

Zee laughed.

Quiet.

Real.

Then footsteps approached.

Ner.

His eyes had changed over the year.

Pure Gold remained.

Always.

But dark-red sometimes moved beneath it when hunger sharpened or Bloodsong rose close to the surface.

His voice had changed too.

Not deeper simply from age.

Richer.

Layered when power entered it.

He could feel injured blood before wounds appeared in sight.

Could sometimes calm a panicked heart with a single tone.

Could make spilled blood reveal who it had belonged to through resonance.

He hated when people treated that as a trick.

Zee had learned not to.

Ner sat on Zee’s other side.

“Three?”

Zee looked over.

“How do you know?”

“I can hear it.”

“Their blood?”

Ner nodded toward Zee’s chest.

“Inside you.”

Zee went still.

That was new.

“What does it sound like?”

“Mostly like you ate badly.”

Rez laughed.

Zee shoved him.

Ner smiled.

Then his expression softened.

“You all right?”

Zee looked at Aurelia’s name.

No one replaced her.

No hand did what hers had done.

No voice reached the same place.

“No.”

Ner nodded.

No attempt to repair the answer.

His shoulder leaned against Zee’s.

Rez remained on the other side.

Far above, the Dragon Link opened faintly.

Zareth was in Drakonis.

Mountain wind.

Heat.

A council chamber.

Then warmth.

The four remained connected even when not together.

But the empty place beside Aurelia’s grave stayed empty.

Zee had stopped expecting otherwise.

That year, the stories changed.

The Blood Hunter stopped meaning a reckless prince who happened to kill predators.

It began meaning something else.

If Zee Darkheart accepted your hunt—

he usually finished it.

⸻

Seventeen

At seventeen, Zee compelled thirty-two Vampires without looking at half of them.

That was not the plan.

The plan had been negotiation.

Rez blamed Zee.

Zee blamed the Vampires.

Ner blamed everyone.

Zareth found the entire situation extremely entertaining until someone shot him with a ballista.

Then he became less charitable.

The Crimson Marsh settlement had spent six months raiding villages beneath Vesper protection, taking blood from humans and witches under the claim that ancient feeding rights predated Lucien’s border agreements.

Rez arrived with signed treaties.

The Vampire lord laughed at them.

“Paper.”

Rez remained seated across the long stone table.

“Law.”

“Your law.”

“Your signature is on it.”

“My grandfather’s.”

“Then your House inherited the benefits and obligations.”

The lord smiled.

“You sound like your father.”

Rez smiled back.

“Thank you.”

Zee stood behind him in black, silent enough that three Vampires repeatedly forgot he had changed position.

Nanda Parbat habits had become instinct.

He watched wrists.

Throats.

Weapons.

Heartbeats.

Exit angles.

The Vampire lord looked toward him.

“The Blood Hunter.”

Zee’s expression did not change.

“Apparently.”

“I expected more.”

“People usually do.”

Ner sat near the wall reading the treaty annotations.

He looked up.

“Your grandfather also agreed that feeding on protected settlements would terminate your marsh rights.”

The lord’s eyes narrowed.

“You are the singing Witch.”

Ner closed the document.

“Nereus.”

Zee’s jaw tightened.

Ner glanced toward him.

He did not need rescuing from a bad title.

Zee let it go.

Progress.

The Vampire lord leaned back.

“We are done.”

Rez nodded.

“Then you stop feeding beyond your territory.”

“No.”

Silence.

Rez stood.

“Then you understood the negotiation incorrectly.”

Every Vampire in the chamber moved.

Thirty-two.

Some old.

Some young.

All armed.

Zee inhaled.

Bloodlines opened to him.

Family relations.

Sired lines.

Age differences.

Three recently fed.

One poisoned.

Two carrying enchanted blood from witches they had bitten.

He knew which one would move first.

Before she did.

Zee whispered:

“Sit.”

The first Vampire stopped.

Only her.

Everyone stared.

Her knees bent.

She sat.

The lord’s face changed.

“Compulsion.”

Zee smiled faintly.

“No.”

He looked across the room.

His predatory presence changed.

Vampire Zee.

No Witchcraft.

No Crimson spell.

His will pressed outward through sound, blood, fear, and the instincts every Vampire understood when a stronger predator entered territory.

“Everyone.”

Twenty heads turned.

Twelve did not.

Zee did not raise his voice.

“Sit down.”

Twenty obeyed.

The others resisted.

Zee felt every resistance separately.

Old minds.

Wards.

Training.

One wore a charm blocking eye-based domination.

Zee noticed.

Interesting.

His eyes shifted toward the Vampire with the charm.

The man deliberately stared at the floor.

Zee spoke.

“You too.”

The Vampire’s body jerked.

He remained standing.

Barely.

Zee felt the command catch somewhere beyond eyes.

Voice.

Blood.

Predatory hierarchy.

Not perfected.

Not effortless.

But there.

The Vampire’s knees trembled.

Then hit stone.

The remaining eleven reacted.

Weapons came free.

Rez sighed.

“You could have waited.”

“They were going to attack.”

“I know.”

“Then why complain?”

“Tradition.”

The chamber erupted.

Zee moved.

Assassin technique inside Vampire speed.

One throat struck.

One elbow broken.

A pressure point beneath one jaw shut down another attacker’s balance before supernatural strength finished the problem.

Rez turned the room into geometry.

“Left!”

Zee moved left before asking.

Blue-White Mana froze two floor sections, controlling movement.

“Ner, upper balcony!”

Pure Gold split into six narrow boundaries, turning the balcony into a cage.

Zareth crashed through the outer wall because the ballista crew had made the poor decision of involving him.

Stone exploded.

Rez shouted:

“There was a door!”

The Dragon Link returned absolute indifference.

Zee laughed while disarming a Vampire.

Then the Vampire lord tried escaping.

Zee smelled it before he moved.

Fear.

Blood.

Intent.

Wolf pursuit joined Vampire blood sense.

Zee disappeared.

He caught the lord outside the settlement half a mile away.

No magic.

The lord stared.

“How?”

Zee smiled.

“You ran where frightened things run.”

The lord attacked.

Zee ended it in six movements.

He could have killed him.

Instead he compelled him.

The lord resisted.

Hard.

Zee pushed.

Blood ran from one nostril.

Not the lord’s.

Zee’s.

The domination strained something inside his Vampire nature.

He enjoyed the contest.

“Look at me.”

The lord squeezed his eyes shut.

Zee’s smile deepened.

“No.”

He stepped close.

“You do not get to hide from me that easily.”

The command struck again.

The Vampire’s eyes opened against his will.

There.

A threshold.

Not ordinary compulsion anymore.

Still imperfect.

Still needing focus.

But evolving.

“Kneel.”

The lord knelt.

“Release every captive.”

“Yes.”

“Honor the treaty.”

“Yes.”

“Remember exactly how helpless this felt.”

The lord’s face twisted.

“Yes.”

Zee released him.

He could have drained him.

Wanted to.

Did not.

Not mercy.

Utility.

Fear would travel faster if the lord survived.

By winter, three settlements surrendered captives before Zee ever crossed their borders.

Reputation had become a weapon.

Zee began using it deliberately.

⸻

The relationship with Ner changed that same year.

Not during a battle.

Not while someone was bleeding.

Not under moonlight with some ridiculous speech.

It happened in Vesper’s western kitchen at two in the morning.

Ner was stealing cake.

Zee caught him.

“You said you were going to sleep.”

Ner froze with half a slice in his hand.

“You were not supposed to be here.”

“I live here.”

“So do I.”

“That weakens your argument.”

Ner took a bite.

Zee stared.

“You are eating my cake.”

“Lucien’s cake.”

“Everything in Vesper eventually becomes mine through Rez.”

“That is not how inheritance works.”

“You sure?”

“Yes.”

Zee stepped closer.

Ner did not move.

Seventeen years of friendship sat between them.

Childhood.

Blood.

Death.

Aurelia.

Ner’s second heartbeat beginning where none should have.

Countless almost-moments.

Looks.

Touches.

Things everyone except them had stopped pretending not to understand.

Zee reached for the cake.

Ner moved it away.

Their bodies ended up closer.

Neither laughed.

Zee looked at his mouth.

Ner noticed.

“Zee.”

“What?”

“You are doing it again.”

“Looking?”

“Yes.”

“I know.”

Ner stopped breathing for half a heartbeat.

“That is new.”

Zee’s crimson eyes lifted.

“I got tired of pretending.”

Ner’s expression softened.

“Took you long enough.”

Zee frowned.

“You knew?”

“Everyone knew.”

“I hate everyone.”

“I know.”

Ner set the cake down.

Then kissed him.

Simple.

Brief.

Enough to silence Zee Darkheart completely.

Ner pulled back.

Zee stared.

“You—”

“Yes.”

“You did that.”

“Very observant.”

Zee kissed him back.

Longer.

Still seventeen.

Awkward enough that their noses bumped and Ner laughed against his mouth.

Zee laughed too.

No grand declaration.

They already loved each other.

That had been the problem.

Now they stopped lying about what kind of love had grown beside friendship.

Later, Rez found them sitting on the kitchen floor sharing the stolen cake.

He looked at their joined hands.

Then at both of them.

“No.”

Zee smiled.

“What?”

“I waited years.”

“For?”

“This.”

Ner covered his face.

Rez pointed.

“I deserve recognition.”

“You deserve to leave,” Zee said.

Rez stole the last piece of cake and ran.

Zee chased him through the palace.

Ner followed laughing.

For one night, grief did not disappear.

It simply made room.

⸻

Eighteen

At eighteen, Zee stopped living at Vesper full-time.

He did not leave because Lucien asked.

Lucien never did.

He did not leave because Rez wanted distance.

Rez hated the decision.

He did not leave because Ner or Zareth had become less important.

The opposite.

He left because he finally understood the difference between being loved somewhere and belonging beneath someone else’s roof forever.

Vesper was home.

It was not his kingdom.

Darkheart was his blood.

It was not yet his rule.

Drakonis loved Zareth.

Not Zee.

Good.

Zee needed something that existed because people chose him.

The first place was ugly.

An abandoned fortress on no kingdom’s favored border.

Half the northern wall had collapsed.

The well tasted metallic.

The towers leaned.

There were rats large enough that Zee briefly considered recruiting them as guards.

Rez stared at the ruin.

“This?”

Zee stood inside the broken courtyard.

“Yes.”

“There are better forts.”

“They belong to people.”

“This one belongs to someone.”

“Who?”

Rez checked the parchment.

“A dead baron whose heirs abandoned it sixty years ago.”

Zee smiled.

“Exactly.”

Ner walked through a doorway that immediately collapsed behind him.

He looked back.

“No.”

Zee laughed.

Zareth landed on a nearby hill because the courtyard could not hold him.

The Link carried disgust.

“This is temporary.”

The Dragon remained unconvinced.

Zee looked around.

No banners.

No throne.

No inherited expectation.

Perfect.

People arrived anyway.

First, a Witch family driven from a southern kingdom because one daughter had demon ancestry.

Zee allowed them inside.

Then three Wolves who refused a clan lord’s order to kill mixed-blood infants.

Then two Vampires who had broken from a nest feeding on unwilling humans.

Then mercenaries.

Not saints.

People.

Some needed protection.

Some wanted employment.

Some wanted Zee.

That distinction mattered.

He made rules.

Few.

Simple.

No slavery.

No trafficking.

No forced feeding on people under his protection.

No hunting children.

No killing inside the fortress unless defense demanded it or Zee authorized judgment.

No one belonged to him merely because he protected them.

And if someone brought danger through the gates knowingly—

they answered for it.

Rez read the first version.

“This is not enough law.”

Zee smiled.

“It is enough for forty people.”

“It will not be enough for four hundred.”

“Then I will write more.”

Rez stared.

Zee looked toward him.

“What?”

“You are planning for four hundred.”

Zee glanced across the courtyard.

People repaired stone.

A Witch reinforced the well.

A Vampire and a Wolf argued over roof beams.

Ner stood teaching two younger witches how not to walk directly through a Golden boundary while he repaired a collapsed arch.

Zareth slept outside while three children dared each other to touch his tail.

The Dragon knew.

He pretended not to.

Zee’s face softened.

“Maybe.”

Rez smiled.

“There he is.”

“Who?”

“The king.”

Zee looked at him.

“No.”

“Not yet.”

Zee’s expression darkened.

“Do not call me that.”

Rez nodded.

He understood why.

Victor.

Crown.

Control.

Not yet.

Still, people began coming.

Not because law said Zee owned them.

Because his name meant something.

To predators, threat.

To people no crown wanted, possibility.

He accepted both uses.

By eighteen, Zee could enter a settlement without guards and still change the entire mood.

His horns had matured farther, curving back in larger crimson-black arcs.

Permanent scales covered portions of his shoulders, ribs, forearms, and upper spine.

His body had filled into adult shape without being finished—taller, broader, built by supernatural movement rather than ornamental training.

His Dragon durability had increased enough that an ordinary sword shattered against one scale patch during a border fight.

His fourth nature still did not wake completely.

No wings.

No full Dragon.

But the shoulder structures beneath his back had become impossible to mistake.

Zareth noticed every change.

Through the Link came pride.

And impatience.

Zee sent back:

I know.

No spoken telepathy.

Just shared understanding.

That year, Zee took no crown.

But eighty-seven people began calling the ruined fortress home.

Not Darkheart subjects.

Not Vesper refugees.

His people.

That frightened Victor more than any battle had.

⸻

Nineteen

At nineteen, Zee killed twelve people before breakfast and slept perfectly well that night.

They were not innocent.

That distinction remained.

They belonged to a supernatural raiding company that had burned two villages after the villagers refused to provide bodies for blood sport.

Zee did not arrive with an army.

Armies were loud.

He arrived alone.

Rez hated the plan.

Ner hated that he did not hate it.

Zareth thought it was efficient.

The raid camp contained thirty-seven fighters.

Zee killed twelve.

Compelled nine to disarm each other.

Drove six into fleeing routes where allied Wolves captured them.

Left seven unconscious through pressure points and poisoned needles.

Three surrendered before he touched them.

He spared those three.

Choice.

The first death happened in darkness.

Knife.

Carotid.

Zee caught the body before it hit dirt.

The second was a Witch.

One precise force spell shifted her casting hand into the path of her own binding sigil.

Her magic locked her arm.

Zee broke her neck.

No flourish.

Third.

Wolf.

Tracked by scent after he fled beneath a suppression field.

Wolf Zee moved low through underbrush, silent and relentless.

When the raider turned to fight, Zee met him with claws.

Not Witchcraft.

Not Vampire speed.

He wanted the hunt.

He enjoyed it.

The raider realized that halfway through.

Fear changed his scent.

Zee smiled.

The fourth and fifth were Vampires.

He compelled one to freeze.

The other carried an anti-compulsion charm.

Zee smelled Witch blood woven into the enchantment.

He cut the cord without touching the Vampire’s body.

Then compelled him too.

“Do not move.”

The Vampire’s muscles locked.

Zee circled.

“You thought that would stop me?”

The man whispered:

“Yes.”

“Good.”

Zee fed.

Not completely.

Enough to weaken.

Enough to taste bloodline.

The Vampire had consumed demon blood recently.

Zee recognized the foreign layer instantly now.

His blood sense had become frighteningly precise through years of feeding.

He could distinguish possession residue from voluntary ingestion.

Curse from inheritance.

Poison from disease.

Foreign magic carried in blood from magic produced by the body itself.

The Vampire lied.

Zee smelled it.

Killed him.

Fed fully.

Crimson adaptation moved through Zee’s regeneration.

Years of Vampire blood had changed how fast his body recovered after severe injury.

Not ordinary healing.

His blood now prioritized structural damage almost intelligently.

Bones first if movement mattered.

Blood volume first if feeding had depleted him.

Poison isolation before tissue repair.

His body was learning survival around him.

Sixth.

Demon.

It hid inside another man’s shadow.

That trick would have fooled Zee at fifteen.

At nineteen, demon blood history had sharpened Zee’s presence perception.

Shadow wrong.

No heartbeat.

No scent.

Still there.

He stabbed it before it emerged.

The Demon begged when Zee pinned it.

Actually begged.

Once, begging would have complicated everything.

Now Zee listened for information.

There was none.

“Please.”

Zee looked at the burned village behind them.

“No.”

He fed.

Demon blood remained unpleasant.

His body remained fascinated.

Years of consuming supernatural enemies had made him harder to suppress, harder to poison, harder to bind, and increasingly resistant to hostile environments that depended on corrupting the body’s supernatural balance.

No borrowed demonic tricks.

No copied spell.

Only Zee becoming more difficult to affect the same way twice.

Seven through twelve died through combinations.

Assassin silence carrying Vampire speed.

Wolf instinct identifying an ambush before Witch sight confirmed it.

Crimson Mana redirecting one arrow into another.

Dragon durability allowing him to deliberately accept a blade so he could trap the attacker’s arm against his own scales.

Then fangs.

Always eventually blood.

When the surviving commander surrendered, Zee stood over him covered in red.

“Mercy.”

Zee crouched.

“Why?”

The commander stared.

“What?”

“Give me a reason.”

“I surrendered.”

“That is a reason not to kill you during the fight.”

The man swallowed.

“What else do you want?”

“Something that makes you useful alive.”

Silence.

Zee smiled faintly.

There.

The begging changed.

Not moral appeal.

Information.

Names.

Routes.

Employers.

One employer had ordered the village burned.

Zee listened.

Then spared the commander.

Not because mercy was good.

Because a living witness would destroy the employer more efficiently than a corpse.

Rez met him outside the camp.

“You kept him alive.”

“Yes.”

“I am proud.”

Zee stared.

“Do not make it weird.”

Rez laughed.

Ner arrived minutes later, Pure Gold tracing through the prisoners’ blood to identify which among them had actually participated in the killings and which had been forced into the company under blood-contract coercion.

His Bloodsong had grown frightening too.

He could hear lies in circulation sometimes—not thoughts, not magical truth detection, but changes in blood resonance when emotion and intent sharpened.

He made mistakes.

Corrected them.

Never pretended certainty.

One prisoner had been compelled into service.

Ner proved it.

Zee spared him immediately.

Another had volunteered.

Killed children personally.

Zee learned that through evidence, not instinct alone.

He executed him.

Ner watched.

Did not stop him.

Did not approve either.

Later, under canvas while rain struck the camp, Ner washed blood from Zee’s hands.

Not because Zee needed help.

Because he wanted to.

Zee looked at him.

“You hate when I kill slowly.”

Ner continued cleaning one knuckle.

“Yes.”

“You did not say anything.”

“You already knew.”

Zee’s expression changed.

Ner looked up.

“I am not here to issue permission.”

Good.

That was why their love survived Zee’s descent.

Ner did not exist to fix him.

Zee did not need Ner to pretend every choice was right.

They kissed with blood still drying on Zee’s throat.

Gentle.

Then Zee went outside and ordered an execution.

Both were him.

That year, some kingdoms stopped calling Zee a prince entirely.

They called him lord.

Hunter.

Monster.

Protector.

Blood King, though he had no crown.

Zee corrected none of them.

Names were useful only when people acted differently after hearing them.

Increasingly, they did.

⸻

Twenty

At twenty, Victor finally understood that Zee had become impossible to contain without touching him.

And Victor had promised himself, years ago, never to touch that kind of violence again.

Not after the infant.

Not after watching death fail.

So he used House Darkheart.

Again.

Only now the House resisted.

The first open fracture came when Lord Merek Darkheart refused Victor’s order to expel three families who had sworn protection to Zee’s growing fortress.

Victor called it treason.

Merek called it prudence.

Two more nobles sided with Merek.

Then five.

Then twelve.

Not all loved Zee.

Some feared him more than Victor.

Some simply believed the future had shifted.

Victor saw every vote as another line of an ancient prophecy tightening around his throat.

He would sometimes wake hearing the words.

Every blade raised against him shall sharpen what it seeks to destroy.

The first blade had been Victor’s.

That memory never left.

Then reports came.

Zee survived poisons that once would have crippled him.

Zee broke supernatural compulsions faster.

Zee fed from things ordinary Vampires avoided.

Zee’s hunters crossed borders where Darkheart soldiers no longer could.

Mixed supernatural families traveled voluntarily toward his fortress.

Dragons spoke his name without contempt.

Wolves called him predator and meant respect.

Witches whispered that Crimson Mana responded differently now.

And Victor remembered another fragment.

He shall not inherit the world as it was given.

He stopped sleeping.

No one knew why.

Not his council.

Not Darkheart witches.

Not even the priests who thought the King had simply grown paranoid with age.

Only Victor knew the entire prophecy.

Only Victor understood why every report felt like a countdown.

Zee knew none of it.

He spent his twentieth year doing exactly what Victor feared without ever knowing fear had predicted the shape.

He expanded the fortress.

Not into a kingdom.

Not yet.

Into territory.

People patrolled under Zee’s mark.

Not a crown.

A simple Crimson cut across black cloth.

No ancient symbolism.

No prophecy.

Just something visible at night.

Rez mocked the design.

“It looks like somebody spilled wine on a funeral banner.”

Zee stared.

“You helped choose it.”

“I was seventeen.”

“You were eighteen.”

“Even worse.”

Ner liked it.

Zareth tried burning one and discovered the material Zee’s witches used was more fire-resistant than expected.

The Link carried offense.

Zee laughed for several minutes.

At twenty, laughter happened less often.

That made everyone notice when it came.

He was fully dangerous now.

Not because he had reached his final strength.

Far from it.

Because experience had caught up to power.

Zee no longer entered fights to discover what he could do.

He entered knowing.

Blood tracking.

Wolf pursuit.

Mass compulsion.

Precise Witchcraft.

Dragon durability.

Assassin skill.

Crimson adaptation.

He used whichever nature solved the problem cleanest.

Sometimes none required combination.

Vampire Zee could dismantle a room alone.

Wolf Zee could hunt for days.

Witch Zee could control a battlefield with movements small enough enemies did not realize spells had been cast.

Dragon Zee could stand through force that broke stone and answer with Crimson heat that made older Dragons take him seriously.

Still no wings.

Still no completed awakening.

Still unfinished.

That fact annoyed him less than it once had.

He had learned unfinished did not mean weak.

Then Victor made the decision that ended everything.

He declared every Darkheart noble, soldier, witch, servant, or blood-relative who swore direct loyalty to Zee guilty of treason.

He ordered their lands seized.

Their titles stripped.

Their children removed from succession.

And those already inside Castle Darkheart who had publicly supported Zee—

imprisoned.

Not killed.

Victor had learned some lessons.

Containment.

Always containment.

Forty-three people disappeared into Darkheart cells in one day.

Lord Merek among them.

The order reached Zee at sunset.

He read it once.

Rez stood opposite the table.

Ner beside him.

Zareth outside, the Dragon Link already darkening with anger.

Theron and Seraphine waited near the wall.

Zee placed the decree down.

No shouting.

No broken furniture.

That version of him was years gone.

“What do you want to do?” Rez asked.

Zee looked toward Castle Darkheart on the map.

Victor had spent twenty years deciding what happened to people because they stood too close to his son.

Aurelia was gone.

No one stood between them now.

Zee touched the seal.

“Bring everyone home.”

Ner watched him.

“Darkheart?”

Zee nodded.

Theron’s expression sharpened.

Seraphine went still.

Rez asked the obvious question.

“How?”

Zee looked up.

His crimson eyes held no hesitation.

“I am going to my father.”

“Negotiation?”

“No.”

Silence.

Zee folded the decree.

He did not smile.

Did not threaten.

Did not need to.

“The old reign ends.”

Outside, Zareth roared.

The sound rolled across the unfinished fortress and through the people who had chosen Zee without a crown.

Some looked toward him.

Some bowed.

Zee hated that once.

At twenty, he let them.

Far away in Castle Darkheart, Victor woke from a dream with the final words of the prophecy echoing through his chamber.

The world shall break before it teaches him how to die.

He sat alone beneath the crown and understood that the future was no longer approaching.

His son was.

And this time Aurelia would not be there to save either of them.

Chapter Sixty-One

The Prophecy and the Son

At twenty-one, Zee Darkheart entered Castle Darkheart without being invited.

No one stopped him.

That was the first difference.

At fifteen, guards had watched his horns.

At twenty-one, they watched his hands.

Mature crimson-black horns swept back from his temples in dark arcs polished naturally by age and battle.

Permanent Crimson scales covered his forearms, parts of his neck, shoulders, ribs, upper spine, and patches along his jaw.

His body had finished growing into something years of fighting had already prepared—tall, powerful without excess, every movement economical.

The ridges beneath his shoulder blades had become pronounced structures under skin and scale.

Still closed.

Still no wings.

Still no full Dragon.

Still the First Natural Tribrid carrying a fourth nature that had never needed a new title to make itself real.

His crimson eyes remained unmistakably his.

Everything else about the way he looked at people had changed.

A guard near the entrance shifted his grip.

Zee noticed.

Dominant right hand.

Old left shoulder injury.

Two knives.

One anti-Vampire charm.

Fear elevated pulse.

No intention to attack.

Zee walked past.

Twenty-one had made killing possibilities quieter.

He no longer needed to stare at them.

They existed in the background of every room.

Rez walked at his right.

Twenty-one.

Crown Prince of Vesper.

No boy remained in the way he wore blue-white ceremonial armor or measured the Darkheart court with a future ruler’s patience.

Ner walked at Zee’s left.

Twenty-one.

Pure Golden Mana barely visible beneath his skin.

Vampire stillness and Witch presence coexisting with something stranger in his voice.

Years of Bloodsong development had taught him enough control that entire rooms no longer accidentally matched his heartbeat when he became emotional.

Usually.

His hand brushed Zee’s once as they entered.

Deliberate.

Zee did not look over.

He squeezed Ner’s fingers once.

Released.

Zareth came through the sky.

Twenty-one.

No longer the young Dragon that had barely fit inside Vesper courtyards.

The Crown Prince of Drakonis crossed over Castle Darkheart like a living crimson storm, Teal-and-Gold power flowing between immense scales.

He did not land.

He circled.

Independent.

Watching.

The Dragon Link opened.

Victor.

Below.

Fear.

Zee felt it too.

Not magically.

His Vampire senses could hear his father’s heart from the throne hall.

Fast.

Too fast.

Victor knew.

Zee had brought no army.

That frightened the King more.

The throne room doors opened.

Zee entered.

Twenty-one years collapsed into one room.

Victor Darkheart sat beneath the blackened crest.

Older.

Much older.

The crown looked heavier than it had six years before.

The court gathered along both sides.

Some loyal to Victor.

Some secretly to Zee.

Some loyal only to survival.

The imprisoned supporters had been moved from the cells that morning.

Victor had expected an assault.

He had placed them behind the throne under guard.

Human shields without calling them that.

Zee saw.

His face remained calm.

Victor’s fingers tightened on the throne.

“You came.”

Zee stopped at the center of the hall.

“You knew I would.”

Victor looked toward Rez.

Then Ner.

Then upward as Zareth’s shadow crossed the high windows.

“Always surrounded.”

Zee’s expression did not change.

“No.”

He looked at the prisoners.

“I came for them.”

Victor laughed weakly.

“Of course.”

“Release them.”

“No.”

Zee tilted his head.

No anger.

No threat.

That was worse now.

Victor knew.

“Then we finish.”

A murmur moved through the hall.

Rez did not speak.

Ner did not.

This was Zee’s.

Victor stood.

“You believe this is about prisoners?”

“No.”

“Then what?”

“You.”

The answer landed simply.

Victor descended the throne steps.

Twenty-one years earlier he had carried a blade toward a newborn.

Now he approached a grown man who could hear every change in his heartbeat.

The irony was almost cruel enough to be magic.

It was not.

Victor stopped ten feet away.

“You have no idea.”

Zee frowned.

“About?”

Victor stared.

For a moment he seemed genuinely confused.

Then horrified by the confusion.

“You do not know.”

Zee looked toward Rez.

Rez knew nothing.

Ner too.

“What am I supposed to know?”

Victor laughed.

One broken sound.

“No.”

He turned away.

Then back.

“You cannot.”

Zee’s assassin instincts tracked every movement.

Victor was not reaching for a weapon.

He was unraveling.

“Father.”

Victor flinched.

Zee had not called him that in years.

“What?”

“What do I not know?”

Victor stared at his son.

Then whispered:

“The prophecy.”

Silence.

Zee’s face went blank.

“What prophecy?”

That question destroyed Victor more completely than any threat could have.

The King stepped backward.

“No.”

Zee looked toward Rez again.

Rez’s eyes sharpened.

Ner shook his head once.

None of them knew.

Zee returned his attention to Victor.

“What prophecy?”

Victor’s breathing changed.

Twenty-one years.

Every decision.

Every fear.

Every attempt at containment.

Every rejection.

Built around words his son had never even heard.

“You are lying.”

Zee’s expression darkened.

“I do not need to lie to you.”

“You must know.”

“I don’t.”

Victor stared.

Zee stepped closer.

“Tell me.”

“No.”

Crimson eyes narrowed.

Not compulsion.

Not yet.

“Tell me what you heard before you killed me.”

The court went utterly still.

Victor’s face collapsed inward.

There.

The newborn death.

The first blade.

The thing no crown could clean.

Zee continued.

“You heard something.”

“Yes.”

“And decided I deserved death before I could speak.”

Victor’s mouth tightened.

“It was not that simple.”

“It was exactly that simple to the infant.”

A sharp breath came from someone in court.

Victor looked around.

The House was hearing too much now.

Good.

No more private fear shaping public law.

Victor’s voice lowered.

“The words came after Blood Rain.”

Zee said nothing.

“The kingdom was still in panic.”

“Witches had lost control of magic.”

“Wolves were mad.”

“Vampires heard—”

“A second heartbeat,” Zee said.

Victor looked at him.

“Everyone knows what happened when I was born.”

“Not this.”

Victor’s face changed.

Then finally, after twenty-one years, he spoke the words that had ruled him.

“When blood falls upward and beasts forget their names, a child of crown and hunger shall open his eyes beneath the blackened throne.”

Zee went still.

Victor continued.

“Three lives shall breathe within one flesh, and every blade raised against him shall sharpen what it seeks to destroy.”

Rez looked toward Zee.

Ner’s breathing stopped for half a heartbeat.

Above them, Zareth’s Link tightened.

Victor’s voice began trembling.

“He shall not inherit the world as it was given.”

The throne room seemed to shrink around him.

“The world shall break before it teaches him how to die.”

Silence.

Nothing answered.

No thunder.

No magic.

No prophecy waking.

Just words.

Old words.

Zee stared at his father.

“That’s it?”

Victor looked as though Zee had struck him.

“That’s it?”

“Yes.”

“You heard that and killed me?”

“You do not understand what it meant.”

“No.”

Zee stepped closer.

“I understand exactly what you did.”

Victor’s face hardened defensively.

“It said every blade would sharpen you.”

“And you chose to become the first.”

Victor stopped.

Zee’s voice remained calm.

“It said I would change the world.”

“You decided that made me guilty of whatever change frightened you.”

“It said the world would break—”

“Before it taught me how to die.”

Zee smiled faintly.

No humor.

“You learned that part was true very quickly.”

Victor’s face whitened.

The newborn.

Blade.

Blood.

Stillness.

Return.

Death ended once.

Zee continued.

“I did not know.”

Victor shook his head.

“You became it anyway.”

“Became what?”

“The prophecy.”

Zee stared.

Victor pointed at him.

“The horns.”

“The blood.”

“The creatures following you.”

“The Houses bending.”

“The monsters fearing your name.”

“The people choosing you.”

“Everything.”

“You are what it warned me about.”

Zee looked down at himself.

Mature scales.

Blood-dark clothing.

Knives hidden where Victor could not see.

The body of a predator shaped by years of choices.

Then back at his father.

“I became me.”

Victor laughed bitterly.

“Same thing.”

“No.”

The word struck harder than a spell.

“The prophecy described possibilities.”

“You built your life around them.”

“I didn’t.”

Victor’s breathing became ragged.

Zee continued.

“I did not leave Darkheart because a prophecy told me to.”

“You drove me out.”

“I did not learn to fight because prophecy demanded it.”

“People hunted me.”

“I did not go to Nanda Parbat because some ancient voice wanted an assassin.”

“I wanted skill.”

“I did not start protecting people because destiny assigned them to me.”

“I chose them.”

“I did not drink supernatural blood because prophecy promised evolution.”

“I liked what it did to me.”

Ner’s eyes shifted toward him.

No judgment.

Truth.

Zee stepped closer.

“And I did not come here because some prophecy said I would.”

His crimson eyes hardened.

“I came because you imprisoned people for choosing me.”

Victor stared.

The throne room held its breath.

Zee spoke quietly.

“You spent twenty-one years obeying those words.”

“I spent twenty-one years trying to stop them.”

“Same thing.”

Victor recoiled.

There.

The irony finally became visible.

Not that Victor caused every event.

He had not.

Aurelia’s death belonged to seven killers.

Nanda Parbat belonged to Zee.

Ner’s transformation belonged to desperation and blood.

Zee’s growing darkness belonged to grief, choice, appetite, survival, and the world he lived in.

But Victor had shaped one part faithfully.

He had treated possibility as guilt.

Fear as proof.

Prophecy as permission.

And his son had grown without even knowing the script.

Victor whispered:

“If I had done nothing…”

Zee’s expression changed.

“You still would not have owned me.”

Victor looked up.

“That is what you still do not understand.”

Zee stepped within arm’s reach.

“I might have loved you.”

That hit.

Victor’s face broke.

Just once.

Small.

Zee saw the father who had existed before terror.

Too late.

“I did love you.”

Zee’s eyes hardened.

“You loved the version of me that had not frightened you yet.”

“No.”

“You killed him.”

Zee let silence do the work.

Then Victor drew a knife.

Not to murder Zee again.

He knew better.

Not even truly to win.

Instinct.

King.

Father.

Man cornered by everything he had spent his life avoiding.

The blade came.

Zee caught his wrist.

Effortlessly.

Twenty-one years.

The first time, Victor’s blade had entered an infant.

This time it stopped inches from Zee’s chest.

Victor strained.

Zee did not move.

“You cannot kill me.”

Victor’s face twisted.

“I know.”

He finally knew.

Then Victor.

“You taught me that.”

The knife fell.

Guards moved.

Rez drew his sword.

Ner’s Gold spread.

Zareth roared above.

Everyone stopped.

Not compulsion.

Authority.

His.

Scales.

Bloodline.

Himself.

Exactly as Zee wanted.

No knife now.

Witchcraft.

Dark Mana tore across the chamber.

Zee remained standing.

Victor stared.

Zee moved.

Vampire speed.

One instant ten feet away.

Next behind Victor.

Pressure point beneath the shoulder.

Wolf instinct read the turn before it happened.

Zee caught the elbow.

Assassin leverage drove Victor to one knee.

One precise force.

Long enough.

Humiliated.

Terrified.

He attacked.

For several minutes.

Not because the fight was close.

Because Victor deserved to understand.

Every blade sharpened what it sought to destroy.

Victor cast suppression.

Zee’s blood adapted around old suppression patterns years ago.

Victor used poison smoke.

Zee smelled it before release and held his breath longer than a Human body could.

Victor threw enchanted silver.

Zee’s accumulated resistance turned agony into damage he could fight through.

Victor bound Zee’s legs.

Crimson Mana surgically severed the weakest line.

No spectacle.

Victor summoned a blade.

Zee took it through the hand deliberately, trapped the weapon between reinforced bone and scale, then broke it.

Finally afraid in a way Zee had never smelled from him before.

Not fear of prophecy.

Fear of the man.

Zee preferred that.

He approached slowly.

“You enjoy this.”

Zee stopped.

“Yes.”

No shame.

“There.”

“You needed me to be one when I was a baby.”

Zee stepped closer.

“I am a monster now.”

Ner’s face changed.

Rez went still.

“To some.”

“Hunters.”

No more room behind him.

“Aurelia would hate this.”

Once.

The darkness wanted more.

Slow.

Painful.

Calmly.

Personal.

Controlled.

Final.

Blood on his teeth.

“Not enough.”

Truth.

“Good.”

Fear.

Real.

Love.

Concern.

No attempt to replace anyone.

Zareth landed outside the throne hall so hard the high windows rattled.

The Link carried one overwhelming truth.

Finished.

Yes.

Victor’s reign was finished.

Then Lord Merek stepped forward.

He looked at Victor’s body.

Then at Zee.

“By blood, you are first heir of House Darkheart.”

Zee said nothing.

Another noble spoke.

“By challenge, the King fell to you.”

Another:

“By the House, there is no stronger claimant.”

Zee looked toward the throne.

Victor’s throne.

Black stone.

Old blood.

Old fear.

He did not want Victor’s crown.

Merek lifted it anyway.

Dark metal.

Heavy.

The same crown Zee had watched from below as a child.

“King Zee Darkheart.”

Zee stared at it.

Then took the crown from Merek.

The court waited.

Zee looked toward the throne.

Toward Victor.

Toward the banners.

Then closed his hands around the crown.

Metal bent.

Gasps.

Crimson Dragon heat moved through his palms.

The old crown cracked.

Zee broke it in two.

One half struck the throne steps beside Victor.

The other remained in Zee’s hand.

Rez smiled.

Ner did too.

Merek stared.

“What are you doing?”

Zee looked at the broken crown.

“His reign ended.”

He dropped the second half.

“I am not wearing it.”

Silence.

“Then how will the House recognize—”

Zee turned.

Every eye followed.

He climbed the throne steps.

Stepped over Victor’s crown.

Not Victor’s body.

That distinction mattered.

He moved the body aside first.

Carefully enough that several people noticed.

Then Zee sat on the black throne.

No crown.

Blood from his father still across one hand.

Crimson scales catching torchlight.

Mature horns framing a face the House had once been taught to fear.

Outside, Zareth roared.

Pure Gold flared once around Ner.

Blue-White Mana answered from Rez.

Not granting Zee authority.

Standing with him.

Lord Merek knelt.

Then another.

Then another.

Some slowly.

Some eagerly.

Some because they loved him.

Some because they feared him.

Some because bloodright demanded it.

Some because Victor was dead.

Some because they had already chosen Zee years ago.

Zee watched each one.

No illusion that everyone kneeling meant everyone loyal.

Future king.

Future assassin.

He would remember faces.

Hands.

Heartbeats.

The ones hesitating.

The ones relieved.

The ones lying.

By the time the last standing Darkheart noble made their choice, the throne room had changed.

Not magically.

Politically.

Personally.

Permanently.

Zee rested one blood-covered hand on the black stone armrest.

Twenty-one.

No children.

No sons.

No completed Dragon awakening.

No full Dynasty spanning the world.

Not yet.

But fully grown.

Fully dangerous.

And finally sitting beneath no father.

Rez looked up at him.

“Do I have to call you Majesty now?”

The throne room froze.

Zee stared.

“No.”

Rez smiled.

“Good.”

Ner laughed.

The sound loosened something in Zee’s chest.

Zee looked toward him.

His partner.

His best friend.

The first strange blood-born being Zee had ever created without knowing creation was possible.

Zee loved him.

Deeply.

That love did not soften the blood on his hands.

Both existed.

Zareth’s amusement rolled through the Link.

Zee looked toward the shattered crown below.

Victor had spent twenty-one years trying to escape a prophecy.

He had killed an infant because he feared the man that infant might become.

The infant returned.

The child survived.

The hunted boy learned to hunt.

The prince learned to kill.

The son learned he had never needed his father’s fear to become dangerous.

And at twenty-one, when Victor finally met the future he had spent his entire life trying to prevent, it was not destiny that entered the throne room.

It was Zee.

Now Victor Darkheart was dead.

The old crown was broken.

And beneath the blackened throne banners of House Darkheart sat a King who had no intention of asking the world whether it approved.

King Zee Darkheart looked over his House.

Then smiled.

Small.

Predatory.

His.

The prophecy had survived the man who feared it.

And House Darkheart had a new King.

Chapter Sixty-Two

The Crimson Demonic Dragon

The God ran for six years.

Not every day.

Not every country.

Not in panic.

Gods did not run like frightened men.

They vanished into temples that did not admit mortals.

Crossed kingdoms through worship.

Changed names.

Changed faces.

Used priests, mercenaries, and monsters as distance.

Zee lived anyway.

He became King.

He built power.

He loved Ner.

He fought beside Rez.

He watched Zareth grow into Drakonis authority.

He buried more enemies than he bothered counting.

But he never forgot the seventh heartbeat that had escaped Aurelia’s death.

Now there was nowhere left to go.

The God stood alone on a black plateau above a dead sea.

No temple.

No followers.

No army.

Only wind.

Zee walked toward him.

The God smiled.

“So.”

Zee said nothing.

“You finally found me.”

Still nothing.

The God’s smile weakened.

Zee’s crimson eyes stayed fixed on him.

Human pupils.

For now.

No guards followed.

Rez knew where Zee had gone.

Ner knew.

Zareth knew.

None had tried to stop him.

This belonged to Zee.

The God tilted his head.

“You look different.”

Zee stopped twenty feet away.

“So do you.”

The God laughed.

“Do you remember my face?”

“No.”

That bothered him.

Zee continued.

“I remember your blood scent.”

The smile disappeared.

Good.

Zee inhaled once.

Divine blood.

Old.

Powerful.

Hidden under incense, cold air, and something metallic.

Same as six years ago.

No mistake.

The God lifted one hand.

Gold-white force slammed across the plateau.

Zee moved before it hit.

Vampire speed.

Assassin angle.

Not away.

Inside.

He crossed half the distance before the God corrected.

A second blast hit Zee in the chest.

Stone shattered beneath him.

He flew backward.

Rolled.

Stopped on one knee.

Blood touched his mouth.

The God smiled again.

“There.”

Zee stood.

“You expected more?”

“I expected grief.”

Zee wiped his lip.

“You are six years late.”

Then disappeared.

⸻

The God was fast.

Not Vampire fast.

Different.

Distance folded around his body through divine authority.

One moment near.

Next far.

Zee stopped trying to chase the body.

Wolf instinct tracked pressure through the ground.

Vampire blood sense followed the divine pulse beneath false distance.

Assassin training watched where the God wanted Zee looking.

Witchcraft touched only what mattered.

The God appeared behind him.

Zee flicked two fingers.

The divine spear changed angle by inches.

Enough.

It missed his spine.

Zee turned.

Claws tore across the God’s face.

Wolf.

Not magic.

The God staggered.

Surprise.

Zee smelled divine blood.

Real.

He smiled.

Slit pupils.

The God touched his cheek.

Looked at the gold-red blood.

“You wounded me.”

“Yes.”

“How?”

Zee attacked again.

No explanation.

The God blocked his knife.

Zee let it go.

Trap.

Left hand caught the wrist.

Right elbow hit the throat.

Dragon durability met divine force when the God countered with a palm strike.

Zee’s bones screamed.

Did not break.

Not all of them.

He grabbed the arm anyway.

Vampire strength.

Wolf leverage.

Assassin precision.

He threw the God across the plateau.

The God stopped in midair.

Zee barely raised one hand.

“Fall.”

Crimson Witchcraft struck.

Simple.

Sharp.

The God dropped hard enough to split black stone.

Zee was on him before the impact finished.

Knife to throat.

The God caught his wrist.

Divine power exploded.

Zee’s hand burned.

Scales blackened.

Regeneration began immediately.

The God kicked him away.

Zee landed badly.

One knee.

One hand.

Breathing harder now.

Good.

The God stood.

“You cannot kill me.”

Zee looked up.

“I heard that before.”

“From whom?”

“My father.”

The God’s face changed.

Zee rose.

“He was wrong too.”

⸻

The fight lasted longer than Zee wanted.

Long enough for the plateau to crack.

Long enough for Zee to bleed from six places.

Long enough for the God to learn that killing Zee was not the same as hurting him.

Divine force crushed his shoulder.

It repaired.

A blade of light opened his abdomen.

His Vampire regeneration pulled the wound closed faster after Zee fed from his own bitten tongue and forced blood back into damaged tissue.

A divine command struck his mind.

“Kneel.”

Zee’s body buckled.

One knee touched stone.

The God smiled.

Then Zee looked up.

Crimson eyes brightened.

His will pushed back.

Vampire compulsion.

Predatory dominance.

Witch resistance.

Years of hostile magic rewritten into Crimson tolerance.

“No.”

The divine command tightened.

Zee’s horns heated.

Scales spread across his shoulders.

The ridges beneath his back burned.

Something deep moved.

Not old adaptation.

Not Demon.

Not Vampire.

Dragon.

The God frowned.

“What is that?”

Zee did not know.

The pressure doubled.

His Dragon blood answered.

For years it had existed beneath everything.

Born with him.

Awakened slowly.

Horns.

Scales.

Heat.

Durability.

Instinct.

Never wings.

Never transformation.

Never Zareth.

Now it simply finished becoming itself.

No ritual.

No voice.

No destiny.

The sleeping line in Zee’s blood opened.

Completely.

His body locked.

Then heat tore through every vein.

Crimson-black scales spread farther over his neck, chest, ribs, and spine.

His horns sharpened.

Darkened.

Became more severe. More crown-like.

The structures beneath his shoulder blades hardened into powerful ridges.

Nothing opened from them.

No wings.

No tail.

No Dragon body.

Zee remained Zee.

But the blood was no longer sleeping.

Dragon.

Fully active.

The God stepped back.

Actually stepped back.

Zee noticed.

That pleased him.

“What are you?”

Zee stood.

The divine command shattered.

“I told you.”

His pupils became slits.

“Zee.”

⸻

The second half of the fight was worse for the God.

Not easy.

Never easy.

But different.

Zee’s Dragon instincts changed how he met force.

He stopped yielding ground unnecessarily.

His body heat climbed.

Divine blades that had cut deep now struggled longer against darkened Crimson scales.

Zee caught one bare-handed.

It burned through his palm.

He held it anyway.

Closed his fist.

“Break.”

Witchcraft and physical force hit together.

The divine weapon fractured.

The God stared.

Zee headbutted him.

Mature horns opened the God’s brow.

Blood ran.

Zee smelled it.

Hunger hit immediately.

Not ordinary hunger.

Curiosity.

Power.

Six years.

Mother.

The God tried to escape.

Zee expected it.

Assassin countertracking had already taught him every visible pattern in the God’s retreat.

Wolf instinct knew which direction fear preferred.

Vampire blood sense found the pulse.

Zee vanished.

Appeared in front of him.

The God stopped.

“No.”

Zee almost smiled.

“There it is.”

The God struck.

Zee took the blow across scaled ribs.

Caught his arm.

Twisted.

Bone cracked.

Divine bone.

The scream was satisfying.

Zee did not hide that.

He drove the God to the ground.

Knee against the spine.

One hand gripping hair.

The God whispered:

“You do not know what happens if you drink me.”

Zee’s fangs descended.

“No.”

That frightened the God more than certainty would have.

“Then stop.”

Zee leaned closer.

“You watched my mother die.”

“I did not strike her.”

“You came with the ones who did.”

“That is not the same.”

Zee’s voice stayed calm.

“It is enough.”

He bit.

⸻

God blood did not taste like power.

It tasted like contradiction.

Cold and burning.

Heavy and weightless.

Ancient enough that Zee’s body rejected it for one violent instant.

Then his Crimson nature took control.

He drank harder.

The God screamed.

Divine blood hit Zee’s Vampire nature first.

His heart hammered.

Then Witch.

Crimson Mana flared.

Then Wolf.

Every predatory instinct became razor-sharp.

Then Dragon.

The newly awakened natural bloodline surged.

And something old answered from deeper inside Zee.

Demon blood.

Years processed.

Years rewritten.

Never gone.

The old Demonic adaptation collided with true divine blood.

The reaction nearly tore Zee apart.

He stopped feeding for half a second.

The God tried to move.

Zee snarled.

Bit deeper.

Kept drinking.

Divine blood rejected Demon influence.

Demonic adaptation rejected divine presence.

Dragon blood reacted to both.

Three incompatible forces crashed through Zee’s body.

None belonged in control.

His Crimson biology refused all of them.

So it rewrote.

Zee screamed against the God’s throat.

Crimson-black fire moved under his scales without burning outside.

His horns lengthened slightly.

Sharpened.

The black near their bases spread farther.

His scales deepened from Crimson into dark crimson-black across broader regions of his torso and arms.

Heat rolled off him in waves.

The God weakened.

Zee did not stop.

Blood.

All of it.

Every last divine drop.

The God’s heartbeat slowed.

Then stopped.

Zee kept feeding until there was nothing left to take.

He released the corpse.

It hit stone dry.

Dead.

The seventh attacker was finished.

Aurelia’s killer had nowhere left to run.

Zee stood.

Then nearly fell.

Something inside him changed permanently.

Not a God nature.

Nothing divine settled cleanly inside him.

No domain.

No stolen authority.

No copied miracle.

The divine blood had become pressure.

The old Demon adaptation had become poison to it.

The Dragon bloodline became the battlefield.

Crimson rewrote the outcome.

The Dragon nature mutated.

Darkened.

Changed.

Not Demon.

Not Dragon alone.

Not God.

Something Zee.

His eyes burned.

When he opened them again, Crimson and Gold existed together permanently.

Not one overtaking the other.

Both.

His pupils returned human as his breathing slowed.

For one moment, Zee simply stood over the dead God.

Then the plateau shook.

Not from magic.

From witnesses.

Far across the broken ridge, surviving priests and soldiers who had hidden during the fight stared at him.

They had seen the Dragon traits fully awaken.

Seen the God fall.

Seen Zee drain him dry.

Seen the transformation afterward.

One priest whispered:

“Dragon…”

Another:

“No.”

His voice shook.

“That is not a Dragon.”

Zee looked toward them.

Every heartbeat accelerated.

Slit pupils returned.

Nobody moved.

A third man whispered the name that would escape the plateau before Zee did.

“The Crimson Demonic Dragon.”

Zee frowned.

He disliked it immediately.

Which meant it would probably survive.

⸻

Ner was the first person to touch his face when Zee returned to Darkheart.

He did not ask permission.

He simply stepped close and placed one hand against Zee’s cheek.

Zee’s pupils shifted human.

Ner noticed.

“You look terrifying.”

Zee sighed.

“Good to see you too.”

Rez walked around him once.

“More scales.”

“Yes.”

“Bigger horns.”

“Yes.”

“Eyes.”

“I noticed.”

Rez stopped in front of him.

“You killed the God.”

“Yes.”

Zareth landed beyond the courtyard.

Then froze.

The Dragon Link struck Zee harder than it had in years.

Recognition.

Shock.

Dragon.

Then—

wrong.

Not wrong as rejection.

Wrong as impossible.

Zee looked toward him.

The Link sharpened.

Zee’s Dragon blood.

Fully awake.

But changed.

Darkened by something Zareth could sense and did not recognize.

Zee walked over.

Placed one hand against Zareth’s snout.

The Dragon inhaled.

Teal-and-Gold Mana stirred.

Zee’s new Crimson Demonic Dragon force answered automatically.

Heavy.

Hot.

Predatory.

Zareth pulled back half an inch.

Zee stared.

Then Zareth pushed his forehead against Zee’s chest harder than necessary.

The Link carried fierce acceptance.

Still Zee.

Good.

That mattered.

Ner joined them.

Rez beside him.

No Aurelia.

That empty place remained.

Zee looked back toward Castle Darkheart.

King.

Tribrid.

Wolf.

Vampire.

Witch.

Dragon blood fully awake and no longer ordinary Dragon blood at all.

A title already spreading behind him.

The Crimson Demonic Dragon.

He had not chosen it.

The world had.

Zee smiled faintly.

“Terrible name.”

Rez laughed.

Ner said, “It is dramatic.”

Zareth sent approval.

Zee looked betrayed.

“Not you too.”

The moment lasted three seconds.

Then the first alarm horn sounded.

Not from Darkheart.

From the northern border.

Rez’s expression changed.

Ner turned.

Zareth lifted his head.

Zee’s smile vanished.

His pupils narrowed into slits.

The God was dead.

The world had seen what Zee became.

And apparently the world had decided the intelligent response was to attack immediately.

Zee flexed one blood-warm hand.

“Good.”

Rez looked toward him.

“That sounded concerning.”

Zee started walking.

“It was.”

Chapter Sixty-Three

The King Is the Wolf

The northern attack lasted twenty-three minutes.

The people who ordered it expected hours.

That was their first mistake.

Their second was assuming King Zee Darkheart would command from behind walls.

The invading force crossed the northern forest before dawn.

Two hundred mercenaries.

Thirty witches.

A dozen Vampires.

Wolf trackers.

Three siege constructs.

No unified supernatural empire.

Just a neighboring lord who saw Victor dead, Darkheart succession changed, and rumors of Zee’s transformation as a narrow opportunity before the House stabilized.

Reasonable.

Wrong.

Zee listened to the report once.

Then looked at Lord Merek.

“How many entered the forest?”

“Two hundred forty-seven confirmed.”

“Civilians?”

“None.”

“Darkheart villages?”

“Evacuated.”

“Good.”

Rez entered the war chamber.

“They are expecting a defensive line here.”

He pointed to the river road.

Zee looked.

Then shook his head.

“No line.”

Merek frowned.

“Majesty?”

“They came through my forest.”

Rez understood first.

“Oh.”

Ner looked between them.

“What?”

Rez smiled faintly.

“He is going hunting.”

Zee’s crimson-and-gold eyes shifted.

Slits.

“Yes.”

⸻

The transformation hurt less than it had when he was younger.

Not because Wolf Zee had become weaker.

Because Zee had finally stopped treating transformation as secondary.

Bones shifted.

Spine changed.

Hands became paws.

Clothing fell around a body becoming something else entirely.

When the transformation finished, a massive four-legged wolf stood where the King had been.

No horns.

No scales.

No Dragon traits.

Wolf.

Complete.

Near-black fur carried subtle deep-crimson undertones beneath moonlight.

His crimson-and-gold eyes remained unmistakable.

Slit pupils now.

Predatory.

Rez crouched.

“Still strange.”

Wolf Zee stared.

Ner smiled.

“You say that every time.”

Rez looked offended.

“Because he usually has hands.”

Zee showed teeth.

Rez stood.

“Yes, yes. Terrifying.”

Zareth’s amusement rolled through the Link from above.

Zee ignored all of them.

Then ran.

⸻

The forest belonged to Zee before it belonged to Darkheart law.

Wolf instinct knew that.

Territory was not parchment.

It was scent.

Movement.

Trees.

Wind.

Who crossed.

Who bled.

Who feared.

Zee ran north without Vampire speed.

Did not need it.

Wolf endurance carried him mile after mile.

His paws barely sounded.

He found the invaders by smell first.

Oil.

Steel.

Sweat.

Vampire blood.

Spell ash.

Fear disguised beneath discipline.

He circled once.

Counted.

Not numerically.

Predator map.

Three groups.

One main column.

Two flanks.

Witches protected center.

Vampires scouting ahead.

Wolf trackers spreading wide.

They expected Darkheart patrols.

Not the King.

Zee followed one scout.

The Wolf mercenary stopped suddenly.

He smelled something.

Turned.

Nothing.

Zee had already moved downwind.

Countertracking.

Nanda Parbat inside Wolf form.

The mercenary continued.

Zee circled ahead.

Waited behind a fallen tree.

The scout passed.

Zee struck.

One bite.

Throat.

Silent.

No feeding.

Not every kill required blood.

He dragged the body beneath brush.

Continued.

Second scout disappeared.

Then third.

By the time the invading commander realized his perimeter had holes, Zee had already entered the column.

Panic began from the outside.

Not the center.

Good.

Fear spread inward.

One mercenary whispered:

“Something is following us.”

Another answered:

“Wolves?”

Zee moved through black trees.

One man saw crimson-and-gold eyes.

Only for a second.

Then nothing.

“The Blood Hunter.”

Wrong name.

Old name.

Still useful.

A Vampire commander hissed:

“He is not here.”

Zee attacked from behind.

The commander never finished the sentence.

Wolf jaws crushed the back of his knee.

He screamed.

Zee released.

Ran before weapons turned.

Did not kill him.

Not yet.

Fear needed a witness.

The commander shouted:

“FORM!”

Too late.

The forest erupted.

Darkheart Wolves came from the western slope.

Not helpless subjects.

Not waiting for Zee.

His people had learned.

They attacked the flank independently.

Darkheart witches hit from elevated ground.

Ner’s Pure Gold flashed far behind the enemy and sealed retreat paths without trapping civilians because there were none.

Rez had positioned all of it before Zee transformed.

King and future king thinking differently.

Zareth remained above, watching for siege constructs trying to break through forest cover.

No one rode him.

No one needed to.

The invasion collapsed into chaos.

That was when Zee transformed back.

Not in front of everyone.

Behind an overturned siege cart.

Human shape returned.

He pulled a black coat from a hidden pack placed earlier.

Nanda Parbat planning.

Then walked into the chaos.

One mercenary charged.

Zee barely moved his hand.

The man flew sideways through a tree.

Witch.

Another cast.

Zee flicked two fingers.

The spell reversed direction.

Hit the caster.

“Sleep.”

Three soldiers dropped.

Vampire Zee surfaced next.

He heard every heartbeat.

One false surrender.

Two genuine.

One man reaching for a poisoned knife behind his back.

Zee looked at him.

“Don’t.”

The man froze.

Not because he chose to.

Compulsion reached through voice and predatory presence.

No eye contact.

The mercenary struggled.

Zee felt resistance.

Pushed.

The hand opened.

Knife dropped.

The man stared.

Zee smiled faintly.

“Better.”

The invading commander finally found him.

Human.

Armored.

No supernatural blood.

Interesting.

He pushed through retreating fighters.

“Darkheart!”

Zee turned.

The commander raised a sword.

“You call this a kingdom?”

Zee looked around.

His Wolves holding territory.

Witches controlling lines.

Ner’s Gold cutting escape from reinforcement routes.

Rez directing prisoners away from active fighting.

Zareth tearing a siege construct apart with his claws rather than burning the forest.

“Yes.”

The commander attacked.

Zee could have killed him five different ways before the blade descended.

He chose assassin technique.

Step inside.

Wrist.

Chapter Sixty-Eight

The Villages That Burned First

The western villages were already burning when Zee arrived.

Three.

Not one line of fire.

Three separate strikes.

Different roads.

Different timing.

Same result.

People running.

Livestock screaming.

Darkheart soldiers dragging families from houses while witches fought flames that did not behave like ordinary fire.

Zee stopped at the edge of the first village.

Wood.

Oil.

Blood.

Spell residue.

Wolf.

Human.

And something metallic beneath it.

“Magic?”

“Yes.”

Fire wrong.

Good.

Wolf instinct.

His castle.

Zee Darkheart had spent most of his life surviving people who decided what he might become was reason enough to act first.

Now, for the first time, he was preparing to do something dangerously similar.

The difference, in his mind, was evidence.

The question was how long that difference would remain enough.

Chapter Seventy

The First Name

Orin Bale lived in a city that worshiped discretion.

No banners.

No guards in uniform.

No royal colors.

Just money.

Old money.

Quiet money.

The kind that paid other people to become violent.

Good.

Bloodsong struck circulation.

“Still.”

One instant standing.

Pressure point beneath the jaw.

Near-black fur.

Crimson-and-gold eyes.

No horns.

No scales.

Just Wolf.

Zee did not.

Claws.

Teeth.

Weight.

No Vampire speed.

No Witchcraft.

Pinned him.

Could kill.

Did not.

Not yet.

Human-shaped.

“Every nature complete.”

Zee straightened.

“Three always were.”

She looked toward the darker scales along his neck.

“And the fourth?”

Zee smiled faintly.

“None of your business.”

This time directly at Ner.

Wrong choice.

Raised one palm.

The spell stopped.

He closed his fist.

It shattered.

Then his other hand flicked.

Wood exploded.

No hurry.

“You protect him because he proves your blood can make more.”

Zee’s face changed.

“No.”

She laughed.

“You love him.”

“Yes.”

No hesitation.

Ner went still.

Not because it was new.

Because Zee said it here, covered in blood, while walking toward someone he intended to kill.

Both true.

Both Zee.

Zee disappeared.

Reappeared behind her.

Knife beneath ribs.

Not fatal.

Yet.

Assassin placement.

She gasped.

Zee whispered:

“Who else did you order killed?”

“Hundreds.”

Truth.

His Vampire blood sense caught no deception.

“How many children?”

“Enough.”

That was the answer.

No remorse.

No coercion.

No uncertainty.

Zee could kill her now.

He wanted to.

“Wait.”

Zee stopped.

Not because Ner commanded.

Because he trusted the reason would matter.

Ner approached.

“Where are the lists?”

Mara’s expression shifted.

Lists.

Good.

Zee smiled faintly.

Ner noticed.

“You forgot the evidence.”

“Yes.”

Mara laughed.

“You two are absurd.”

“Where?”

She resisted.

Ner’s voice changed.

Bloodsong.

“Tell me.”

Mara had wards.

Strong.

Her blood fought the resonance.

Ner pushed with Golden precision around the command, isolating the effect from everyone else.

“Tell me.”

Blood vessels stood along Mara’s neck.

“Lower crypt.”

“Done?”

“Yes.”

“Good.”

Fear entered her.

Finally.

“Wait.”

“You just spent ten minutes explaining why waiting is weakness.”

“I can help you.”

“Probably.”

“I do not want your help.”

Zee pulled the knife free.

Mara stumbled.

Relief.

Wrong.

He caught her by the throat.

Vampire strength lifted her.

She struggled.

“Mercy.”

Zee stared.

At nineteen, he had begun asking why.

At twenty-one, he still did.

“Give me a reason.”

“I know every threat forming against you.”

“Names?”

“I can tell you.”

“Lists?”

“Yes.”

“Where?”

“Crypt.”

Already had it.

No new value.

Mara realized.

Fear deepened.

Zee enjoyed it.

He did not pretend otherwise.

“You are going to kill me.”

“Yes.”

“You are proving me right.”

Zee’s pupils narrowed.

“No.”

His fangs descended.

“You killed people for what they might become.”

He pulled her closer.

“I am killing you for what you already chose.”

Then he fed.

⸻

Mara’s Witch blood hit hard.

Old.

Potent.

Layered with defensive rituals and traces of dozens of supernatural substances she had consumed over years trying to harden herself.

Zee drank all of it.

Not her spells.

Not her knowledge.

Her blood entered Zee and met Crimson biology.

Poison resistance stirred.

Suppression resistance.

Blood analysis.

The foreign mixtures began separating almost instantly.

His body was becoming frighteningly good at deciding what belonged.

Mara weakened.

Her hands stopped moving.

Her heartbeat slowed.

Zee did not stop until it ended.

He dropped the body.

No guilt.

No apology.

Ner watched him wipe blood from his mouth.

“You enjoyed that.”

“Yes.”

“Because she was afraid?”

“Yes.”

“Because of the blood?”

“Yes.”

“Because you killed her?”

Zee thought.

Then:

“Yes.”

Ner nodded.

No approval.

No condemnation.

He simply knew Zee.

That mattered.

⸻

The lower crypt held forty-seven names.

Some marked dead.

Some pending.

Some under observation.

A twelve-year-old Witch with unstable fire magic.

A Vampire child born from an old predatory bloodline.

A Wolf girl whose father had massacred a village.

A mixed-blood infant Mara believed could become dangerous.

Potential.

Nothing more.

“She would have killed them.”

“Yes.”

Then he burned the list.

Not the evidence ledger beside it.

“Why keep one?”

Growth.

Quickly.

No spectacle.

The monastery belonged to no one by sunset.

Did not want it.

He sent the evidence to three kingdoms whose citizens had been murdered.

Let them tear apart the rest of Mara’s network.

Not Orin.

Not Mara.

Dren Solvar.

Beside it:

PRIMARY INTEREST: KING ZEE DARKHEART — BLOOD ACQUISITION ALIVE IF POSSIBLE.

Ner read it.

Then looked toward Zee.

Zee smiled.

Slow.

Predatory.

“Alive?”

“There it is.”

Mara had wanted to kill threats before they matured.

Dren Solvar wanted Zee alive.

For blood.

For study.

For something worse.

The difference was almost refreshing.

Zee tucked the page into his coat.

“Next.”

No rest.

No reset.

The world kept coming.

And King Zee Darkheart was becoming very comfortable meeting it halfway.

Chapter Seventy-Two

The Man Who Wanted the King Alive

Dren Solvar did not hide.

That made Zee suspicious immediately.

He owned an estate outside the coastal city of Valen.

Open gates.

Visible guards.

No blood wards.

No hidden fortress.

No attempt to run.

Ner looked at the estate from the ridge.

“I hate this.”

Zee smiled.

“Good.”

“That was not encouragement.”

“I know.”

Rez had stayed in Vesper.

The aqueduct attack had failed, but three Covenant members remained loose inside his kingdom.

His problem.

His hunt.

Zareth remained in Drakonis.

The Link carried distant mountain heat and irritation at being excluded from a problem that specifically involved Zee’s blood.

Zee sent back amusement.

Then looked toward Ner.

“You stay outside.”

Ner stared.

“No.”

“Dren wants me alive.”

“Yes.”

“So I give him what he wants.”

“That sentence is terrible.”

Zee’s pupils narrowed into slits.

“I want to see how.”

Ner crossed his arms.

“You are using yourself as bait.”

“Yes.”

“You are King.”

“Yes.”

“You are impossible.”

“Yes.”

Ner sighed.

“Fine.”

Zee blinked.

“That was easy.”

“I am coming in thirty seconds after you.”

“That defeats the point.”

“Twenty.”

Zee smiled.

“Thirty.”

“Twenty-five.”

“Done.”

They kissed once.

Quick.

Then Zee disappeared down the ridge.

⸻

Dren Solvar waited in the garden.

Human.

At least mostly.

Not enough to become Vampire.

Repeated doses.

Enhancement.

Other blood too.

Wolf.

Witch.

Something reptilian.

Interesting.

“King Darkheart.”

“Dren.”

“You came alone.”

“No.”

“At least you are honest.”

No weapon visible.

Four guards behind Dren.

Two archers on the roof.

Three heartbeats behind the garden wall.

Zee did not touch it.

“Yes.”

Dren laughed.

“Very good.”

“Common paralytic under the lavender.”

“Less common suppression agent beneath it.”

“And?”

Zee inhaled.

“Dragonbane.”

The smile vanished.

There.

“You really can smell that?”

“Yes.”

Dren set the cup down.

“You are magnificent.”

Zee’s face cooled.

“Do not.”

“Do not what?”

“Talk about me like a specimen.”

“But that is exactly what you are.”

Wrong.

Zee almost killed him there.

Did not.

Information first.

“What do you want with my blood?”

“To understand transformation.”

“Ner.”

“Yes.”

“God blood.”

“Yes.”

“Your Dragon evolution.”

“Yes.”

Dren leaned forward.

“You drank things that should have destroyed you.”

“You became more yourself.”

Dren noticed.

“Demon blood.”

“Dragon blood.”

“Divine blood.”

“Different poisons.”

“Different supernatural species.”

“You do not accumulate foreign powers.”

“You rewrite pressure.”

Zee said nothing.

Dren smiled.

“I understand you better than most.”

“No.”

“Why?”

“Because you think understanding my blood means understanding me.”

The smile thinned.

Zee leaned back.

“What were you planning?”

Dren’s eyes sharpened.

“To capture you.”

“Alive.”

“Yes.”

“How?”

“Would you like to know?”

Zee smiled.

“Yes.”

Dren lifted one finger.

The garden exploded.

⸻

Silver-black cables launched from beneath the stone.

Not magic.

Mechanisms.

Fast.

Zee moved.

One wrapped his ankle.

Another caught his wrist.

A third hit his chest.

The cables activated.

Suppression.

Dragonbane.

Vampire restraints.

Wolf irritants.

Witch-breaking sigils.

Everything at once.

Zee hit the ground.

Dren stood.

“Like that.”

Zee looked down.

Interesting.

His Vampire strength failed first.

Witchcraft became heavy.

Wolf senses flooded with artificial scent.

Dragon blood burned.

Good design.

Dren approached.

“You have been attacked by specialists.”

“I hired engineers.”

Zee flexed one hand.

The cable tightened.

Pain.

His Crimson adaptations reacted.

Not instantly.

Not enough.

Good.

“You see?”

Zee looked at him.

Human pupils now.

Calm.

“You made one mistake.”

“Which?”

“You built restraints for everything you know I am.”

Zee’s hand closed.

Nothing happened.

Dren laughed.

Then Zee smiled.

“Separately.”

His Wolf nature found balance first.

He stopped fighting the restraint and rolled with its tension.

The Vampire suppression expected direct resistance.

None came.

His Witch nature used one tiny gesture.

Two fingers.

Barely moving.

A sigil on the nearest cable rotated half an inch.

Wrong alignment.

The Dragonbane load shifted.

Crimson Demonic Dragon heat surged into the exposed weakness.

One cable snapped.

Dren stopped laughing.

Zee moved.

Vampire speed returned only partially.

Enough.

He caught Dren by the throat.

The other cables dragged behind him.

Dren gasped.

Zee headbutted him.

Horn edge opened his scalp.

Blood.

Mixed blood.

Artificial.

Zee smelled every layer.

Ner’s Golden barrier erupted around the garden.

Twenty-five seconds.

Exactly.

Ner entered.

“You are tied to a statue.”

“Temporarily.”

Dren shouted:

“NOW!”

The hidden fighters moved.

Chaos.

The underground Witch cast first.

Ner’s Gold pierced the floor and broke the spell structure before it rose.

One archer fired.

Zee flicked two fingers.

The arrow bent.

Hit the second archer’s bow.

Wolf attackers came from the wall.

Zee tore one remaining cable free through brute force.

Not Vampire alone.

Dragon durability let the restraint cut deep without stopping him.

He caught the first Wolf by the throat.

Threw him.

Second attacked Ner.

Wrong.

Ner spoke one low Bloodsong note.

The Wolf’s circulation stumbled.

His body dropped to one knee.

Ner sealed him in Gold.

“Alive,” Ner said.

“For now.”

Zee let him.

“You are letting him go.”

Zee’s pupils shifted into slits.

“Wolf.”

Understanding hit Ner.

“Oh.”

Zee transformed.

Near-black Wolf form moved through wet brush without sound.

No horns.

No scales.

No magic.

Just Wolf.

Zee tracked broken fern.

Dren crossed rock.

Zee tracked displaced insects.

Dren entered seawater.

Waited on the beach.

Saw Zee.

Stopped.

“You need me.”

Wolf Zee showed teeth.

“Do you know what this is?”

Human form returned.

Dragon.

Demon.

Vampire.

Mixed.

Badly.

“A weapon.”

“A mistake.”

Veins blackened.

Bones shifted beneath skin.

Strength surged.

Dren screamed.

Supernatural bloods fought inside him.

No stable inheritance.

Just incompatibility.

Zee caught the first punch.

Barely.

Strong.

Dren became faster.

More unstable.

Weakness.

His right leg compensated.

Heart skipping every fourth beat.

One.

Two.

Three.

Skip.

Zee caught him.

“Interesting.”

“You see?”

“Yes.”

“Why?”

“I can give you everything.”

“Already have your ledgers.”

“You need my research.”

“You could become—”

Zee’s face went cold.

“I decide what I become.”

Dren screamed.

Zee drank.

Not because Dren’s blood offered some miraculous new power.

Because Zee wanted to know what artificial supernatural blood tasted like inside a failed vessel.

His body separated everything immediately.

Foreign Vampire enhancement.

Wolf residue.

Witch infusion.

Dragon blood.

Demon corruption.

Nothing stable enough to keep.

Crimson biology rejected most of it.

Not every supernatural blood source deserved adaptation.

Sometimes the correct evolution was refusal.
