Chapter Ninety-Six

Before the Same Sun Set

Cassel Rhune died before dawn.

Zee remained beside the ruined shrine after the Godslayer’s body went cold.

Blood covered the snow.

Most of it was his.

Black Divinity still burned through the wounds Cassel had opened.

One cut crossed Zee’s face.

Another split his shoulder.

A deeper wound remained beneath his ribs where Cassel’s blade had entered and refused to let Vampire healing close it properly.

His scales were cracked.

His hands were burned.

His heart still carried damage from the blade Cassel had driven through it.

Zee stood anyway.

Zareth watched him in human form.

“You need a healer.”

“I need breakfast.”

“You were stabbed through the heart.”

“I noticed.”

“That was not a joke.”

“It hurt like one.”

Zareth stared at him.

Through the Link came irritation wrapped around concern.

You are barely healing.

Zee looked down at the blackened edge of the wound in his side.

His Crimson biology had learned something during the fight.

Not how to use Dark Divinity.

Not how to absorb it.

Only how to resist being opened quite as deeply by it the next time.

Small.

Incomplete.

The burns still hurt.

The wounds still resisted healing.

Black Divinity remained dangerous.

Good.

Zee preferred dangerous things that stayed dangerous.

Ner arrived as morning light reached the mountains.

He took one look at Zee.

“No.”

Zee frowned.

“No what?”

“Whatever you are about to say.”

“I was going to say hello.”

“You were going to say you are fine.”

Zee smiled.

“I am alive.”

“That was not the question.”

Ner approached and touched the skin near Zee’s ribs without touching the wound itself.

Bloodsong reacted immediately.

Then recoiled.

His expression hardened.

“This is wrong.”

“Godslayer.”

“I know.”

“You asked.”

“I did not.”

Zareth looked between them.

“I am going back to Drakonis before this becomes domestic.”

Zee looked at him.

“You are already involved.”

“That is exactly why I am leaving.”

Through the Link came warmth.

Then Zareth shifted.

True Dragon form exploded across the mountain ridge.

Wings opened.

He launched toward Drakonis.

Ner watched him disappear.

Then looked back at Zee.

“We are going home.”

Zee opened his mouth.

Thunder answered first.

Not ordinary thunder.

The sky turned white.

Then black.

Clouds formed in seconds.

The mountain pressure changed hard enough to make stone groan.

Ner looked upward.

“That is not weather.”

Zee smiled faintly.

“No.”

A figure descended through the storm.

Bare feet never touched the ground.

Gold-white armor.

A spear made from condensed lightning.

Eyes filled with blue divine fire.

The air bent around him.

Not because of magic.

Authority.

The mountain itself seemed to recognize him.

Zee’s smile widened.

Ner sighed.

“Of course.”

The God looked at Cassel’s corpse.

Then Zee.

“So.”

Zee wiped blood from his mouth.

“So?”

“You killed the Godslayer.”

“Yes.”

The God’s gaze moved over Zee’s wounds.

“You are weaker than I expected.”

Zee looked at his own bleeding chest.

“Rude.”

The God ignored that.

“I am Kharos.”

The storm intensified.

“Lord of the Tempest Throne.”

Zee’s pupils narrowed.

“Congratulations.”

Ner covered his face briefly.

Kharos’s expression hardened.

“You have killed divine blood before.”

“Yes.”

“You consumed it.”

“Yes.”

“You survived.”

“Yes.”

“And now you have killed one who carried Dark Divinity.”

Zee’s smile disappeared.

Kharos descended another foot.

“Mortals are beginning to mistake survival for authority.”

“I am not mortal.”

“You are not divine either.”

“I know.”

“That distinction will be corrected today.”

Zee glanced toward Cassel’s corpse.

Then back at Kharos.

“You waited until after he cut me apart.”

“I observed an opportunity.”

Zee laughed.

Actually laughed.

Blood ran down his side while he did it.

Kharos frowned.

“You find this amusing?”

“Yes.”

“Why?”

Zee’s fangs descended.

“Because Cassel already reminded me how much I enjoy fighting things that can hurt me.”

The storm stopped moving.

For one second.

Then Kharos attacked.

⸻

Divine lightning struck first.

Zee moved.

Too slow.

The bolt hit his shoulder.

His entire body locked.

Crimson-black scales cracked.

The old Black Divinity wound reopened.

Zee hit the ground.

Kharos raised one hand.

Gravity changed.

Zee slammed deeper into stone.

Ner’s Gold surged.

Kharos looked toward him.

“Kneel.”

Divine authority struck.

Ner’s knees buckled.

He caught himself with one hand.

Gold shook around him.

Zee’s eyes changed.

Slits.

“Do not.”

Kharos looked back.

“Do not what?”

“Order him.”

“You command everyone around you.”

“No.”

Zee pushed against the divine pressure.

Muscles tore.

Dragon force answered.

He stood.

Slowly.

“They choose whether they stay.”

Kharos drove the spear forward.

Zee caught the shaft.

Lightning exploded through his body.

His hands burned.

Still he held it.

Kharos stared.

Zee smiled.

“You keep expecting pain to make me obedient.”

Then Witchcraft struck.

Silent.

One closed fist.

The stone beneath Kharos collapsed.

Not enough to hurt a God.

Enough to shift his footing.

Assassin lesson.

Position first.

Zee pulled.

Vampire strength.

Dragon force.

Kharos stumbled one step.

Wolf instinct saw the opening before thought finished forming.

Zee struck his knee.

Hard.

Divine bone cracked.

Kharos roared.

The storm answered.

A wall of wind threw Zee across the mountain.

He landed badly.

One rib broke.

Then another.

His healing remained slow.

Cassel’s wounds still interfered.

Kharos flew toward him.

“You should already be dead.”

Zee rolled aside as the spear hit stone.

“I hear that often.”

Kharos backhanded him.

Divine strength broke part of Zee’s jaw.

Zee spat blood.

Then laughed again.

Kharos finally looked disturbed.

Good.

⸻

The fight crossed the mountain.

Kharos controlled the sky.

Zee controlled nothing that easily.

So he stopped fighting the sky.

He went into the forest.

Wolf form.

Four-legged.

Near-black fur.

Crimson-and-gold eyes.

No horns.

No scales.

No Dragon features.

Only predator.

Kharos descended after him.

Mistake.

Lightning destroyed trees.

Zee was never where it landed.

Wolf instinct read pressure shifts.

Air displacement.

Static.

Movement.

Kharos raised the spear.

Wolf Zee changed direction before it moved.

Then changed back to human form behind him.

One hand lifted.

“Down.”

Witch force struck Kharos from above.

Divine authority resisted.

For half a second.

Enough.

Zee hit him.

Fist.

Elbow.

Horn.

Claw.

No wasted motion.

Cassel had wounded Zee.

Khandra Parbat had taught him what to do when power could not solve a fight.

Kharos drove lightning into Zee’s abdomen.

Zee convulsed.

The God grabbed him by the throat.

“You are nothing beside divinity.”

Zee’s eyes became very calm.

Human pupils.

Choice.

“Then why did you wait until I was wounded?”

Kharos froze.

There.

Fear did not arrive yet.

But doubt did.

Zee bit his wrist.

⸻

Divine blood entered Zee’s mouth.

Hot.

Storm-heavy.

Powerful.

His Crimson biology reacted immediately.

Not worship.

Not transformation.

Processing.

The divine blood tried to expand.

Zee’s body crushed it down.

No God nature.

No storm authority.

No divinity.

Only nourishment.

Pressure.

Adaptation.

Kharos screamed and ripped free.

Zee swallowed.

The old Black Divinity wounds burned violently.

For one terrible second, divine blood and anti-divine residue collided inside him.

Then Zee’s body separated them.

Not perfectly.

Enough.

The next time Kharos’s authority crashed into Zee, it still hurt.

But Zee recognized the pressure sooner.

Braced sooner.

Survived cleaner.

Small.

Not immunity.

Just Zee learning.

Kharos saw it.

“You are changing.”

“I always am.”

“That is the abomination.”

Zee wiped divine blood from his mouth.

“No.”

His eyes narrowed into slits again.

“That is the consequence.”

Then he attacked.

⸻

By sunset, the storm was dying.

So was Kharos.

One divine arm hung broken.

His spear was gone.

Zee had thrown it into a ravine after breaking three of his own fingers taking it.

Kharos’s regeneration kept repairing wounds.

Zee kept reopening them.

Witchcraft disrupted position.

Wolf instinct predicted retreat.

Vampire speed closed distance.

Assassin technique targeted the same damaged joints.

Crimson Demonic Dragon force endured impacts that should have shattered him.

Zee himself looked worse.

Blood everywhere.

One eye swollen.

Three black Godslayer wounds still open.

Scales broken.

Breathing heavy.

Still smiling.

Kharos backed toward the edge of the mountain.

The God finally smelled afraid.

Zee stopped.

Enjoyed it.

Fully.

Deliberately.

Kharos understood.

“You could finish this.”

“Yes.”

“Then why are you waiting?”

Zee stepped closer.

“Because you came here believing you were above fear.”

Kharos’s divine fire flickered.

Zee smiled.

“I wanted you to meet it.”

Kharos raised one trembling hand.

“You cannot kill what I am.”

Zee reached him.

“I already have.”

He bit.

Kharos screamed.

Zee fed deeply.

Divine regeneration fought.

Then weakened.

Storm clouds collapsed overhead.

Kharos struck Zee.

Once.

Twice.

The third blow barely moved him.

Zee kept drinking.

The God’s heartbeat slowed.

Divine light dimmed.

Fear became panic.

Zee pulled back before the final beat.

Kharos sagged in his grip.

“Please.”

There.

A God begging.

Zee’s face remained calm.

He could have prolonged it.

Wanted to.

Instead he chose enough.

“Now you understand.”

He broke Kharos’s neck.

Then tore the remaining divine life from him through blood.

The storm stopped.

Completely.

Kharos died.

Permanently.

No escape.

No avatar.

No return.

The Godslayer lay dead before dawn.

The God lay dead before sunset.

Same day.

Zee looked toward the darkening sky.

“Long day.”

Then the river below the mountain rose upward.

⸻

Not flooded.

Rose.

A column of water climbed from the valley against gravity.

Ner moved beside Zee.

Gold ready.

Zee watched.

Water spiraled through the air.

Divine blood from Kharos’s corpse had reached cracks in the mountain.

Underground streams.

The water reacted violently.

Then became still.

Impossible stillness.

A woman stepped from it.

No gasp.

No struggle.

No wet stumble.

She walked through suspended water as if crossing a palace floor.

Dark hair fell down her back.

Pearl-black armor covered her shoulders and waist.

A crown of dark silver rested against her head.

Not decorative.

Royal.

Her eyes were deep blue-black.

Not glowing.

Worse.

Watching.

She looked at Kharos’s corpse.

Then Cassel’s blood still dried across Zee.

Then at Zee himself.

The wounds.

The divine blood.

The broken scales.

She showed no awe.

Only irritation.

“You killed a god.”

Zee looked at Kharos.

“Yes.”

“You killed a Godslayer this morning.”

“Yes.”

Her gaze moved toward the river still climbing behind her.

“And somehow both became my problem.”

Zee smiled.

“Long day.”

She stared at him.

For one second.

Then:

“I already dislike you.”

Zee’s smile widened.

“Good.”

The woman looked toward the water.

“You have made the ocean angry.”

Zee glanced at the dead God.

“Tell it to wait.”

Ner started laughing.

The Queen did not.

Not yet.

⸻

Chapter Ninety-Seven

The Queen Beneath the Water

Her name was Nymeris Thalryn.

She did not offer it immediately.

First she ordered Zee away from Kharos’s corpse.

Zee looked at her.

“No.”

Nymeris looked at him.

“That was not a request.”

“That is unfortunate.”

“You are standing beside a divine rupture connected to every underground current beneath this mountain.”

Zee glanced downward.

“Still sounds like a request.”

Ner stood several feet away, enjoying this far too much.

Nymeris noticed.

“You find this entertaining?”

“Extremely.”

“Why?”

Ner smiled.

“People usually need longer before ordering him around.”

Zee looked at him.

“Whose side are you on?”

“Mine.”

Fair.

Nymeris stepped closer to the dead God.

The river responded.

Water curled around her wrist.

Not Bloodsong.

Not ordinary Witchcraft.

Older.

Oceanic.

Pressure moved through it.

Zee felt something beneath the surface.

Abyss.

Depth.

The sensation of water so deep sunlight had never reached it.

Nymeris touched two fingers to Kharos’s blood.

The river convulsed.

Her expression hardened.

“You killed the holder of a Tempest Throne beside a watershed connected to the deep currents.”

Zee leaned against a broken stone because his body had finally started objecting to the day.

“And?”

“And divine authority does not simply vanish politely.”

“What did it do?”

“It fell.”

Zee frowned.

“Into what?”

“The water.”

That got his attention.

Nymeris looked toward the river.

“Kharos’s death created a pressure fracture through the current network. My eastern boundary felt it before he finished dying.”

“Your boundary?”

Now she finally looked directly at him.

“I am Queen Nymeris Thalryn.”

The water behind her rose higher.

“Reigning Queen of Nhalaris.”

Ner’s expression changed.

Zee’s did not.

He had never heard the name.

Nymeris noticed.

“Of course surface kings forgot.”

Zee smiled faintly.

“You hid underwater.”

“We survived underwater.”

“Same result.”

“No.”

The answer carried enough authority that even Zee stopped smiling for half a second.

Good.

He liked her better already.

⸻

Nhalaris was older than several kingdoms Zee knew.

That was all Nymeris volunteered.

Not where it stood beneath the ocean.

Not how many people lived there.

Not how its armies moved.

Only enough.

An ancient underwater civilization.

Its own laws.

Its own military.

Its own magic.

Its own throne.

Its royal bloodline had carried a relationship with the Abyss longer than surface records remembered.

Siren blood lived inside that inheritance.

Old.

Hereditary.

Royal.

Not every bearer expressed it the same way.

Nymeris did.

But not like Ner.

Her voice did not command blood.

It affected water.

Pressure.

Resonance through deep currents.

The ocean heard her differently than people did.

Zee studied her.

She caught him.

“What?”

“Nothing.”

“You are staring.”

“I am looking.”

“That is what staring is.”

“No.”

Ner laughed again.

Nymeris looked toward him.

Then stopped.

Something passed through the air.

Small.

Almost inaudible.

Ner’s Bloodsong answered automatically.

One low resonance beneath his heartbeat.

Nymeris’s eyes sharpened.

Ner’s smile vanished.

“There is something in your voice.”

Nymeris studied him.

“There is something impossible in yours.”

Zee looked between them.

Ner stepped closer.

Not threatened.

Curious.

“Siren?”

Nymeris’s expression changed by only a fraction.

“Partly.”

Ner’s Gold moved faintly around his fingers.

“My mother’s line.”

Nymeris watched the resonance around him.

“That is not ordinary Siren blood.”

“No.”

“What happened to you?”

Ner glanced at Zee.

Nymeris followed the look.

Then closed her eyes briefly.

“Of course.”

Zee frowned.

“What does that mean?”

“It means I have known you less than an hour and you have already become responsible for two separate problems.”

“Only two?”

Nymeris stared.

Ner laughed again.

Good.

⸻

Then Nymeris noticed Zee’s wounds properly.

Her humor disappeared.

“What did that?”

“Godslayer.”

“And where is he?”

“Dead.”

She looked toward the ruined shrine above them.

Then at Kharos.

“And that?”

“Also dead.”

Nymeris stared at him.

Zee waited.

Finally:

“What?”

“You killed both today?”

“Yes.”

“You killed a Godslayer before sunrise.”

“Yes.”

“Then fought a true God while those wounds were still open.”

“Yes.”

“And killed him before sunset.”

“Yes.”

Nymeris looked at Ner.

“Is he always like this?”

Ner considered.

“Unfortunately.”

Zee looked offended.

Nymeris looked back at the black wounds.

“Dark Divinity.”

Zee’s eyes sharpened.

“You know it.”

“I know of it.”

“Godslayers?”

“Yes.”

“How many?”

Nymeris smiled faintly.

“Surface kings really do believe nothing exists until they personally meet it.”

Zee stood straighter.

“That was unnecessarily insulting.”

“It was accurate.”

“Worse.”

Nymeris’s gaze returned to the wounds.

“You are resisting it.”

“A little.”

“You did not absorb it.”

“No.”

“Good.”

Zee frowned.

“Everyone keeps saying that.”

“Because attempting to hold Dark Divinity without being chosen by it would be an excellent way to destroy yourself.”

“I was not planning to.”

Nymeris looked at the dead God.

“You drank him.”

“That is different.”

“How?”

“I wanted his blood.”

She stared again.

Ner stepped between the conversation before it became circular.

“He does not become what he drinks.”

Nymeris looked at him.

“No?”

“No.”

“He changes around pressure.”

Nymeris returned her attention to Zee.

That interest was different.

Not awe.

Assessment.

“Everything that tries to kill you teaches you how to survive it.”

“Usually.”

“That sounds exhausting.”

Zee paused.

Most people called it terrifying.

Monster.

Impossible.

Weapon.

Nymeris called it exhausting.

He looked at her more carefully.

She noticed.

“What?”

“Nothing.”

“You did it again.”

“Still looking.”

She rolled her eyes.

⸻

Zareth arrived before full dark.

Human form this time.

He walked into the valley, saw Nymeris standing beside Zee, and immediately opened the Link.

Dangerous.

Zee answered mentally.

I noticed.

Zareth looked at him.

You smiled.

I smile around dangerous people.

That is the problem.

Nymeris looked toward Zareth.

“You are Drakonis.”

Zareth stopped.

“Crown Prince Zareth Drakonis.”

“I know the blood.”

Zareth’s eyes narrowed.

“You know Dragon blood?”

“My people know what reaches the deep.”

“Dragons do not live underwater.”

“No.”

Nymeris’s expression remained calm.

“But dead ones sink.”

Silence.

Zareth stared.

Zee looked at her.

“That was dark.”

Nymeris glanced toward him.

“You killed two immortal threats before dinner.”

“Fair.”

Zareth privately sent:

I like her less now.

Zee answered:

You like her more.

A pause.

Unfortunately.

⸻

The real problem surfaced after sunset.

The river split.

Not physically.

Magically.

One current flowed downstream.

Another pulled backward beneath it.

Nymeris knelt beside the water.

Her face changed.

Queen now.

No irritation.

No jokes.

Responsibility.

“My eastern ward is weakening.”

Zee crouched beside her despite the pain in his ribs.

“What happens if it breaks?”

“Pressure from the Abyss enters channels not built to hold it.”

“Meaning?”

“Villages beneath the shelf collapse.”

“How many people?”

Nymeris looked at him.

“Eleven thousand under the eastern reach.”

That number changed Zee instantly.

Not because they were his.

Because he understood the look on her face.

Calculation.

Distance.

Time.

People.

A ruler trying to decide which disaster could be allowed because not all of them could be stopped.

He knew that expression.

She saw recognition in him.

Not sympathy.

Recognition.

“You understand.”

“Yes.”

Nymeris looked back toward the water.

“Most kings ask what happens to their trade.”

“I hate trade meetings.”

“That may be the first sensible thing you have said.”

Zee almost smiled.

Then pain tore through his side.

He hid it badly.

Nymeris noticed.

“You are injured.”

“I remain aware.”

“And you are considering helping.”

“Yes.”

“You cannot even stand properly.”

“I am standing.”

“You are leaning on a rock.”

“The rock is supportive.”

Ner turned away because he was laughing.

Nymeris stared at Zee for a long moment.

Then something changed.

Not affection.

Respect.

Small.

Earned.

“You do not know my people.”

“No.”

“You have never seen Nhalaris.”

“No.”

“You owe us nothing.”

Zee looked toward the unnatural current.

“I killed the God.”

“Yes.”

“That made the fracture.”

“Yes.”

“Then part of it is mine.”

Nymeris studied him.

That answer mattered.

Not because Zee took blame for everything.

Because he took responsibility for what was actually his.

She understood that too.

⸻

They worked through the night.

Not to repair the entire oceanic boundary.

Impossible.

Only to stop the fracture from widening.

Nymeris controlled the water.

Ner used Bloodsong resonance to identify where living currents carried the divine disturbance.

Zee used Witchcraft to break divine residue from the stone without touching Nymeris’s Abyssal magic directly.

Zareth carried collapsed boulders from the river channel in human form until he became irritated and shifted into true Dragon form to move the rest.

By midnight, the reverse current weakened.

Nymeris stood waist-deep in the river.

Her voice changed.

Not louder.

Deeper.

The water responded like something remembering its Queen.

Ancient Siren resonance moved through the current.

Not compulsion.

Not Bloodsong.

A royal call through water itself.

The fracture closed.

Mostly.

Nymeris emerged from the river.

For the first time, she looked tired.

Zee noticed.

Did not comment.

Queens disliked obvious observations as much as kings did.

Good.

⸻

By morning, the rumors had already started.

Cassel Rhune.

True Godslayer.

Dead.

Kharos.

True God.

Dead.

Same day.

Killed by the same man.

Surface reports disagreed on everything else.

Some claimed Zee had stolen Dark Divinity.

False.

Some claimed he had become a god.

False.

Some claimed he had killed Kharos with Cassel’s weapon.

False.

One report called him:

THE MAN WHO KILLED GODS.

Zee read it and frowned.

“That is dramatic.”

Zareth looked over his shoulder.

“You say that like you are not.”

“I am tasteful.”

Ner laughed.

Nymeris looked genuinely confused.

“Do surface people always name everything?”

“Yes,” Zee said.

“No,” Ner said simultaneously.

Nymeris looked between them.

“I see.”

Zee burned the report.

⸻

Nymeris prepared to return to Nhalaris before noon.

The river rose around her again.

Zee stood nearby.

Still wounded.

Still bleeding slightly beneath fresh bandages.

She looked at him.

“You owe my kingdom a visit.”

Zee stared.

“I do not do underwater.”

“You will.”

“That sounded like an order.”

“It was.”

Zee smiled.

Nymeris did not.

Then almost did.

Almost.

Ner noticed.

Zareth noticed.

Zee did not care.

There was nothing romantic in it.

Something stranger had begun.

Two rulers who understood responsibility.

Two people accustomed to being obeyed.

Two kingdoms that had existed without needing each other.

Until one dead God connected them through water.

Zee folded his arms.

“What happens if I refuse?”

Nymeris stepped backward into the rising river.

“I will come back.”

“That sounds threatening.”

“It is diplomatic.”

“Surface diplomacy is better.”

“No.”

She sank without splashing.

Then stopped.

Only her face remained above the impossible water.

“Ner.”

He looked at her.

“We should speak again.”

Bloodsong hummed faintly.

Ner nodded.

“I think so.”

Then Nymeris looked at Zee one last time.

“Try not to kill another god before I repair the damage from this one.”

Zee considered.

“No promises.”

Her eyes narrowed.

“King Darkheart.”

“Queen Thalryn.”

Then she vanished beneath the water.

The river fell normally.

Silence returned.

Zareth looked at Zee.

“She is going to become a problem.”

Zee smiled.

“Probably.”

Ner stepped beside him.

“You like her.”

“As a person.”

“I know.”

Zee looked at him.

“No jealousy?”

Ner stared.

“You are gay.”

“Correct.”

“And I have eyes.”

“Also correct.”

Ner smiled.

“Besides, I like her too.”

Zareth groaned.

“Excellent. Now there are three of you.”

Zee looked toward the river.

Somewhere far beneath oceans surface kingdoms barely understood, Queen Nymeris Thalryn ruled an ancient civilization tied to the Abyss and old Siren blood.

Zee knew almost nothing about her.

She knew almost nothing about him.

That was fine.

They had time.

A reason to meet again was enough.

Behind them lay the blood of a Godslayer.

Ahead of them lay the corpse of a God.

Before the same sun had set, Zee Darkheart had killed both.

And before the next sun fully rose, another kingdom had entered his life.

Not through conquest.

Not prophecy.

Not destiny.

Through consequence.

The world had become larger again.

And darker with it.

Chapter Ninety-Eight

The Kingdom Beneath the Ocean

Three months passed before Zee visited Nhalaris.

Nymeris reminded him twice.

The third message contained no words.

Only a sphere of seawater floating above the Darkheart council table.

Zee stared at it.

Rez stared at Zee.

Ner smiled.

Zareth leaned back in his chair.

“She is getting impatient.”

Zee looked at him.

“You sound pleased.”

“I am.”

The sphere burst.

Water hit Zee directly in the face.

Silence.

Rez started laughing first.

Ner followed.

Zareth did not even try hiding it.

Zee wiped water from his eyes.

“I hate her.”

Ner stood.

“No, you don’t.”

“I am reconsidering.”

A folded shell rested where the sphere had been.

Zee opened it.

One sentence.

COME BELOW, SURFACE KING.

Zee’s eye twitched.

⸻

Nhalaris did not sit on the ocean floor.

It existed inside it.

That distinction became clear when Nymeris opened the passage.

Zee, Ner, and Zareth stood on a black coastal cliff while seawater climbed upward into an arch.

Not a portal.

A road.

Water held apart by pressure and ancient magic.

Nymeris waited beyond it.

Dark armor.

Silver-black crown.

Completely dry despite standing inside the sea.

“You came.”

Zee stepped through.

“I was assaulted by correspondence.”

“You ignored two requests.”

“They were very long.”

“They were six sentences.”

“Exactly.”

Ner walked behind him.

Zareth entered in human form.

Nymeris looked toward the Dragon prince.

“No true form below the inner gates.”

Zareth raised an eyebrow.

“Why?”

“Because you are enormous.”

Fair.

Zee smiled.

Zareth privately sent:

I dislike this kingdom already.

Zee answered:

You dislike doors.

Correct.

⸻

The descent took nearly an hour.

Not because they walked downward.

Because Nhalaris moved around them.

Currents shifted.

Stone opened.

Water became corridors.

Then suddenly—

the ocean disappeared.

A city stretched beneath a living dome of deep-blue pressure.

Towers of black coral.

Silver bridges.

Bioluminescent gardens.

Water channels flowing upward along walls.

Siren guards in dark armor.

Others without visible Siren traits.

Families.

Merchants.

Soldiers.

Children.

An entire civilization hidden beneath the surface kingdoms.

Zee stopped.

Nymeris noticed.

“What?”

“Nothing.”

“You are staring again.”

“This one is deserved.”

That almost made her smile.

Almost.

Ner’s Bloodsong hummed faintly.

Dozens of distant voices answered the city around him.

Not directly.

Resonance.

Ancient Siren blood everywhere.

His expression changed.

Nymeris looked toward him.

“Too much?”

“A little.”

She nodded.

No mockery.

“Do not listen to everything.”

“I am not trying.”

“That is usually when it is worst.”

Ner looked at her.

Recognition.

Not identical power.

But experience.

That mattered.

⸻

The Nhalaris council hated Zee immediately.

That helped.

Seven ministers.

Three military commanders.

One Abyssal priestess.

None bowed.

Good.

Zee did not ask them to.

One minister spoke first.

“You killed Kharos.”

“Yes.”

“You ruptured our eastern current.”

“Yes.”

“You entered Nhalaris armed.”

Zee looked down at himself.

“I am always armed.”

Nymeris closed her eyes.

The minister continued.

“Your presence threatens the stability of this court.”

Zee looked toward Nymeris.

“Do they always speak like this?”

“Yes.”

“That sounds exhausting.”

“It is.”

The minister looked offended.

Good.

Then another woman placed a map of the eastern current across the table.

The damage remained.

The fracture they closed on the surface had prevented collapse.

It had not repaired the deeper channels.

Three villages still operated under emergency pressure wards.

Nymeris looked toward Zee.

“This is why I summoned you.”

“Ordered.”

“Yes.”

Zee smiled.

“What do you need?”

No argument now.

Work.

Nymeris pointed.

“Divine residue embedded itself into an old Abyssal boundary.”

Zee studied the map.

“And if we remove it?”

“The boundary may fail.”

“If we leave it?”

“It spreads.”

“How many people?”

“Eight thousand seven hundred within the affected reach.”

Zee’s humor disappeared.

There.

Same burden.

Different kingdom.

Nymeris noticed.

“You understand why I did not wait politely.”

“Yes.”

“Good.”

Zee looked toward the map.

“Then we fix it.”

One minister objected.

“He is the reason it exists.”

Zee looked at him.

“Yes.”

The man paused.

Zee continued.

“That is why I am helping.”

No defensiveness.

No excuse.

Just responsibility.

Nymeris watched him carefully.

Another small piece of trust moved into place.

⸻

The repair took four days.

Zee did not command Nhalaris.

That was important.

Nymeris did.

Her engineers.

Her Siren wardens.

Her military.

Her laws.

Zee listened.

Mostly.

On the second day he ignored one safety order and nearly got crushed under deep-current pressure.

Nymeris found him afterward bleeding from both ears.

“You are impossible.”

“I survived.”

“That is not the same as listening.”

“I listened.”

“You did the opposite.”

“I heard you first.”

Nymeris stared.

Ner turned away to hide a smile.

Zee looked toward him.

“Do not.”

“I said nothing.”

“You are thinking loudly.”

“Zareth says the same thing.”

Through the Link from another chamber:

Because you are both annoying.

Zee smiled.

Good.

⸻

The final breach sat beyond Nhalaris’s eastern shelf.

Open ocean.

Dark enough that even Zee’s Vampire sight struggled.

Nymeris entered the water first.

Not swimming.

Belonging.

The ocean carried her.

Ner followed inside a Golden breathing sphere.

Zee had one too.

He hated it.

“This is humiliating.”

Nymeris’s voice reached them through water resonance.

“You cannot breathe underwater.”

“I do not need much air.”

“You need some.”

“Technicality.”

She ignored him.

Zareth remained in human form until the passage widened.

Then shifted.

True Dragon form filled the dark water.

No fire.

No flight.

But enormous strength.

The Dragon Link carried his displeasure.

I hate swimming.

Zee answered:

You look majestic.

I will drown you.

I cannot permanently die.

Then I will drown you repeatedly.

Nymeris looked back.

“You two are arguing.”

Zee frowned.

“How do you know?”

“You both look irritated.”

Fair.

⸻

The divine residue had become a knot of storm-light beneath the shelf.

Nymeris anchored the current.

Ner used resonance to locate living pressure around it.

Zareth held the collapsing rock.

Zee entered the center.

The old Black Divinity scars across his body burned.

Not because Dark Divinity was present.

Because divine pressure recognized wounds that had once denied divinity.

Useful.

Painful.

Zee smiled.

Nymeris saw.

“You enjoy pain too much.”

“Only interesting pain.”

“That sentence is deeply concerning.”

Zee raised one hand.

Witch precision.

No giant blast.

He separated divine residue thread by thread.

Nymeris held the current around it.

Their magic did not merge.

Did not need to.

They worked beside one another.

Queen.

King.

Each controlling what belonged to them.

The final divine strand broke.

The ocean surged.

Zareth roared through the water.

Ner’s Gold snapped outward.

Nymeris lifted both hands.

Her voice changed.

Deep Siren resonance moved through miles of water.

The current obeyed.

Not like compulsion.

Like inheritance.

The Abyss recognized her.

The rupture closed.

Completely.

Nhalaris survived.

⸻

That night, Nymeris invited them to dinner.

Not diplomacy.

Dinner.

A distinction Zee noticed immediately.

No ministers.

No guards at the table.

Only Zee.

Ner.

Zareth.

Nymeris.

Zee looked around.

“Where is everyone?”

“I dismissed them.”

“Why?”

“Because I wanted one meal without hearing someone explain why your existence threatens oceanic stability.”

Zee smiled.

“Reasonable.”

Nymeris poured wine.

Ner looked toward the food.

“Is that still moving?”

“Yes.”

“No.”

Zareth picked it up and ate it.

Ner stared.

Zareth shrugged.

“Dragon.”

Zee laughed.

Nymeris finally did too.

Not almost.

Actually.

The sound changed something.

Small.

Not romance.

Ease.

By the end of the night, Nymeris no longer called Zee Surface King every time she addressed him.

Only half the time.

Progress.

⸻

Chapter Ninety-Nine

The People Behind the Crowns

Nymeris came to Darkheart six months later.

Without warning.

Zee found her in Southhold arguing with a mason.

He stopped in the street.

“Why are you here?”

Nymeris looked over.

“To see whether your kingdom actually functions.”

The mason glanced between them.

Zee frowned.

“You could have started at the castle.”

“I have seen castles.”

She gestured toward Southhold.

“I wanted this.”

Homes.

Markets.

Wolf children chasing Vampire children through muddy streets.

Witches repairing protective runes on the school.

Former Rell workers building their own shops.

Kael arguing with a guard.

Tessa yelling at three patients.

Amara carrying lumber despite not being asked.

Nymeris watched all of it.

“This is not what surface reports describe.”

“Surface reports are written by people who dislike me.”

“They describe an army of hybrids.”

“I have four.”

“Five, if you count Rez.”

“He is Vesper.”

Nymeris glanced at him.

That answer mattered.

“You could claim him.”

“He would punch me again.”

“Again?”

Zee said nothing.

Nymeris smiled.

“I need that story.”

“No.”

⸻

Ner found them near the school.

Nymeris greeted him before Zee.

That offended Zee unnecessarily.

“You like him more.”

Nymeris looked at Ner.

“Yes.”

Ner smiled.

Zee stared at both of them.

“This alliance is becoming hostile.”

“Good,” Nymeris said.

Ner’s Bloodsong reacted when she stepped close.

Her Siren resonance answered more clearly now.

Still different.

Ner listened.

“You carry something deeper than the surface Siren lines I have encountered.”

Nymeris’s expression sharpened.

“My House descends from the royal Abyss line.”

“Does every Thalryn inherit it?”

“No.”

“Every Queen?”

“No.”

Ner nodded.

No more questions.

Nymeris noticed.

“You stopped.”

“You would tell me if you wanted me to know.”

She looked at Zee.

“Keep him.”

Zee blinked.

“I was already planning to.”

Ner laughed.

⸻

Nymeris stayed three weeks.

Not as guest decoration.

She attended councils.

Argued over Safe Road expansion.

Insulted Darkheart drainage systems.

Improved them.

Visited Kael’s training yards.

Asked Tessa about hybrid medicine.

Let Amara take her hunting through the southern forest and returned covered in mud, furious, and apparently happier.

She spent one afternoon with Rez when he arrived from Vesper.

The two argued about trade law for four hours.

Zee left after twenty minutes.

Cowardice sometimes meant survival.

Zareth arrived on the fifth day.

He and Nymeris immediately disagreed about whether oceanic territory included Dragon flight paths over open sea.

Neither yielded.

Zee watched them for half an hour.

Ner stood beside him.

“This is your fault.”

“I did nothing.”

“You introduced them.”

“I did not control the result.”

“That is usually your defense.”

Fair.

⸻

The attack came on Nymeris’s seventeenth day.

Not against her.

Against Southhold.

Again.

A mercenary company from a western kingdom wanted refugees returned for unpaid taxes and military desertion.

Different motive.

Same ugly assumption.

That people remained owned after leaving.

This time Southhold responded before Zee did.

Bells rang.

Children entered shelters.

Witch barriers rose.

Wolf trackers moved outside the walls.

Vampire defenders took rooftops.

Kael commanded the eastern street.

Tessa moved medical teams.

Amara vanished into the trees.

Zee stood beside Nymeris on the tower.

She watched.

“You are not moving.”

“I am.”

“You are standing.”

“I am watching first.”

Old Zee would already have been in the enemy line.

Nymeris understood the change.

“Your people know what to do.”

“Yes.”

“That bothers you.”

“Yes.”

“Why?”

“Because they learned by being attacked.”

Nymeris looked toward the battlefield.

“So did mine.”

There.

Same burden again.

Then the mercenaries broke through the western barrier.

Zee’s pupils narrowed.

“Now.”

He moved.

Nymeris moved too.

Not because Zee asked.

Because civilians were threatened.

⸻

Zee hit the first line in human form.

Crimson-black scales spreading over his arms.

One-word Witchcraft breaking weapons.

Vampire speed cutting through formation.

Wolf instinct reading motion.

Controlled.

Dark.

Efficient.

Nymeris fought differently.

Water erupted from underground wells.

Not enough to flood Southhold.

Enough to tear mercenaries off their feet.

Her voice carried through it.

Abyssal resonance.

Pressure.

Direction.

One man tried reaching a child shelter.

Nymeris slammed him into stone with a column of water.

Zee looked over.

“That was excessive.”

Nymeris stared.

“You broke someone’s leg with your face ten seconds ago.”

“Horn.”

“That does not improve it.”

Good.

They fought well together.

Not perfectly.

Zee pushed.

Nymeris contained.

Nymeris controlled space.

Zee hunted openings.

Neither commanded the other.

Neither needed to.

When the mercenary commander surrendered, Zee stopped.

Immediately.

That mattered after Rell.

Nymeris noticed.

He heard the commander’s heartbeat.

Smelled fear.

Wanted blood.

Still chose prison.

Nymeris said nothing.

She did not need to.

⸻

Afterward, they found six dead Darkheart citizens.

Three soldiers.

Three civilians.

Not clean.

Never clean.

Zee stood over the bodies.

Nymeris beside him.

No one spoke for a while.

Then she said:

“You count them all as yours.”

“Yes.”

“Even people who arrived months ago.”

“Yes.”

“Even if they were born elsewhere.”

“Yes.”

Nymeris looked toward him.

“That is why they keep coming.”

Zee’s jaw tightened.

“That is why they keep dying too.”

“No.”

He looked at her.

She did not soften the answer.

“They die because other rulers still think leaving is theft.”

Zee said nothing.

Nymeris continued.

“You are responsible for what happens under your protection.”

“Yes.”

“You are not responsible for the existence of cruelty beyond it.”

Zee almost argued.

Then stopped.

Not because she had absolved him.

She had not.

She was drawing the same distinction Ner often demanded of facts.

Responsibility without delusion.

Queen thinking.

Zee understood.

That was rarer than sympathy.

⸻

Later that night, Zee found Nymeris sitting alone on the southern wall.

No crown.

Hair loose.

She looked less like Queen of Nhalaris.

Still unmistakably one.

He sat beside her.

For once, neither began with an insult.

Nymeris spoke first.

“When I was nineteen, a pressure collapse killed two hundred people beneath the western shelf.”

Zee looked at her.

She had never told him anything personal before.

“I ordered the evacuation too late.”

“Why?”

“I believed the wardens when they said the barrier would hold.”

Silence.

“It did not.”

Zee understood immediately.

“How long did you blame yourself?”

Nymeris laughed without humor.

“I have not stopped.”

“There.”

She looked at him.

“That is stupid.”

“Yes.”

“Was that supposed to help?”

“No.”

He leaned back.

“I blame myself for people dying where I am not.”

“That is also stupid.”

“Yes.”

They sat in silence.

Then Nymeris smiled faintly.

“Good.”

“What?”

“Now we are both stupid.”

Zee laughed.

There.

Not diplomacy.

Not alliance.

Friendship.

Something deeper than usefulness.

Chosen slowly.

Earned.

⸻

Nymeris remained another week.

When she finally left, Darkheart children knew her name.

Tessa had forced her to take three medical books back to Nhalaris.

Amara had given her a hunting knife.

Kael had somehow lost money to her playing cards.

Rez sent trade proposals.

Zareth claimed he still disliked her.

Nobody believed him.

Ner walked with her to the river passage.

Zee followed.

Nymeris looked between them.

“Nhalaris will send a permanent diplomatic vessel to the coastal river.”

Zee raised an eyebrow.

“That sounds suspiciously like friendship.”

“It is administration.”

“Of course.”

She looked at Ner.

“And I want you to visit.”

Ner nodded.

“I will.”

Then at Zee.

“You too.”

“I just went.”

“Six months ago.”

“Recently.”

“No.”

Zee sighed.

Nymeris stepped toward the water.

Then paused.

“Zee.”

His expression changed.

She rarely used his name without sarcasm.

“What?”

“If Darkheart is attacked beneath the coastline, send for me.”

He stared.

Nymeris continued.

“If Nhalaris is attacked near the surface, I will send for you.”

Not treaty language.

More personal.

Trust.

Zee nodded once.

“Done.”

She entered the river.

Then looked back.

“And fix your drainage.”

Zee’s face hardened.

“I knew you ruined the moment on purpose.”

Nymeris smiled.

Then vanished beneath the water.

Ner stood beside him.

“You love her.”

Zee looked at him sharply.

“Not like that.”

“I know.”

Zee looked back toward the river.

Chosen family had never needed one shape.

Aurelia had taught him that blood mattered.

Rez had taught him blood was not required.

Zareth had taught him connection could begin before language.

Ner had taught him love could survive change.

Nymeris was teaching him something else.

Two rulers could become family without either surrendering a crown.

And somewhere in the months ahead, that friendship would continue growing.

Not toward prophecy.

Not toward destiny.

Toward choices neither of them had made yet.

For now, that was enough.

Chapter One Hundred

The Year the Sea Came Ashore

Zee turned twenty-five while standing knee-deep in seawater that should not have existed.

Darkheart was forty miles inland.

That made the situation irritating.

Nymeris found it worse.

She stood in the flooded market of Southhold with water curling around her boots.

“This is not mine.”

Zee looked at the water.

“It came from your direction.”

“The ocean is not one enormous bucket I personally manage.”

“That sounds irresponsible.”

Nymeris stared at him.

Ner laughed behind them.

“You two have known each other too long.”

It had been more than a year since Zee killed Kharos.

Long enough that Nymeris no longer arrived at Darkheart as a foreign Queen.

She still arrived with guards.

Still carried Nhalaris authority.

Still argued with Zee before most meals.

But Southhold knew her.

Darkheart children recognized her.

Nhalaris had begun recognizing Zee too.

Not all of them liked him.

That was fine.

Zee liked very few councils himself.

⸻

The flood came from beneath the earth.

Tessa discovered the first body.

Not drowned.

Drained.

A Vampire woman lay beside an underground spring with every drop of blood gone.

No bite marks.

No wounds.

Kael crouched beside her.

“What does that?”

Ner touched the water.

His Bloodsong recoiled.

“Something beneath us.”

Nymeris knelt immediately.

Her expression changed.

“What?”

Zee asked.

She looked toward the flooded street.

“Abyssal current.”

“You said it was not yours.”

“It is not.”

“Convenient.”

Nymeris ignored him.

“There are currents beneath the world older than Nhalaris.”

That got Zee’s attention.

“How old?”

“Old enough that my people built around some instead of disturbing them.”

Amara arrived from the northern road.

“Tracks.”

“What kind?”

She shook her head.

“Nothing I know.”

Good.

Zee smiled.

Nymeris noticed.

“Why are you happy?”

“New monster.”

“You have terrible instincts.”

“Usually effective.”

⸻

The thing emerged after sunset.

It came through the flooded well.

Long.

Pale.

Almost transparent.

No eyes.

Too many joints.

Its mouth opened across its chest.

Three Darkheart soldiers attacked first.

One died before Zee reached them.

The creature touched him.

His blood left his body through unbroken skin.

Tessa shouted:

“Do not let it touch you!”

Zee was already moving.

The creature struck.

He caught one limb.

Instant mistake.

Blood pulled toward his skin.

Vampire instinct screamed.

Crimson biology resisted.

His veins darkened.

He tore free.

“Annoying.”

Nymeris raised both hands.

Water slammed the creature against stone.

It twisted inside the pressure.

Not swimming.

Using water like flesh.

Nymeris’s eyes narrowed.

“It belongs to the Deep Below.”

Zee looked at her.

“That sounds dramatic.”

“It is trying to drink your kingdom.”

“Fair.”

The creature lunged.

Zee disappeared beneath it.

Vampire speed.

Claws opened its underside.

No blood.

Only black fluid.

Amara attacked from the flank in Wolf form.

Kael bound two limbs with Witchcraft.

Ner hit the creature with Bloodsong.

Nothing.

He frowned.

“No heartbeat.”

Tessa shouted from behind a shield line:

“Then stop trying to talk to it!”

Ner glared.

“I was not talking.”

“You were singing.”

“Different.”

The creature broke Kael’s chains.

Nymeris’s water caught it again.

Zee understood.

“Hold the upper half.”

Nymeris looked at him.

“Why?”

“Because I want the lower half.”

“That sentence was horrifying.”

“Hold it.”

She did.

Zee moved.

Silent Witchcraft compressed the stone beneath the creature.

Wolf instinct tracked every joint.

Dragon force entered his arms.

He caught two limbs.

Pulled.

The creature screamed.

Not from a mouth.

From the water.

Nymeris flinched.

“There.”

Zee saw it.

A black organ beneath the translucent body.

Not heart.

Anchor.

He drove his hand through the creature.

Closed his fist.

“Break.”

The anchor ruptured.

The thing collapsed.

Water hit the street all at once.

Zee stood dripping.

Nymeris stared at him.

“You put your hand inside it.”

“Yes.”

“Without knowing what it was.”

“Yes.”

“You are twenty-five now.”

Zee frowned.

“So?”

“I had hoped age would improve you.”

“It has.”

Ner walked past them.

“It has not.”

⸻

The flooding stopped before dawn.

But the damage remained.

Seven dead.

Thirty-one injured.

Two streets destroyed.

A section of Southhold evacuated.

Nymeris stayed.

Not because diplomacy required it.

Because Darkheart needed water engineers.

Nhalaris sent them.

Zee did not ask twice.

That mattered.

Months earlier, he would have tried solving everything himself.

Now he accepted help without pretending it made him smaller.

Nymeris noticed that too.

She said nothing.

Also progress.

⸻

The attack was not the only reason she stayed.

Three days later, Nhalaris received news.

A surface kingdom had begun dumping cursed iron into a coastal trench to poison an underwater trade route.

Nymeris read the report in Zee’s council chamber.

Her face went still.

Zee recognized the expression.

Queen.

Not woman.

Not friend.

Ruler.

“How many affected?”

“Two settlements.”

“Dead?”

“Twenty-three.”

Zee stood.

Nymeris looked at him.

“This is Nhalaris.”

“Yes.”

“You do not need to come.”

“I know.”

That answer stopped her.

Zee reached for his coat.

Ner smiled faintly.

Nymeris frowned.

“Why?”

Zee looked toward her.

“You stayed.”

Simple.

She understood.

⸻

They went together.

Not Darkheart saving Nhalaris.

Not Nhalaris needing rescue.

Two kingdoms responding because one had been harmed.

Nymeris led.

Zee followed her law beneath the coast.

Ner coordinated resonance through the poisoned current.

Zareth guarded the surface approach from the air.

Kael stayed in Darkheart.

Tessa stayed with Southhold.

Amara remained on the Safe Roads.

Nobody abandoned their own responsibilities simply because Zee moved.

The world had finally become too large for that.

Good.

The coastal kingdom responsible for the poisoning expected an underwater retaliation.

It did not expect Zee.

Its commander looked from Nymeris to him.

“This is not Darkheart territory.”

Zee smiled.

“I know.”

“Then why are you here?”

Nymeris answered first.

“Because you killed my people.”

Zee answered second.

“And she is mine.”

Silence.

Nymeris turned slowly.

Zee realized how that sounded.

He corrected immediately.

“Family.”

Nymeris kept staring.

Ner covered his mouth.

The enemy commander looked confused.

Zee sighed.

“Bad phrasing.”

Nymeris finally looked back toward the soldiers.

“We discuss that later.”

“Preferably never.”

⸻

The cursed-iron stores burned before sunrise.

The poison routes were destroyed.

The civilians working the docks were evacuated before the military warehouses collapsed.

The commander who ordered the dumping tried escaping by ship.

Nymeris sank the ship.

Zee caught the commander before he drowned.

The man looked relieved.

Then Zee handed him to Nymeris.

Relief disappeared.

Good.

Her kingdom.

Her judgment.

Zee did not take it from her.

That mattered more than killing the man himself.

⸻

When they returned to Darkheart, Nymeris found Zee on the western balcony.

“You called me family.”

Zee looked out over the city.

“Yes.”

“You corrected yourself very quickly.”

“It sounded possessive.”

“It did.”

“I hate ownership.”

“I noticed.”

Silence.

Nymeris stepped beside him.

“So?”

“So what?”

“Was it true?”

Zee looked at her.

She was not asking as Queen.

That made the answer easier.

“Yes.”

Nymeris looked away toward Darkheart.

Then nodded.

“Good.”

No speech.

No ceremony.

No promise.

Family did not always arrive through blood.

Sometimes it arrived through flooded streets, broken currents, arguments, and someone showing up because you stayed when their people needed you.

For the first time, Nymeris Thalryn was no longer merely the Queen beneath the water.

She was one of Zee’s people.

Not subject.

Not lover.

Not subordinate.

Family.

And Zee was becoming the same to her.

⸻

Chapter One Hundred One

The Question of Heirs

The conversation began because Rez insulted everyone.

Which was normal.

Darkheart hosted its first formal summit with Nhalaris that winter.

Vesper attended.

Drakonis attended.

No alliances merged.

No crowns surrendered authority.

The entire point was cooperation without ownership.

Rez called it:

“A room full of powerful people agreeing not to become one country.”

Nymeris looked at him.

“That may be the first useful description anyone has given.”

Zee frowned.

“I explained it better.”

“No,” Ner said.

Zareth nodded.

“You absolutely did not.”

Zee looked around the table.

“I hate this family.”

Rez smiled.

“Family?”

Zee realized too late.

Nymeris looked down at her wine.

Ner smiled.

Zareth sent laughter through the Link.

Zee decided murder remained socially inappropriate.

For now.

⸻

The summit lasted four days.

Trade.

Safe Roads.

Coastal protections.

Refugee passage.

Monster boundaries.

Shared warnings about divine disturbances.

Nothing world-ending.

That was important.

Kingdoms also survived through boring agreements.

Zee hated those most.

On the final night, the subject changed.

Succession.

A Nhalaris minister asked Nymeris whether she intended to name an heir.

Silence.

Nymeris placed her cup down.

“Not tonight.”

The minister bowed.

But the question remained.

Later, Zee found her alone beside Darkheart’s inner lake.

She stood several feet from the water.

Interesting.

Usually Nymeris moved toward water instinctively.

Tonight she watched it.

Zee approached.

“You scared your minister.”

“He will recover.”

“Unfortunate.”

Nymeris glanced toward him.

“You are avoiding your own council.”

“Yes.”

“Why?”

“They are discussing grain.”

She nodded sympathetically.

“Tragic.”

Zee sat on the stone wall.

Nymeris remained standing.

After a moment, he asked:

“Why did that question bother you?”

She looked toward him.

“It did not.”

“Lie.”

“You are irritating.”

“Yes.”

Nymeris exhaled.

“My House expects continuity.”

“Heir.”

“Yes.”

“You do not want one?”

Her expression changed.

“That is not the same question.”

Zee understood immediately.

Good.

He waited.

Nymeris looked toward the lake.

“I want children.”

Zee said nothing.

“I do not want a child because ministers are worried about succession.”

“Fair.”

“I do not want someone born carrying a kingdom before they learn their own name.”

That hit something inside him.

Zee’s childhood.

Crown.

Prophecy.

Fear.

Victor.

He looked away.

Nymeris noticed.

“You understand.”

“Yes.”

“Of course you do.”

Silence settled.

Then she asked:

“What about you?”

Zee frowned.

“What about me?”

“Children.”

He almost laughed.

Then realized she was serious.

“I have not thought about it.”

Nymeris looked at him.

“That is a lie.”

Zee narrowed his eyes.

“You are becoming annoying.”

“I learned from you.”

Fair.

He looked toward the lake.

Had he thought about children?

Yes.

Not often.

Never safely.

For years, survival had been the only future he trusted.

Then kingship.

Darkheart.

Ner.

His people.

Now twenty-five.

Immortal.

A kingdom growing around him.

Zee finally answered.

“I think about what they would inherit.”

Nymeris did not mistake the meaning.

“Power.”

“Enemies.”

“Your name.”

“My blood.”

“Your history.”

“Yes.”

Nymeris came closer.

“And what would they inherit that you actually want them to have?”

That question was worse.

Zee thought.

“A home.”

Nymeris waited.

“People who love them.”

Another pause.

“The right to choose who they become.”

There.

Nymeris smiled faintly.

“Then perhaps you have thought about it.”

Zee looked toward her.

“Do not become smug.”

“Too late.”

⸻

Ner joined him later that night.

Zee was already in bed.

Not sleeping.

Ner knew.

“What happened?”

“Nymeris asked if I want children.”

Ner stopped removing his coat.

Then looked at Zee.

“And?”

“I threatened her.”

Ner stared.

“With what?”

“Being annoying.”

“That is not a threat. That is your personality.”

Zee threw a pillow.

Ner caught it.

Then sat beside him.

“So?”

Zee looked at the ceiling.

“I do.”

Ner did not react dramatically.

That made Zee look toward him.

“You knew?”

“I suspected.”

“How?”

“You stare at every child in Darkheart like you are checking whether the world is bothering them.”

“That proves nothing.”

“It proves several things.”

Zee rolled his eyes.

Ner became quieter.

“Do you want one now?”

“No.”

Immediate.

Clear.

Ner nodded.

“Good.”

Zee frowned.

“Good?”

“You answered without fear.”

That made Zee think.

He had not said no because children frightened him.

He said no because he was not ready.

Different.

Ner leaned against him.

“Someday?”

“Maybe.”

“Then someday.”

Simple.

No jealousy.

No permission.

Partner.

Zee wrapped an arm around him.

“What if my child is like me?”

Ner smiled faintly.

“Impossible?”

“Yes.”

“Annoying?”

“Ner.”

“Fine.”

Ner became serious.

“If your child is powerful, then your child is powerful.”

“That sounds simple.”

“It is not.”

Zee looked at him.

Ner continued.

“But power is not a crime.”

No.

Zee knew that better than anyone.

⸻

Nymeris returned to Nhalaris after the summit.

For the next year, the question of children remained exactly that.

A question.

No decision.

No plan.

Life continued.

Darkheart expanded another Safe Road.

Nhalaris opened its first permanent surface embassy.

Rez strengthened Vesper’s independence while still coordinating with both kingdoms.

Zareth took greater responsibility inside Drakonis.

Kael became one of Darkheart’s most respected field commanders.

Tessa expanded battlefield medicine into three permanent clinics.

Amara trained mixed patrols through the southern forests.

Ner traveled between Darkheart and Nhalaris twice, learning more about ancient Siren resonance without becoming one of them.

Zee kept ruling.

Kept hunting.

Kept killing enemies he consciously chose to kill.

Kept feeding.

Kept enjoying fear.

Kept learning where choice ended and impulse began.

And Nymeris became normal inside his life.

That may have been the strangest part.

She appeared for council without announcement.

He visited Nhalaris without complaining every single time.

Sometimes they worked.

Sometimes they argued.

Sometimes they sat in silence and understood the same burden without explaining it.

Years of trust did not arrive through one dramatic oath.

It accumulated.

One decision at a time.

⸻

Near the end of Zee’s twenty-sixth year, Nymeris came to Darkheart alone.

No royal escort.

No diplomatic vessel.

She found Zee in the training courtyard with a twelve-year-old Wolf boy hanging from his back.

The child was trying to choke him.

Poorly.

Zee continued walking.

“You are too high.”

The boy tightened his arm.

“I almost have you.”

“No.”

Nymeris watched.

Zee noticed.

“What?”

“Nothing.”

“You are staring.”

“I am looking.”

Zee narrowed his eyes.

“That is mine.”

“I improved it.”

The boy finally released Zee and dropped to the ground.

“Again?”

“Tomorrow.”

The child ran off.

Nymeris watched him leave.

Then looked at Zee.

“You would be good at it.”

Zee’s expression changed.

“Do not.”

“I said one sentence.”

“You knew what you were doing.”

“Yes.”

He sighed.

Nymeris smiled.

Then became serious.

“I have been thinking.”

“Dangerous.”

“Zee.”

He stopped.

Her tone was different.

Not Queen.

Not joking.

Something personal.

“What?”

Nymeris looked toward the empty courtyard.

“About heirs.”

Zee said nothing.

“About children.”

Still nothing.

“And about whether bloodlines should continue because kingdoms demand it…”

She looked at him.

“…or because the people carrying them actually choose to.”

Zee’s eyes sharpened slightly.

There it was.

Not a decision.

Not yet.

But the question had changed.

No longer:

Do either of them want children?

Now:

What would it mean to choose one?

Nymeris held his gaze.

“We should talk.”

Zee glanced toward the castle.

“Now?”

“No.”

That surprised him.

“When?”

“When neither of us is speaking as King or Queen.”

Zee understood.

No councils.

No succession.

No kingdoms deciding for them.

Personal.

Choice.

“Nymeris.”

“I know.”

“No decisions.”

“I know.”

“Absolutely.”

“Never.”

Good.

Now he was beginning to consider making one deliberately.

Not an heir.

Not a weapon.

Not a prophecy.

A child.

But not yet.

Not until the choice belonged completely to the people making it.

Chapter One Hundred Two

The Child They Chose

They spoke three nights later.

No council.

No ministers.

No crowns.

Just Zee and Nymeris inside a quiet room overlooking Darkheart.

For once, there was nobody left to interrupt them.

“I know.”

“You do not get to say that like it makes this smaller.”

“I know.”

Her voice sharpened.

“If anything happens to him because of what you have done…”

Water rose around her.

Dark.

Abyssal.

“There will not be enough of Darkheart left to remember your name.”

Zee accepted the threat.

Not because he feared Nymeris.

Because he understood exactly where it came from.

Mother.

He looked toward the windows.

Outside, Nhalaris remained mobilized.

Darkheart remained alert.

Rez had already received reports of sea movement.

Zareth knew what a full conflict would mean.

Ner knew too.

Nymeris knew most of all.

If she declared war now—

everyone would ask why.

Why would Nhalaris threaten Darkheart immediately after an impossible supernatural birth disturbance?

Why would two allied rulers suddenly become enemies?

What had happened between them?

What were they hiding?

Aidan himself prevented the war.

That realization made Nymeris angrier.

Zee saw it.

She hated being trapped by the protection she opposed.

But she did not give the order.

Not yet.

Sea gates remained ready.

Diplomacy fractured.

The threat stayed alive.

So did Aidan.

⸻

Only five people outside the minimum birth healers who had already been stripped from public record retained the full truth.

Zee.

Nymeris.

Ner.

Rez.

Zareth.

The circle closed.

Small.

Deliberate.

Dangerous to expand.

Rez stood near the door.

Face pale.

“You understand what you just did?”

“Yes.”

Zareth’s voice was quieter.

“The world cannot feel him.”

“Yes.”

Ner looked toward Aidan.

Bloodsong touched the infant gently.

Aidan’s heartbeat answered.

Still there.

Still himself.

Just hidden.

Nymeris sat with him in her arms.

Zee approached slowly.

She almost told him not to.

Then stopped.

Not forgiveness.

Aidan still had a father.

Even if she hated him right now.

She allowed Zee to take him.

Nothing more.

Zee held his son.

Aidan moved.

Then wrapped his hand around Zee’s finger again.

Same as before.

No understanding of kingdoms.

No understanding of war.

No understanding of Systems.

Seals.

Legacy.

Erasure.

Only warmth.

Heartbeat.

Father.

The System rested silently around three locked foundations.

The Legacy preserved what the world no longer knew.

Ocean, Abyss, and Siren blood remained inside him untouched.

The room was quiet.

For the first time since Aidan opened his eyes—

the world was not staring.

Zee looked down at him.

Fear returned.

Not of the child.

Never.

Of the future.

Of what Aidan would think when he learned.

Of whether the difference between Victor and Zee would matter to the son whose childhood had been rewritten before it began.

Zee touched his forehead to Aidan’s.

Then whispered:

“You can hate me when you are old enough to choose to.”

Nymeris closed her eyes.

Ner looked away.

Rez said nothing.

Even Zareth’s Link went quiet.

Zee held his son closer.

Alive.

Hidden.

Wanted.

Chosen.

Aidan Darkheart existed.

Son of Zee Darkheart.

Son of Nymeris Thalryn.

Prince by blood of Darkheart.

Prince by blood of Nhalaris.

Carrier of Witch.

Vampire.

Wolf.

Ocean.

Abyss.

Siren.

The world knew none of it now.

But his family did.

And someday—

Aidan would too.

For now, the world had forgotten him.

And Zee Darkheart had finally given his son the one thing nobody had ever given him at birth.

Time.

Chapter One Hundred Two

The Child They Chose

They spoke three nights later.

No council.

No ministers.

No crowns.

Just Zee and Nymeris inside a quiet room overlooking Darkheart.

Ner had gone to sleep hours earlier.

Zareth was in Drakonis.

Rez had returned to Vesper.

For once, there was nobody left to interrupt them.

Nymeris stood near the window.

Zee sat across from her.

Neither wasted time.

“I want a child,” Nymeris said.

Zee nodded.

“I know.”

“And not because Nhalaris needs an heir.”

“Good.”

She looked toward him.

“Do you?”

Zee did not pretend he misunderstood.

“Yes.”

The word felt stranger aloud.

Not frightening.

Real.

Nymeris sat across from him.

“I do not want to create someone already indebted to a throne.”

“Neither do I.”

“I do not want ministers choosing what my child means.”

“No.”

“I do not want Nhalaris deciding why he exists.”

“No.”

Zee leaned forward.

“And I do not want Darkheart doing it either.”

Nymeris held his gaze.

“A child first.”

“Heir second.”

“If he wants the throne.”

“If either throne is still relevant by then.”

Nymeris smiled faintly.

“That sounds like something only an immortal King would say.”

“Probably.”

Silence followed.

Not uncertainty.

Weight.

They both understood exactly what they were discussing.

Not politics.

Not obligation.

A person.

A life that did not exist yet.

Nymeris spoke first.

“If we do this, I want him because we chose him.”

“Yes.”

“Not because our bloodlines would be impressive together.”

“Yes.”

“Not because Darkheart and Nhalaris would gain something.”

“Yes.”

“Not because the world expects a continuation.”

Zee looked at her.

“I spent too much of my childhood being told what my existence meant.”

His voice hardened slightly.

“I will never do that to mine.”

Nymeris nodded.

“Then we agree.”

Zee stared at her for a long moment.

“Are we actually doing this?”

“Yes.”

He laughed once.

Not from humor.

Something close to disbelief.

Nymeris smiled.

“You look terrified.”

“I have fought Gods.”

“And?”

“This is worse.”

“Good.”

Zee frowned.

“Why good?”

“Because you understand it matters.”

That ended the last uncertainty.

They chose.

Not King and Queen.

Not Darkheart and Nhalaris.

Zee.

Nymeris.

Two people who wanted a child.

⸻

Zee told Ner before sunrise.

Ner stared at him for exactly three seconds.

Then:

“You and Nymeris.”

“Yes.

“Are having a child.”

“Yes.”

Ner sat back.

Zee narrowed his eyes.

“Say whatever terrible thing you are thinking.”

Ner smiled.

“I was wondering whether the world is prepared for your blood combined with hers.”

Zee stared.

“That was my first thought too.”

“Of course it was.”

Ner became quieter.

“You want this?”

“Yes.”

“Really?”

Zee did not hesitate.

“Yes.”

Ner nodded.

Then smiled differently.

Warm.

“You are going to be unbearable.”

“I already am.”

“You are going to inspect the child every four minutes.”

“No.”

“Every three?”

Zee threw something at him.

Ner caught it.

Then stood and crossed the room.

No jealousy.

No awkwardness.

No competition.

He wrapped his arms around Zee.

“You are going to be a father.”

Zee went still.

That sentence landed harder than expected.

Then he held Ner back.

“Yes.”

Ner whispered against his shoulder:

“That child is going to be loved stupidly.”

Zee smiled.

“Violently.”

“That too.”

⸻

There was nothing romantic in what followed.

Nothing disguised.

Nothing confused.

Zee remained gay.

Nymeris remained his chosen family.

Ner remained the person Zee returned to at night.

The decision to create a child did not alter any of that.

When conception finally happened, it was private.

Intentional.

Briefly handled.

And completely chosen.

No accident.

No prophecy.

No drunken mistake.

No cosmic intervention.

Zee Darkheart and Queen Nymeris Thalryn deliberately created a child together because they wanted him.

Everything after began there.

⸻

The first two months were ordinary.

Mostly.

Nymeris hated being watched.

Zee watched constantly.

“You are staring.”

“I am listening.”

“To what?”

“The heartbeat.”

Nymeris stopped.

Then looked at him.

“You can hear it already?”

“Yes.”

That softened something in her face.

For approximately three seconds.

Then:

“Stop hovering.”

“I am not hovering.”

“You have visited Nhalaris seven times this month.”

“That proves nothing.”

“You live on land.”

“Technicality.”

Nymeris sighed.

Ner, seated nearby, smiled into his drink.

⸻

By the fourth month, the water started moving around Nymeris without permission.

Not violently.

Responding.

A cup trembled when the child shifted.

A shallow basin formed ripples whenever Nymeris rested.

Ocean currents beneath Nhalaris began subtly bending toward the palace.

Nymeris noticed first.

She said nothing for two days.

Then summoned Zee.

He arrived with Ner and Zareth.

Nymeris stood beside an indoor pool.

The water was completely still.

“Watch.”

She placed one hand over her stomach.

The child moved.

The pool rippled.

Zee’s expression sharpened.

Again.

The water moved before Nymeris did anything.

Ner stepped closer.

His Bloodsong hummed.

Then stopped.

He frowned.

“What?”

Zee asked.

Ner listened harder.

“There are two resonances.”

Nymeris looked toward him.

“Two heartbeats?”

“No.”

Ner shook his head.

“One heartbeat.”

Then quieter:

“More than one answer inside it.”

Zee’s face changed.

Zareth moved closer.

Dragon senses focusing.

He stared at Nymeris’s stomach.

Then at Zee.

That is not normal.

Zee answered through the Link.

I know.

Nymeris looked between them.

“You are doing the private conversation.”

“Yes.”

“What did he say?”

Zareth answered aloud.

“Your child feels wrong.”

Nymeris’s eyes narrowed.

Zareth corrected.

“Powerful.”

Zee looked at him.

“Better.”

⸻

By the sixth month, Zee could distinguish patterns.

Not awakened powers.

Foundations.

Something Witch-like responded whenever spellwork happened nearby.

Something predatory answered blood.

Something lupine reacted to the moon and movement.

None fully surfaced.

None behaved like Zee had at birth.

That mattered.

Zee had been born awake.

Everything alive at once.

This child was different.

Compressed.

Deep.

Waiting.

Then there was Nymeris.

Ocean.

Abyss.

Siren resonance.

Not part of the other three.

Separate.

Hereditary.

The unborn child carried that too.

Zee did not name what he was feeling yet.

He did not want to.

Ner did.

One night in Darkheart, he pressed Gold lightly against Nymeris’s wrist.

His expression changed.

“There is something in him that answers me.”

Nymeris looked down.

“Siren?”

“Partly.”

“Bloodsong?”

“No.”

Immediate.

Clear.

Ner shook his head.

“Nothing like mine.”

Good.

Different.

His expression remained uneasy.

“But deep.”

Zee looked toward him.

“How deep?”

Ner met his eyes.

“Enough that I do not think birth is going to be quiet.”

That sentence remained.

⸻

By the seventh month, Zareth stopped joking.

Mostly.

He stood beside Zee on the Nhalaris balcony while deep water rolled against the pressure dome.

“You are terrified.”

Zee looked at him.

“No.”

Through the Link came:

Lie.

Zee sighed.

“I am concerned.”

Zareth smiled.

“That is what Kings call fear.”

Zee looked toward Nymeris in the room behind them.

“She is strong.”

“Yes.”

“The child is stable.”

“Yes.”

“I have checked.”

“Constantly.”

Zee ignored that.

Zareth became serious.

“What are you afraid of?”

Zee listened to the heartbeat.

Steady.

Too steady.

Not Human.

Not ordinary supernatural.

Layered.

“I do not know yet.”

That was worse.

⸻

They chose the name in the eighth month.

No ceremony.

No council.

Nymeris was lying in bed, irritated because Zee had convinced three healers to examine her in one day.

“This is excessive.”

“You said the same thing yesterday.”

“It was true yesterday too.”

Zee sat beside her.

“What about Aidan?”

Nymeris stopped.

Looked at him.

“Aidan.”

“Yes.”

She repeated it softly.

Then smiled.

“Aidan Darkheart.”

Zee looked toward her.

“Thalryn too.”

“By blood.”

“Yes.”

“Prince of Nhalaris.”

“If he wants it.”

“Prince of Darkheart.”

“If he wants that too.”

Nymeris laughed.

“Everything with you becomes conditional on choice.”

“Yes.”

She placed one hand over her stomach.

“Aidan.”

The child moved.

Zee heard the heartbeat accelerate.

Then settle.

He smiled.

There.

Their son had a name.

Not prophecy.

Not destiny.

Aidan.

Chosen because they chose it.

⸻

Labor began during a stormless night.

That was the first wrong thing.

The ocean moved anyway.

Every current around Nhalaris reversed.

Not violently.

All at once.

Nymeris doubled over.

The palace pressure wards activated without command.

Deep bells rang through the city.

Zee stood so quickly his chair shattered behind him.

“What happened?”

Nymeris grabbed the edge of the table.

“He is coming.”

Ner entered seconds later.

His face pale.

“I heard it.”

Zee looked toward him.

“What?”

Ner’s Bloodsong trembled.

“The heartbeat.”

Zee already heard it.

But now—

another rhythm beneath it.

Then another.

Not separate hearts.

Separate structures.

Witch pressure surged through the room.

Every spell ward in Nhalaris lit at once.

Far above the ocean, Darkheart Witches turned toward the same direction without knowing why.

Vampires across distant roads stopped feeding.

For one second, all of them heard an impossible heartbeat beneath their own.

Wolves across three kingdoms went silent.

No howling.

No frenzy.

Silence.

The entire ocean around Nhalaris drew inward.

Nymeris screamed.

Abyssal resonance rolled through the palace.

Zee stood beside her.

And remembered blood raining from the sky.

Witches losing power.

Wolves losing themselves.

Vampires hearing something impossible.

His own birth.

His own beginning.

His own world deciding he was wrong before he could speak.

Zee went cold.

“No.”

Nymeris looked at him through pain.

“What?”

The heartbeat struck again.

Crimson pressure rolled through the room.

Not awakened.

Compressed.

Immense.

Worse because it was waiting.

Zee stared at Nymeris.

At their unborn son.

At the entire supernatural world already beginning to respond.

And understood.

“This is happening again.”

The ocean shook.

Aidan Darkheart was coming.

⸻

Chapter One Hundred Three

The Child the World Forgot

Aidan Darkheart was born before dawn.

The moment he opened his eyes, the ocean stopped moving.

Every current around Nhalaris froze.

Not slowed.

Stopped.

For three heartbeats.

Then the Abyss answered.

A pressure wave traveled outward from the underwater kingdom.

Darkheart wards activated hundreds of miles away.

Witches felt Crimson power move beneath their magic.

Vampires heard a second heartbeat where none should exist.

Wolves went silent.

Beneath the ocean, Siren voices vanished for five full seconds.

And far beyond the kingdoms of men, something divine turned its attention toward the world.

Somewhere else—

a bearer of Dark Divinity opened his eyes.

⸻

Zee heard none of that first.

He heard Aidan cry.

Small.

Angry.

Alive.

Nymeris held him against her chest.

Exhausted.

Sweating.

Furious at everyone who came too close.

Queen disappeared.

Mother remained.

Aidan’s skin was warm.

His heartbeat was impossible.

One rhythm.

Four inheritances.

Three great supernatural foundations compressed beneath infancy.

Witch.

Vampire.

Wolf.

Complete.

Not awakened.

Not like Zee.

Zee had entered the world as all three.

Fully active.

Aidan had entered carrying all three like sealed storms beneath his blood.

And beyond them—

Nymeris.

Ocean.

Abyss.

Siren.

Separate.

Hereditary.

Not another Authority.

Something older in another direction.

Zee approached slowly.

Nymeris looked at him.

“Take him.”

Zee froze.

For a man who had fought Gods, the child terrified him more than anything ever had.

Not because of what Aidan might do.

Because of what the world would do to him.

Nymeris held him out.

Zee took his son.

Aidan immediately grabbed one of Zee’s fingers.

Tiny hand.

Impossible strength hidden beneath it.

Zee stopped breathing.

Ner stood several feet away.

He had never seen Zee look like that.

No King.

No Blood Hunter.

No Crimson Demonic Dragon.

Just father.

Aidan opened his eyes.

Dark.

For now.

Zee listened to the heartbeat.

Then whispered:

“Hello.”

Aidan tightened his grip.

Zee smiled.

Then his Vampire senses reached deeper.

And the smile disappeared.

⸻

Three foundations.

All complete.

Witch.

Vampire.

Wolf.

Not awake.

Waiting.

And too deep.

Far too deep.

Zee had never felt anything like it.

His own birth had been explosive because everything came alive at once.

Aidan’s was worse in another way.

Everything was already there.

Finished beneath the surface.

Like doors waiting for the child to become strong enough to open them.

Zee’s Crimson blood recognized the structures instantly.

His son carried the same roots.

But denser.

Broader.

Changed by Nymeris’s royal blood.

The total potential made something cold move through Zee.

Aidan could surpass him.

The thought produced no jealousy.

No anger.

Only fear.

For Aidan.

Zee looked toward the ceiling.

He could feel attention gathering.

Magic searching.

Divine awareness probing.

Bloodline sensing beginning across distances.

The birth had announced something.

Not a name.

Not yet.

But enough.

Nymeris saw Zee’s expression.

“What?”

Zee looked at Aidan.

Then at her.

“We have to hide him.”

Nymeris’s face became still.

“No.”

Immediate.

Zee expected it.

“The world felt him.”

“No.”

“Nymeris—”

“No.”

Aidan began crying again.

Nymeris took him back.

Her voice remained low.

“He was born minutes ago.”

“That is exactly the problem.”

“He has a name.”

“I know.”

“He has a kingdom.”

“I know.”

“Two.”

“I know.”

“He is my son.”

Zee’s eyes hardened.

“And mine.”

“Then do not speak about erasing him.”

“I said hide.”

Nymeris stared.

“What do you think hiding means when the world has already begun looking?”

Silence.

Zee knew.

She knew he knew.

He answered anyway.

“Records.”

Her expression changed.

“Zee.”

“Bloodline tracking.”

“No.”

“Divine observation.”

“No.”

“Birth declarations.”

“Stop.”

“Royal recognition.”

“STOP.”

Water exploded across the chamber.

The walls shook.

Aidan cried harder.

Nymeris instantly pulled the pressure back.

Mother first.

Even furious.

Zee stepped closer.

“The world knows something was born.”

“Then let them know.”

“They will come.”

“Let them.”

“You do not understand.”

Nymeris’s eyes turned cold.

“Do not say that to me.”

“I lived it.”

“And I have ruled Nhalaris through wars you have never seen.”

“This is different.”

“Because it happened to you?”

“Because I know the sequence.”

Zee’s voice sharpened.

“Birth.”

“Fear.”

“Classification.”

“Hunting.”

“People deciding what the child means before the child can speak.”

Nymeris stood despite the healers trying to stop her.

Aidan against her chest.

“I will defend him.”

“The ocean.”

“Yes.”

“Godslayers?”

“Yes.”

“Yes.”

“They failed to kill me because I cannot die.”

Nymeris went silent.

Zee stepped closer.

“He can.”

That landed.

For the first time, fear entered her expression.

Not surrender.

Fear.

Zee continued.

“I was killed before I understood what death was.”

Nymeris stared at him.

“My father did it.”

“I know.”

“I spent childhood being hunted because adults were afraid of what I might become.”

“I know.”

“I will not give him that childhood.”

Nymeris’s jaw tightened.

“You told me you wanted your child to choose who he becomes.”

“Yes.”

“Then let him.”

“He has to survive long enough to choose.”

There.

The center.

Neither moved.

Aidan cried between them.
